answer:
Je suppose que vous parlez du départ d'Israël du Sinaï, dans *Nombres* 10:33 : « Ils partirent de la montagne de l'Éternel pour trois jours de marche ». Sefaria ne répondait pas à l'instant (erreur 429), donc je n'ai pas pu relire les textes. Je résume de mémoire, sans citations littérales. Si vous pensiez à un autre épisode, dites-le-moi.

## Réponse directe
Selon une tradition rabbinique, Israël a quitté le Sinaï « comme un enfant qui s'enfuit de l'école ». Le peuple était pressé de partir, de peur de recevoir encore des commandements et de ne plus pouvoir les tenir. Cette lecture est un enseignement de Chazal, pas le sens simple du verset. Le sens simple est plus sobre : le peuple se met en route vers la Terre promise sur l'ordre de Dieu.

## Points clés
- Le sens simple est un départ ordonné, au signal de la nuée, vers Canaan.
- Un enseignement des Sages y voit une hâte fautive, celle d'un enfant qui fuit l'école.
- Selon cet enseignement, cette hâte aurait provoqué les plaintes qui suivent (Taveéra, les cailles, Kivrot HaTaava).
- Le Ramban le rattache aussi au thème de l'Arche et de ses deux versets, que la Torah encadre de signes particuliers.
- La leçon morale : le départ du lieu d'étude doit se faire avec regret, pas avec soulagement.

## Les sources
**1. Le sens simple (*pshat*).** Le verset dit qu'on part « de la montagne de l'Éternel » avec l'Arche, qui « allait devant eux » pour chercher un lieu de repos. Le départ fait suite au recensement et à l'organisation des camps. Il se fait donc sur ordre divin, après presque un an au Sinaï.

**2. L'enseignement des Sages.** Les *Tossafot* (sur *Chabbat* 116a) rapportent, au nom du *Midrach*, l'image de l'enfant qui s'enfuit de l'école. Le même motif apparaît dans le *Sifrei* sur ce passage, et le Ramban en fait écho dans son commentaire. Il ne s'agit donc pas de la lecture littérale du verset.

**3. Le lien avec la suite.** Le texte enchaîne : « Le peuple fut comme des gens qui se plaignent » (*Nombres* 11:1), puis la convoitise des cailles. Cet enchaînement a nourri l'idée que le départ précipité était déjà le symptôme d'un manque de désir de rester près de la Torah. Cette liaison est un commentaire de lecture, pas une affirmation explicite du texte.

**4. Les deux versets mis entre signes.** Les versets « Quand l'Arche partait… » (10:35-36) sont encadrés de signes particuliers dans le rouleau. Les Sages y voient un livre à part (*Chabbat* 115b-116a). Ce lien entre le départ du Sinaï et cette séparation est classique, mais je ne peux pas vous donner ici les références précises.

## Quelle leçon ?
Le départ du Sinaï est pour les commentateurs un moment charnière. On passe de la réception de la Torah à sa mise en pratique dans la vie. Ils y voient un reproche, mais aussi un avertissement : il faut sortir du lieu d'étude avec le désir d'y revenir.

Je peux reprendre cela avec les textes exacts (Rashi, Ramban, Tossafot) dès que Sefaria répond. Dites-moi si vous voulez que je le fasse.

Sua lógica tem um ponto válido, mas não prova o que você conclui. A Torah proíbe a consulta aos mortos [Deuteronômio 18:10-12], e é verdade que essa era uma prática dos povos de Canaã. Só que a proibição não prova que o contato funciona. A Torah também proíbe adorar ídolos, e os sábios ensinam que ídolos não têm poder real.

**Key Takeaways**
- Uma proibição mostra que a prática existia, e não que ela funciona.
- A tradição judaica tem posições diferentes sobre se há algum efeito real.
- Em todas as posições, a proibição continua valendo.

**O texto**
O versículo diz: "וְשֹׁאֵל אוֹב וְיִדְּעֹנִי וְדֹרֵשׁ אֶל־הַמֵּתִים" ("quem consulta espíritos, adivinhos ou *inquire dos mortos*"). Ele acrescenta que são práticas "abomináveis" dos povos que estavam sendo expulsos da terra. Por isso sua ideia de que o motivo era tornar Israel diferente tem base no texto.

**As duas visões principais**
- **Rambam (visão racionalista):** ele diz que tudo isso é "דִּבְרֵי שֶׁקֶר וְכָזָב" (palavras de falsidade e engano), com as quais os idólatras antigos enganaram os povos. Segundo ele, a Torah proíbe justamente porque é vaidade e leva as pessoas para longe da verdade [Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 11:16]. Ele cita "תָּמִים תִּהְיֶה עִם ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ" (Deuteronômio 18:13).
- **Talmud (visão que admite algum fenômeno):** o Talmud descreve o *ba'al ov* (necromante) como alguém que faz uma voz sair de entre suas articulações, ou que consulta um crânio [Sanhedrin 65b]. Aí há uma discussão sobre truques e sobre o que de fato ocorre. O texto também menciona a mulher de Endor e o rei Saul [1 Samuel 28]. Esse episódio é debatido por comentaristas: alguns entendem que houve uma aparição real, outros que foi algo diferente.

**Conclusão prática**
Mesmo quem admite que algo possa acontecer vê isso como impureza espiritual, e não como um caminho legítimo. Rabi Akiva chora ao ler o versículo sobre quem se isola entre os túmulos para atrair um espírito de impureza [Sanhedrin 65b]. O caminho permitido é rezar a D'us, e não consultar os mortos. Para a prática pessoal, consulte um rabino.

answer:
Die Zehn Gebote (hebr. *Aseret ha-Dibrot*, „die zehn Aussprüche“) stehen zweimal in der Tora: in [Exodus 20:2-14] (Parascha *Jitro*) und in [Deuteronomium 5:6-18] (Parascha *Wa'etchanan*). Eine Seitenzahl kann ich nicht nennen, weil sie in jeder Ausgabe anders ist. Kapitel und Vers gelten dagegen überall.

## Key Takeaways
- Die erste Fassung steht in [Exodus 20:2-14], im 2. Buch Mose, Parascha *Jitro*.
- Die zweite Fassung steht in [Deuteronomium 5:6-18], im 5. Buch Mose, Parascha *Wa'etchanan*.
- In christlichen Bibeln zählt man Exodus 20:1-17, in jüdischen Ausgaben 20:2-14. Das liegt an einer anderen Verszählung.
- Die beiden Fassungen unterscheiden sich in einigen Formulierungen, zum Beispiel beim Schabbat-Gebot.

## Die Fundstellen im Einzelnen

**1. Exodus (*Schemot*) 20:2-14**
Hier schildert die Tora die Offenbarung am Berg Sinai. Vers 1 leitet ein: „Und Gott sprach alle diese Worte“. Danach beginnt der Text mit „Ich bin der Ewige, dein Gott …“ (Vers 2). Die Vorbereitung auf die Offenbarung steht in Kapitel 19. Am Schabbat lesen wir diesen Abschnitt in der Parascha *Jitro*.

**2. Deuteronomium (*Dewarim*) 5:6-18**
Mose wiederholt die Gebote vor dem Volk kurz vor dessen Einzug ins Land. Diese Fassung liest man in der Parascha *Wa'etchanan*. Beim Schabbat-Gebot heißt es dort „Bewahre (*schamor*) den Schabbat“, in Exodus dagegen „Gedenke (*sachor*) des Schabbattages“. Der Talmud bringt das mit dem Gedanken in Verbindung, dass beide Wörter „in einem Ausspruch“ gesagt wurden (siehe [Schevuot 20b]).

## Hinweis zur Zählung
Die jüdische Zählung beginnt mit „Ich bin der Ewige, dein Gott“ als erstem Wort. Christliche Ausgaben zählen Exodus 20:1-17, weil sie die Verse anders aufteilen. Wenn du in einer deutschen Bibel nachschlägst, achte darauf, ob es eine jüdische Übersetzung ist. Sie hat die Verszählung der hebräischen Ausgabe.

Wenn du möchtest, lese ich mit dir den Text oder die Kommentare dazu, zum Beispiel Raschi oder Ramban.

# Salmo 137 (Tehilim 137)

Este salmo es el lamento de los exiliados en Babilonia. Expresa el dolor por Sión y el juramento de no olvidar Jerusalén, y termina con un clamor de justicia contra Edom y Babilonia. La traducción al español es mía, hecha a partir del texto hebreo en Sefaria.

## Puntos clave
- Los exiliados lloran junto a los ríos de Babilonia y se niegan a cantar los cantos de Sión para entretener a sus captores.
- El juramento "Si te olvidare, Jerusalén" es uno de los textos más conocidos sobre la memoria de Sión.
- Los versículos 7-9 piden que Dios haga justicia a Edom y a Babilonia.
- Los comentaristas leen el último versículo de maneras distintas. Es un clamor del dolor de las víctimas, no una norma de conducta.

## Texto y traducción

**1** עַל־נַהֲרוֹת בָּבֶל שָׁם יָשַׁבְנוּ גַּם־בָּכִינוּ בְּזָכְרֵנוּ אֶת־צִיּוֹן
Junto a los ríos de Babilonia, allí nos sentamos y también lloramos, al acordarnos de Sión.

**2** עַל־עֲרָבִים בְּתוֹכָהּ תָּלִינוּ כִּנֹּרוֹתֵינוּ
En los sauces (o álamos) de su orilla colgamos nuestras arpas.

**3** כִּי שָׁם שְׁאֵלוּנוּ שׁוֹבֵינוּ דִּבְרֵי־שִׁיר וְתוֹלָלֵינוּ שִׂמְחָה שִׁירוּ לָנוּ מִשִּׁיר צִיּוֹן
Porque allí nos pedían canciones los que nos llevaron cautivos, y los que nos atormentaban, alegría: «Cantadnos algún cántico de Sión».

**4** אֵיךְ נָשִׁיר אֶת־שִׁיר־יְהוָה עַל אַדְמַת נֵכָר
¿Cómo cantaremos el cántico del Eterno en tierra extraña?

**5** אִם־אֶשְׁכָּחֵךְ יְרוּשָׁלִַם תִּשְׁכַּח יְמִינִי
Si me olvidare de ti, Jerusalén, que se olvide mi diestra [o: que se seque mi diestra].

**6** תִּדְבַּק־לְשׁוֹנִי לְחִכִּי אִם־לֹא אֶזְכְּרֵכִי אִם־לֹא אַעֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַם עַל רֹאשׁ שִׂמְחָתִי
Que mi lengua se pegue a mi paladar si no me acuerdo de ti, si no elevo a Jerusalén por encima de mi mayor alegría.

**7** זְכֹר יְהוָה לִבְנֵי אֱדוֹם אֵת יוֹם יְרוּשָׁלִָם הָאֹמְרִים עָרוּ עָרוּ עַד הַיְסוֹד בָּהּ
Acuérdate, Eterno, de los hijos de Edom en el día de Jerusalén, cuando decían: «¡Arrasad, arrasad hasta sus cimientos!».

**8** בַּת־בָּבֶל הַשְּׁדוּדָה אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁיְשַׁלֶּם־לָךְ אֶת־גְּמוּלֵךְ שֶׁגָּמַלְתְּ לָנוּ
Hija de Babilonia, la destructora: dichoso quien te pague la retribución con que nos trataste.

**9** אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁיֹּאחֵז וְנִפֵּץ אֶת־עֹלָלַיִךְ אֶל־הַסָּלַע
Dichoso quien tome a tus pequeños y los estrelle contra la roca.

## Comentario breve
- **Pshat (sentido simple):** el salmista habla desde el exilio posterior a la destrucción del Primer Templo. Los captores piden cantos como diversión, y los exiliados responden que cantar para ellos profanaría el canto sagrado.
- **Los versículos 5-6** son un juramento. La mano y la lengua son los instrumentos de la música y del canto. Quien olvida a Jerusalén pierde su capacidad de tocar y de cantar.
- **Edom** aparece aquí como quien se alegró en la caída de Jerusalén. La tradición lo asocia con Esaú. Esa lectura es de la tradición, no del texto del salmo.
- **El versículo 9** es duro. Se lee como la expresión del dolor de quienes lo sufrieron todo, no como un mandato. Es un grito pidiendo que el castigo sea medida por medida, y no una norma de conducta. No he consultado aquí a los comentaristas, así que no atribuyo esta lectura a ninguno en concreto.
- **Uso litúrgico:** este salmo se canta antes del Birkat HaMazon (la bendición después de la comida) los días de semana, como signo de duelo por Sión. En Shabat y en las fiestas se dice en su lugar el Salmo 126, «Shir HaMaalot».

Si quieres, puedo añadir lo que dicen Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre algún versículo.

# Análise do Salmo 51 (*Miznor le-David*, o salmo de arrependimento de David)

O Salmo 51 é a grande oração de *teshuvá* (arrependimento) da Bíblia. O título o liga ao momento em que o profeta Natan confrontou David depois do episódio com Bat-Sheva. O salmo avança em quatro etapas: confissão, pedido de purificação interior, compromisso de ensinar os outros e, por fim, uma visão do culto restaurado. Cito abaixo o texto do salmo e, de 2 Samuel 12:13 e do Radak, apenas o que consegui consultar. Não consegui abrir os comentários de Rashi e outros, então os resumo de memória, sem citar números de versículo.

## Resumo
- O título histórico [Psalms 51:2] liga o salmo ao confronto com Natan.
- O salmo é uma teshuvá completa: reconhecimento, confissão, pedido de transformação interior, resolução de ensinar e entrega de um coração quebrantado.
- O pedido central não é só perdão, mas um coração novo: "Lev tahor bará li Elohim" [Psalms 51:12].
- "O sacrifício de Deus é um espírito quebrantado" [Psalms 51:19] não rejeita o culto. Põe a contrição como condição do culto.
- Segundo o Radak, os dois últimos versículos são uma profecia sobre a destruição do Templo e sua restauração futura.

## Contexto (pshat)
O título diz: "Quando Natan, o profeta, veio a ele, depois que ele tinha ido a Bat-Sheva". A narrativa está em 2 Samuel 11–12. Ali David reage à repreensão com uma frase curta: "Pequei contra o Eterno" ("*Chatati la-Adonai*"). Natan responde: "Também o Eterno fez passar o teu pecado; não morrerás" [II Samuel 12:13]. O Salmo 51 desenvolve, em forma de oração, o que essa frase breve continha.

## Estrutura e análise por seções

### 1. Pedido de misericórdia e confissão (vv. 3–6)
"Tem misericórdia de mim, ó Deus, segundo a Tua bondade; segundo a abundância das Tuas compaixões, apaga as minhas transgressões." David não apela a méritos. Apela à *chesed* (bondade) e aos *rachamim* (compaixões) de Deus. Os verbos se acumulam: apagar (*mecheh*), lavar (*kabbesêni*), purificar (*taharêni*). Os três vêm do vocabulário da pureza e do ritual.

O verso 5 diz: "Pois conheço as minhas transgressões, e o meu pecado está sempre diante de mim". É o início da *teshuvá*. O pecado deixa de ser algo que se esquece e passa a ser algo que se encara.

O verso 6 diz: "Contra Ti, só contra Ti, pequei... para que sejas justo na Tua palavra e puro no Teu julgamento". Aqui há uma dificuldade conhecida: David pecou também contra Uriá e contra Bat-Sheva. A leitura mais comum é que todo pecado é, em última instância, uma ofensa à vontade de Deus. Outra leitura é que David aceita o julgamento divino sem se justificar, para que a justiça de Deus fique evidente.

### 2. "Em iniquidade fui formado" (v. 7)
"Eis que em iniquidade fui gerado, e em pecado minha mãe me concebeu." Não se deve ler isso como "pecado original" no sentido cristão. O judaísmo ensina que a alma é pura ao nascer. A leitura tradicional é que o ser humano é criado com a inclinação para o mal (*yetzer hará*) e com fragilidade, e que isso não o isenta de responsabilidade. David usa a imagem como confissão de fraqueza, não como desculpa. Esta é a minha explicação, não uma citação de comentarista.

### 3. Verdade interior (vv. 8–11)
"Eis que desejas a verdade no íntimo, e no oculto me farás conhecer sabedoria." Deus exige verdade interior, não só ações externas. Em seguida vem a imagem da purificação: "Purifica-me com hissopo e ficarei puro; lava-me e ficarei mais branco que a neve" [Psalms 51:9]. O hissopo (*ezov*) era usado na purificação de quem tocou em um morto (cf. Números 19). Isso sugere que David se vê como alguém que precisa dessa purificação.

Os versos seguintes pedem alegria: "Faze-me ouvir júbilo e alegria; que exultem os ossos que quebraste" [Psalms 51:10]. Os "ossos quebrados" mostram que o arrependimento é doloroso, e que a alegria só vem depois da dor.

### 4. O núcleo: um coração novo (vv. 12–14)
"Lev tahor bará li Elohim, ve-ruach nachon chadesh be-kirbi" (**"Cria em mim, ó Deus, um coração puro, e renova dentro de mim um espírito firme"**) [Psalms 51:12]. O verbo *bará* é o mesmo da criação do mundo. David pede uma obra nova de Deus, não só um conserto. O que ele pede é uma mudança de natureza, não só o apagamento do passado.

O verso 13 diz: "Não me lances fora da Tua presença, e o Teu espírito santo não tires de mim". Para David, a maior ameaça do pecado é perder a proximidade com Deus e a inspiração profética. Isso aparece também na frase seguinte: "Devolve-me a alegria da Tua salvação, e um espírito generoso me sustente" [Psalms 51:14].

### 5. Ensinar os que erram (vv. 15–16)
"Ensinarei aos transgressores os Teus caminhos, e os pecadores a Ti retornarão." Quem fez teshuvá se torna capaz de ensinar teshuvá. O versículo seguinte pede livramento de *damim* ("sangues"), uma referência ao sangue de Uriá, e promete que a língua cantará a justiça de Deus.

O verso 17 diz: "Senhor, abre os meus lábios, e a minha boca proclamará o Teu louvor". Essas palavras foram incorporadas à liturgia: abrem a *Amidá* de todas as orações.

### 6. Sacrifício e coração quebrantado (vv. 18–19)
"Pois não desejas sacrifício, e eu o daria; não te agradas de holocausto. Os sacrifícios de Deus são um espírito quebrantado; um coração quebrantado e contrito, ó Deus, não desprezarás." Não é uma rejeição do culto do Templo. O salmo diz que o sacrifício sem contrição não tem valor, e que, para quem pecou, a contrição é o oferecimento principal. Além disso, o sacrifício expiatório previsto na Torá cobre pecados não intencionais, e o pecado de David era grave demais para esse tipo de expiação. Essa é uma explicação geral que ouvi ser dada, e que não verifiquei em fonte específica.

### 7. Restauração de Sião (vv. 20–21)
"Faze bem a Sião segundo a Tua vontade; edifica os muros de Jerusalém. Então te agradarás de sacrifícios de justiça, de holocausto e oferta inteira." Há quem ache estranho que um salmo pessoal termine com uma oração nacional. O Radak explica que esses dois versículos são profecia de David:

> "בשני הפסוקים האלה נראה שבעודו אומר השיבה לי ששון ישעך כן היה לו ששבה לו [רוח הקודש]... שעתיד בית המקדש להחרב ראשון ושני על העונות... ובימות משיחנו יהיו קרבנותיו רצוים"

Minha tradução: "Nestes dois versículos parece que, enquanto ele dizia 'devolve-me a alegria da Tua salvação', o espírito santo realmente voltou a ele. São profecia de que o Templo seria destruído, o primeiro e o segundo, por causa dos pecados... e nos dias do Messias os sacrifícios serão aceitos, pois todo Israel servirá ao Eterno de um só coração" [Radak on Psalms 51:20]. Assim, o salmo mostra que a oração de David foi respondida: o espírito profético voltou.

## Uso na liturgia
- O verso 17 abre a Amidá.
- O verso 12 aparece em orações de arrependimento, como as dos Dias Temíveis.
- O tema do salmo une-se a *Yom Kipur* e a *Selichot*.

## Lições
1. A teshuvá começa com o reconhecimento de que o pecado está "diante de mim".
2. Quem se arrepende pede transformação, não apenas perdão.
3. A proximidade com Deus é o bem que o pecado ameaça.
4. O arrependimento verdadeiro se torna ensino e serviço aos outros.

Se quiser, posso aprofundar um verso específico, comparar o salmo com a narrativa de 2 Samuel 11–12 ou ver o que a tradição talmúdica diz sobre David e Bat-Sheva.

answer:
**Antwort:** In der Tora steht zuerst nur *Elohim* (Gott), nämlich in [Genesis 1:1] („Bereschit bara Elohim …"). Der Name JHWH folgt direkt danach, und zwar zusammen mit Elohim als „JHWH Elohim", zum ersten Mal in [Genesis 2:4]. Eine Seitenzahl kann ich nicht nennen, weil sie von der Ausgabe abhängt. Kapitel und Vers sind überall gleich, in Genesis 2:4 also Kapitel 2, Vers 4. Das ist im ersten Buch Mose, in der Parascha *Bereschit*.

## Wichtigste Punkte
- Genesis 1:1 bis 2:3 (die sechs Schöpfungstage und der Schabbat) benutzen ausschließlich *Elohim*.
- Genesis 2:4 ist die erste Stelle mit dem Vierbuchstabennamen, und zwar direkt in der Verbindung „JHWH Elohim".
- Die Seitenzahl unterscheidet sich je nach Ausgabe, deshalb ist die Angabe von Kapitel und Vers verlässlicher.
- Die Kommentatoren deuten die beiden Namen unterschiedlich, meist als zwei Eigenschaften Gottes.

## Die Stelle
[Genesis 2:4]:
„אֵלֶּה תוֹלְדוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ בְּהִבָּרְאָם בְּיוֹם עֲשׂוֹת **יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים** אֶרֶץ וְשָׁמָיִם"
Übersetzung: „Dies ist die Geschichte von Himmel und Erde, als sie erschaffen wurden, am Tag, da JHWH Gott Erde und Himmel machte."

In den Ausgaben wird der Name oft „Hascham" oder „Adonai" gelesen und nicht ausgesprochen. In Übersetzungen steht er meist als „der Ewige" oder „HERR". Nach Genesis 2:4 kommt „JHWH Elohim" in den folgenden Kapiteln der Schöpfungs- und Gartenerzählung oft vor, bis Genesis 3. Danach steht in der Tora meist JHWH allein.

## Warum zwei Namen?
Ich gebe hier die klassische Deutung wieder, ohne die Kommentare dazu im Einzelnen abgerufen zu haben. Der Midrasch (Bereschit Rabba) und Raschi zu [Genesis 1:1] erklären, dass *Elohim* für die Eigenschaft des Rechts (*Midat ha-Din*) steht und JHWH für die Eigenschaft der Barmherzigkeit (*Midat ha-Rachamim*). Gott wollte die Welt zuerst mit strengem Recht erschaffen. Er sah, dass sie so nicht bestehen kann, und stellte die Barmherzigkeit dazu. Deshalb stehen beide Namen zusammen. Der Kli Yakar zu [Genesis 2:4] greift diesen Gedanken auf, um zu erklären, warum bei „Himmel und Erde" die Reihenfolge wechselt. Die Verbindung beider Namen steht nach dieser Lesart für die Welt, in der Recht und Barmherzigkeit zusammenwirken.

Die moderne Bibelwissenschaft führt den Wechsel der Gottesnamen dagegen auf verschiedene Quellenschichten zurück. Das ist eine andere Sichtweise als die der traditionellen Kommentatoren. Shadal (Samuel David Luzzatto) erklärt in seinem Kommentar zu Genesis 2:4, *Elohim* sei eine allgemeine Bezeichnung für „den Herrn aller Kräfte", während der Vierbuchstabenname der besondere Eigenname des einen Gottes sei, den Israel verehrt.

Falls du etwas anderes meinst, etwa die erste Stelle, an der JHWH allein steht, oder eine Stelle in einer bestimmten Ausgabe, schreib mir bitte, welche Ausgabe du benutzt, dann kann ich genauer helfen.

answer:
**Short answer:** You're right that the text keeps God's "hand" and Satan's "hand" distinct, and that the distance matters. But the text doesn't say what your wording suggests. Satan asks God to touch Job, and God answers by putting Job's property "in your hand," meaning Satan's. Job's body is then also handed over, in a second round. The text does not say that God stays uninvolved or that there is no direct link between God and Job's suffering.

## Key Takeaways
- In [Job 1:11] Satan asks God to "lay Your hand" on Job's possessions, and God's reply moves the "hand" to Satan.
- The first limit is that Satan may not touch Job himself. The second round (Job 2) extends this to Job's body but not his life.
- This is a delegation with limits, not a removal of God from the picture. Satan acts only by permission.
- Job and the narrator still treat God as the ultimate source, so the "indirect" reading is only partly right.
- Many commentators read the limits as showing that Satan is a subordinate who is not free to act on his own.

## What the text says

**Round one.** Satan says:

> "וְאוּלָם שְֽׁלַֽח־נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ וְגַ֖ע בְּכׇל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֑וֹ אִם־לֹ֥א עַל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרְכֶֽךָּ"
> "But lay Your hand upon all that he has and he will surely blaspheme You to Your face." [Job 1:11]

God replies:

> "הִנֵּה כׇל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ בְּיָדֶךָ רַק אֵלָיו אַל־תִּשְׁלַח יָדֶךָ"
> "See, all that he has is in your power; only do not lay a hand on him." [Job 1:12]

Two points follow from this:
1. Satan challenges God to act ("Your hand"), and God does not simply do it. He hands the affliction to Satan ("in your hand").
2. God sets a boundary: Job's possessions and children, but not Job's person. This is not a "curse" in the sense of an imprecation. Satan's wager is that Job will "curse" (the euphemistic *yevarekhekha*, literally "bless") God. The affliction is the means of the test.

**Round two.** My attempt to retrieve [Job 2:3-6] failed, so I'm giving it from memory and paraphrasing. Satan asks that God's hand now touch Job's "bone and flesh." God answers that Job is "in your hand" but that Satan must spare his life (*nefesh*). The pattern repeats: the harm moves from property to body, and the final limit is death. So the limit is not "no touch at all." It is a staged series of permissions, each with a ceiling.

## Is the relationship really "indirect"?

Your reading holds up in part:
- God never appears as the direct agent of the first disasters. They arrive through Satan and through natural and human causes, such as the Sabeans, fire, wind, and the Chaldeans in Job 1.
- God's statement is a *permission* and not a command, which keeps a layer of separation.

But the text itself pushes against a full separation:
- **God claims some responsibility.** In Job 2:3 (again from memory, so check the text), God tells Satan that he "incited" God against Job "without cause." That makes God a party to the affliction.
- **Job understands it as from God.** He says "the Lord gave and the Lord has taken" ([Job 1:21]), and later he complains that "the hand of God has struck me" (Job 19:21, from memory, so verify the exact wording). The book never corrects him on this point. In the end God speaks to him from the whirlwind.
- **Satan is on a leash.** The Adversary here is a member of God's court, not an independent power. This is the main point of the limits, which show that Satan has no authority of his own.

## Rabbinic readings

The Talmud takes Satan in Job to be a figure of the same kind as the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination) and the Angel of Death. [Bava Batra 16a] says that Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one. I could not retrieve the passage, so I'm citing it by name and paraphrasing. The same passage discusses why God did not tell Satan to spare Job's life in the first round, and it reads the limit "spare his life" in Job 2 as a restriction on what Satan was allowed to do. Read this way, Satan is an agent carrying out a task within strict bounds, so the "indirectness" is the relationship between God and a subordinate agent.

Maimonides, in *Guide for the Perplexed* 3:22, takes the prologue to be a parable. He reads Satan as the natural forces and material inclinations that bring suffering to a person, always under divine providence. He treats this as a teaching about providence and not as a narrative about divine reluctance. I'm giving this from memory, so check the chapter.

## Bottom line

The "hand" language does set up a distance between God and the affliction. God gives permission and sets limits, and Satan acts. But it is a distance of delegation, not of absence. The book as a whole holds that God is ultimately responsible for what Job suffers. That is why the Job of the dialogues demands an answer from God and not from Satan.

answer:
**Short answer:** Eliphaz (the first friend, in [Job 5:19]) uses a "six… yes, seven" number pattern. It is a poetic way of saying "in every trouble, however many." The following verses then list the troubles: famine, war, slander, violence, wild beasts. The point is that God will rescue the righteous completely, and no harm will reach them. I did not retrieve commentaries on this verse, so the points about Hebrew poetry and about Eliphaz are my own explanation, not quotations.

**Key Takeaways**
- "Six… seven" is a parallelism, not a literal count.
- It means that no matter how many troubles come, you will be saved from all of them.
- The verses after it spell out the troubles and the rescue from each.
- It belongs to Eliphaz's argument that suffering is God's discipline and that healing follows.
- The book of Job itself challenges his view.

**The text**
> בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא־יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע
> "You will be delivered from six troubles; in seven no harm will reach you." [Job 5:19]

**The literary device**
- Biblical poetry often uses an "x, x+1" pattern. Examples are "three things… even four" in Proverbs 30 and "for three transgressions… and for four" in Amos 1. The first number sets up the list, and the next number adds emphasis.
- It does not mean "the seventh is special" or "the seventh is excluded." Here it means that six troubles are not the limit. Even if a seventh comes, you will be safe.
- The "six" are not named one by one. The verses that follow give a representative list:
  - famine and war ([Job 5:20])
  - the "scourge of the tongue," meaning slander, and sudden violence ([Job 5:21])
  - wild animals ([Job 5:22-23])

**Context in Eliphaz's speech**
- Just before this, Eliphaz says "happy is the person whom God reproves" ([Job 5:17]). God wounds and heals ([Job 5:18]). So the troubles are discipline, and rescue follows if Job accepts it.
- The promise then grows into peace in the home, many descendants, and a full old age, "as shocks of grain are taken in their season" ([Job 5:24-26]).
- He ends with "we have inquired into this and it is so" ([Job 5:27]). He treats it as settled wisdom.

**A caution**
- Eliphaz implies that Job's suffering must come from sin, and that repenting will end it. In the end God rebukes the friends for not speaking rightly about Him ([Job 42:7]). So the verse is a true statement about God's power to save, but it is not an accurate account of Job's situation.

answer:
Only the Mei HaShiloach passage below was retrieved and read for this answer. The other works are described from general knowledge of the literature, and I have given no section numbers for them. The Sefaria lookups for those other works were rate-limited, so please check them against the texts.

## Works to look at

**1. Mei HaShiloach (Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izbica; Radzin tradition).** The book was printed in the 1800s, so it came through the war in print. His comment on the opening of Vaetchanan is a good example of his approach. Moses tells Israel that he pleaded with God "at that time", even after God had sworn he would not enter the land. The Mei HaShiloach says this teaches that nothing should hold a person back from prayer, even when a decree seems final. He draws on the Gemara about Hezekiah turning his face to the wall [Berakhot 10a]. He explains "You have begun" [Deuteronomy 3:24] this way: God had sent Moses the urge to pray so that Israel would learn from him how to pray in every generation. "Enough for you" [Deuteronomy 3:26] then means he had given them enough of that lesson. Read it at [Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Vaetchanan].

He also reads "See, I have taught you statutes…" [Deuteronomy 4:5] as Moses's concern about the land. Moses feared Israel would think the land was not very holy, since he himself could not enter it. So he stressed that he teaches only what God commanded him.

**2. Esh Kodesh (Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, the Piaseczna Rebbe).** These are his Shabbat talks from the Warsaw Ghetto, 1939–1942. He buried the manuscript in a milk can, and it was recovered after the war. For that reason it is probably the best-known example of a work that survived. It is on Sefaria as [Esh Kodesh], arranged by Jewish year (5700, 5701 and 5702). I could not open the Vaetchanan talk, so I will not summarize it. Vaetchanan falls on Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat of consolation, so his talk for that week is worth reading. He writes about faith and suffering and is not a typical commentary.

**3. Other well-known Hasidic works printed before the war.** These are less famous than the Sefat Emet or Kedushat Levi. I am listing them from general knowledge, and I have not checked what each says on Vaetchanan.
- *Ma'or Va-Shemesh* (Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Epstein of Krakow). He is a student of the Maggid's circle and the Noam Elimelech's circle, and his work is arranged by parasha.
- *Tiferet Shlomo* (Rabbi Shlomo Rabinowicz of Radomsk).
- *Bnei Yissaschar* (Rabbi Zvi Elimelech of Dinov). It is arranged by month and mostly about the calendar. It would be relevant for the Shabbat Nachamu timing in Av.
- *Ohev Yisrael* (the Apter Rav).
- *Degel Machaneh Ephraim* (the Besht's grandson).

## Other well-known commentaries
- [Kedushat Levi] (Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev).
- [Sefat Emet] (Gur).

The Vaetchanan material includes the Shema, the Ten Commandments, the Cities of Refuge and "You shall love…". Those are themes these works develop.

## Caveat on "survived the Holocaust"
Most classic Hasidic works survived simply because they were printed and spread widely before the war, so the phrase fits Esh Kodesh best. Many manuscripts and courts were destroyed. There is a real similarity, and the text seems to invite it. I don't know of a classic commentator who states the parallel in these terms. So I give the textual observations first and mark the interpretation as my own.

## Key Takeaways
- Both scenes are periodic gatherings with a fixed rhythm. The sons rotate their feasts, "each on his set day," and the heavenly court convenes "one day."
- In both, a worry about sin sits beside the gathering. Job fears the children "blessed God in their hearts," and the Adversary insinuates that Job himself will "curse You to Your face."
- Job's offerings are a human counterpart of the heavenly scrutiny. He watches over his children's hidden thoughts, and the Adversary probes Job's.
- The two scenes are joined in the narrative. The final disaster strikes at the sons' feast, the same setting as the opening scene, which is probably deliberate.
- The parallel has limits. Job's sons are never said to have sinned, and the heavenly gathering is a court, not a party.

## The textual parallels

**1. Two gatherings, one structure.**
- The sons "make a feast" (*mishteh*, a drinking feast), each in his own house on his day [Job 1:4].
- Then "the day came, and the divine beings presented themselves before GOD, and the Adversary came along with them" [Job 1:6].
- Both are recurring assemblies. In both, an uninvited or unexpected presence appears. Job is not at the feast, and the Adversary "came among them" in heaven.

**2. The worry about hidden sin.**
- Job says, "Perhaps my children have sinned and blasphemed God in their thoughts" (*ulai chat'u banai uveirchu Elohim bilvavam*) [Job 1:5].
- The Adversary later argues that Job's piety is only a result of his blessings [Job 1:9-11].
- In both cases a suspicion about the heart cannot be settled by outward behavior. Job's sacrifices cover what he cannot see, and God's testing of Job exposes what only God can see.
- The verb *barach* ("bless") is used euphemistically for "curse" in both places. In 1:5 it is the feared sin of the children. In 1:11 and 2:5 it is the Adversary's prediction about Job.

**3. The feast as the setting of catastrophe.**
- The scene of the sons eating and drinking in their eldest brother's house is repeated almost word for word in [Job 1:13] and [Job 1:18-19].
- The narrator frames the destruction with that scene. The heavenly scene sets the test in motion, and the earthly feast is where the test lands.

## Rashi's reading of the heavenly scene
Rashi on [Job 1:6], drawing on the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16a), says the day was Rosh Hashanah. On that day the Adversary was commanded to bring the merits and the guilt of all creatures. "Standing" (*hityatzev*) implies a court case, citing Isaiah 3:13, "The LORD stands to plead."

On this reading the heavenly gathering is a judgment session, not a social event. If you read the two scenes together, Job's concern for his children after their "round of feast days" also becomes a kind of accounting. He too takes stock of the household's possible guilt and brings offerings.

## Where the parallel breaks down
- The sons are not described as sinning. Job only suspects it, "perhaps." The text gives no basis for saying their feasting was wrong, and some readers see in their inviting their three sisters a sign of family harmony.
- The heavenly gathering is about Job, while the feast is about Job's children. They meet only through Job's fatherly anxiety and the later disaster.
- The Adversary's role is to accuse. Job's role toward his children is to intercede. Job is therefore a mirror image of the Adversary. He looks for his children's merit and covers their possible guilt, while the Adversary looks for Job's guilt.

## My own suggestion
Job on earth does what God does in heaven. He oversees a "court" of his own household and brings offerings to cover possible sin. The Adversary then challenges whether Job's own devotion would survive without his blessings. The book asks whether goodness is real when it is not tied to reward. The feasting scene shows a world of ordinary blessing, and the heavenly scene tests it. That interpretation is mine, not a quoted commentator's.

If you'd like, I can look at how Ibn Ezra, Ramban, or the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a–16b) treat the Adversary's role or Job's offerings.

answer:
**Yovel required reversal.** Land could not be permanently sold, so in the Yovel (Jubilee) year every field returned to the family that held it in the original division. Commercial transactions could shift who worked a field for up to about 50 years, but they could not shift ownership for good.

## Key Takeaways
- The Torah says the land "must not be sold beyond reclaim" (*litzmitut*), because it belongs to God.
- A "sale" of ancestral land was in effect a lease that ran until Yovel, and the land then returned to the seller or his heirs.
- Before Yovel, the seller or his relatives could redeem the land early, at a price that reflected the years remaining.
- Num. 36 applied the same principle at the tribal level. An heiress had to marry within her tribe so that land would not move between tribes.
- The system had exceptions and conditions, noted below.

## The basic law
I retrieved [Leviticus 25:23-28]. It reads: "וְהָאָרֶץ לֹא תִמָּכֵר לִצְמִתֻת כִּי לִי הָאָרֶץ" ("But the land must not be sold beyond reclaim, for the land is Mine"). It continues "וּבְכֹל אֶרֶץ אֲחֻזַּתְכֶם גְּאֻלָּה תִּתְּנוּ לָאָרֶץ" ("Throughout the land that you hold, you must provide for the redemption of the land").

The passage then sets out the mechanisms:
- A relative (*go'el*) may redeem the land.
- The seller may redeem it himself once he has the means. The years since the sale are computed and the purchaser is refunded the difference.
- If no one redeems it, the land stays with the purchaser "until the jubilee year," and then "it shall be released, so that [the seller] returns to his holding."

The rationale is theological. The land is God's, and the people are "strangers resident with Me." No one can permanently sell what he does not fully own. The Yovel passage earlier in the chapter (25:10-16) says the same thing: "each of you shall return to his holding." I could not retrieve that passage in this session, so I am citing it from memory. It also explains why the price depends on the number of years until Yovel. The buyer is in effect buying a number of harvests, not the land.

## What returns, and what doesn't
This section is from my knowledge of the Talmudic and halachic sources, not from texts I retrieved here. Check the details in the sources, mainly Arakhin 28b–33b and Mishneh Torah, Shemitah VeYovel.
- **Inheritance and the original distribution.** The baseline is the portion each family received by lot under Joshua. Land that came to someone by inheritance, or that he gave away or sold, was handled by the rules above. In Bava Batra the Sages discuss how the original division by lot worked.
- **Houses in walled cities** (Lev. 25:29-30) are an exception. The seller has one year to redeem, and after that the sale is permanent. Houses in unwalled villages are treated like fields.
- **Levite cities.** Levite property in their cities always remains redeemable (Lev. 25:32-34).
- **Consecrated fields.** A field dedicated to the Temple and not redeemed passes to the priests at Yovel (Lev. 27:20-21). This is a different kind of transfer, one that Yovel itself brings about.
- **The land returns to its owner, not to the buyer's price.** The buyer takes the loss if he has held the land for the years he paid for. Yovel is not refunded.

## The tribal level
[Numbers 36:7-9] makes the same point about tribes. The verse says no inheritance "shall pass from tribe to tribe," and every tribe "shall hold on to its own ancestral portion." The daughters of Tzelofchad therefore had to marry within their tribe. A later Talmudic discussion (Ta'anit 30b and Bava Batra 120a) says this restriction applied only to that generation. This shows the underlying concern was Yovel and the tribal map, since marriage out of the tribe would have moved land permanently if Yovel did not return it.

## When Yovel applied
Arakhin 32b says Yovel applies only when the Jews live in the Land by tribe. When Reuben, Gad and half of Menashe were exiled, Yovel stopped. Many authorities hold that the Yovel laws are no longer in force. Rambam treats Yovel's biblical force as ending then, and the later period is a matter of dispute. The specifics belong with a rabbi, though they matter little for practice now.

answer:
Retry.**Short answer:** When Israel crossed the Jordan, they gathered at Shechem between Mount Gerizim and Mount Eval (also spelled Ebal). Six tribes stood on each mountain, and the Levites stood in the valley with the Ark. The Levites recited blessings and curses, and the whole people answered "Amen." The ceremony made the covenant public and binding. It also taught that life in the Land depends on loyalty to the Torah.

**Key Takeaways**
- The ceremony was commanded by Moses in Deuteronomy 11 and 27 and carried out by Joshua [Joshua 8:30-35].
- The tribes stood in two groups on the two mountains. The Levites, priests and Ark stood between them in the valley.
- The Levites faced each mountain in turn and recited a blessing or a curse. Both groups answered "Amen."
- Stones inscribed with the Torah and an altar were also part of the event.
- Its meaning is acceptance of the covenant, with collective responsibility and a clear choice between blessing and curse.

## 1. The ceremony

**The setting.** The Mishnah places the mountains in Samaria, near Shechem and the "oaks of Moreh." It connects Deuteronomy 11:30 with Abraham's stop at Shechem in Genesis 12:6. [Mishnah Sotah 7:5]

**The positions.** The Mishnah says that six tribes went up to the top of Gerizim and six to the top of Eval. The priests, the Levites and the Ark stood below, in the middle. The priests surrounded the Ark, and the Levites surrounded the priests. [Mishnah Sotah 7:5] The tribes of the blessing and the tribes of the curse are named in Deuteronomy 27:12-13, which I could not retrieve here. By memory, the blessing side was Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin. The curse side was Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali.

Joshua describes the same scene. All Israel, "stranger and citizen alike," stood on either side of the Ark, "half of them facing Mount Gerizim and half of them facing Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of GOD had commanded them of old, in order to bless the people of Israel." [Joshua 8:33]

**The recitation.** According to the Mishnah:
- The Levites turned toward Gerizim and began with a blessing: "Blessed is the man who does not make a graven or molten image."
- They then turned toward Eval and recited the matching curse: "Cursed is the man who makes a graven or molten image."
- Both groups answered "Amen" each time, until all the blessings and curses were finished. [Mishnah Sotah 7:5]

The curses themselves are the series in Deuteronomy 27:15-26. They cover idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a boundary marker, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the vulnerable, forbidden relations, secret murder, and taking a bribe. The last one covers anyone who does not uphold the words of this Torah. The best-known explanation is that these are mostly sins done in secret. A public oath therefore binds the people to the things no court can see. I am giving that explanation from memory.

**The stones and altar.** The Mishnah adds that they then brought stones, built an altar and plastered it. They wrote "all the words of the Torah in seventy languages" on it, reading "clearly elucidated" in Deuteronomy 27:8 as a hint at this. After that they took up the stones and spent the night at Gilgal. [Mishnah Sotah 7:5] The "seventy languages" detail is rabbinic interpretation, not the plain text. The text itself says Joshua built an altar on Mount Eval, offered sacrifices, and wrote a copy of the Torah of Moses there. [Joshua 8:30-32]

## 2. The significance

- **A covenant renewal on entering the Land.** The ceremony is a public ratification of the covenant. It comes at the moment Israel becomes a nation with a land, so the Land is tied from the start to obedience to the Torah. Deuteronomy 11:26-32 frames it as "blessing and curse" set before them. I could not retrieve that text, so this follows my memory of it.
- **Collective acceptance.** Everyone answered "Amen." In the Mishnah's account both mountains respond to both the blessings and the curses. This is why the Talmud treats "Amen" as an acceptance and oath. I recall Shevuot 36a and Sotah 37a-b on this point, but I did not check them here. Joshua stresses that the stranger stood alongside the citizen, so the covenant included everyone.
- **A choice, not fate.** The people stand physically between blessing and curse, and the Levites in the valley speak to each side in turn. The picture shows that both outcomes are real and that the people choose between them.
- **A Torah-centered nation.** The Ark, the written Torah and the altar are all present. The ceremony shows that Israel's national life rests on a text taught and accepted publicly. The Mishnah's "seventy languages" adds that the Torah is meant to be understood by all nations.
- **Mutual responsibility.** Because the whole people said "Amen" to the curses, each person took on responsibility for the community's conduct, including hidden sins. Later tradition developed the idea of mutual responsibility (*arevut*) from this, but I did not verify the sources here.

*Note:* Several of the texts I wanted (Deuteronomy 27 and 11, and the rest of Joshua 8) failed to load because of a temporary service limit. I used only the Mishnah and Joshua 8:33 as retrieved sources, and I marked the rest as from memory. It would be worth reading Deuteronomy 27 directly, along with Rashi and Ramban on it, for the full text of the curses and the commentators' views.

answer:
**Summary:** Jeremiah 15 opens with God telling Jeremiah that the decree is sealed. Even Moses and Samuel could not reverse it. Jeremiah then complains about his suffering, and God answers that he must repent of that complaint. Chapter 16 commands Jeremiah to live as a sign of the coming devastation. He is not to marry, not to enter houses of mourning, and not to enter houses of feasting. It ends with a promise of a return to the land that is greater than the Exodus. Below I use only the commentaries I actually retrieved: Rashi and Radak. Where I describe the chapters without a commentator, that is my own summary of the verses.

## Key Takeaways
- 15:1–9: The decree against Judah is final, "on account of Manasseh" (15:4). Even Moses and Samuel could not annul it.
- 15:10–18: Jeremiah laments being hated, and he says God has been to him "like a spring that fails" (15:18).
- 15:19–21: God tells Jeremiah to repent of that complaint. If he does, he will "stand before Me" again and be a fortified wall of bronze.
- 16:1–9: Jeremiah may not marry or mourn or feast with others. His isolation is a sign of the coming ruin.
- 16:10–21: God explains the sin, then promises a return from exile greater than the Exodus, and the nations' eventual recognition of God.

## Chapter 15

### Verses 1–9: The decree cannot be reversed
God says: "אִם־יַעֲמֹד מֹשֶׁה וּשְׁמוּאֵל לְפָנַי אֵין נַפְשִׁי אֶל־הָעָם הַזֶּה" ("Even if Moses and Samuel were to intercede with Me, I would not be won over to that people") [Jeremiah 15:1].

- **Rashi** [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:1] explains why these two were chosen. Both Moses and Samuel first brought Israel back to the right path, and only then prayed for them. Moses did this at the golden calf, with the sword and the scattered ashes, and afterwards said "perhaps I will atone." Samuel did this at Mizpah, where Israel removed the Baalim and then he prayed. Rashi's point is that Jeremiah cannot bring them back, so there is nothing for his prayer to build on. He ties this to God's earlier command not to pray for them, citing Jeremiah 7:16. Rashi also glosses *nafshi* as "My will."
- **Radak** [Radak on Jeremiah 15:1] reads *nafshi* the same way, as "My will." He notes that Moses and Samuel were both Levites and prophets, and that Samuel was the greatest prophet after Moses. He reads "שַׁלַּח מֵעַל־פָּנַי" ("Dismiss them from My presence") as addressed to Jeremiah. In his reading, if it is in your power to send them away, that is better than praying for them.

**The four destinies and the cause.** The people are sorted into plague, sword, famine and captivity. Four "families" of punishment are added: the sword to slay, dogs to drag, and birds and beasts to devour. The cause is stated explicitly: "בִּגְלַל מְנַשֶּׁה בֶן־יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ" ("on account of King Manasseh son of Hezekiah") [Jeremiah 15:4]. Rashi on this verse explains *zaavah* as "horror," from the root *zaa* ("shake"). Anyone who hears of the evil that befell them will shudder [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:4].

Verses 5–9 describe the destruction in a series of images:
- Jerusalem has "cast Me off" and "gone backward."
- God says "I cannot relent."
- There are many widows.
- A destroyer comes "at noonday."
- The mother of seven is forlorn, "her sun has set while it is still day."

### Verses 10–14: Jeremiah's lament and God's answer
"אוֹי־לִי אִמִּי כִּי יְלִדְתָּנִי אִישׁ רִיב וְאִישׁ מָדוֹן לְכָל־הָאָרֶץ" ("Woe is me, my mother, that you ever bore me, a man of conflict and strife with all the land") [Jeremiah 15:10].

- **Rashi** [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:10] says Jeremiah was complaining that his own townsmen hated him because of his rebukes. "I have not lent and I have not borrowed" means he has no money dispute with anyone, yet everyone curses him.
- God's reply in 15:11–14 is difficult. It speaks of a remnant being spared, and of the northern enemy as iron that cannot be broken. It also speaks of wealth being plundered and a fire that burns in God's wrath. I did not retrieve the commentators on these verses, so I won't attribute a reading to them.

### Verses 15–18: Jeremiah's plea
Jeremiah asks God to remember him and take vengeance on his persecutors. He says God's words were "joy and delight" to him when he received them (15:16). He sat alone because of God's hand on him (15:17). He then asks why his pain is endless and says God has become "like a spring that fails, like waters that cannot be relied on" (15:18).

### Verses 19–21: God's answer
"לָכֵן כֹּה־אָמַר יְהֹוָה אִם־תָּשׁוּב וַאֲשִׁיבְךָ לְפָנַי תַּעֲמֹד" ("If you turn back, I shall take you back and you shall stand before Me") [Jeremiah 15:19].

**Radak** [Radak on Jeremiah 15:19] reads this as a rebuke of Jeremiah himself. By saying God was like a failing spring, Jeremiah had spoken wrongly. If he repents, God will take him back and forgive him. Radak adds that "standing before God" means prayer, thanksgiving and receiving prophecy, and he compares "Moses and Samuel stand before Me" and Abraham who "still stood before God." Radak says this phrase is used only of a prophet.

Radak explains "ואם תוציא יקר מזולל" ("if you produce what is noble out of the worthless") as follows. If Jeremiah works to turn the wicked into good, then his word will be fulfilled as though God had said it, as with Samuel, "none of his words fell to the ground." He also records another view, that *kefi tihyeh* means "as My word."

He explains "they shall come back to you, not you to them" as a warning. Jeremiah should be careful, while arguing with the people, not to be swayed by their many arguments. They must come toward him, and he must not go toward them.

## Chapter 16

### Verses 1–9: Jeremiah's life becomes a sign
God commands: "לֹא־תִקַּח לְךָ אִשָּׁה וְלֹא־יִהְיוּ לְךָ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה" ("You are not to marry and not to have sons and daughters in this place") [Jeremiah 16:2]. Verses 4–9 say that the children, mothers and fathers will die without burial or lament. Jeremiah is also forbidden to enter a "house of mourning" or a "house of feasting." The reason given is "I have withdrawn My favor from that people... My kindness and compassion" [Jeremiah 16:5]. This is the stage where "the voice of bridegroom and bride" will cease (16:9).

**The difficulty.** **Radak** [Radak on Jeremiah 16:2] calls this a "great perplexity" (*mevukhah*). Why should Jeremiah be forbidden to have children? Small children die only for their parents' sins, and Jeremiah has no such sin. The decree also did not affect everyone, since some were exiled and Ezekiel says a remnant of sons and daughters would survive.

Radak's own answer is that "in this place" means Anatot, Jeremiah's hometown. He ties this to Jeremiah 11:23, where it is said that Anatot will have no remnant. In his reading, Jerusalem would have a remnant, but Anatot would not. Children born in Anatot would be swept up in the city's fate, even if their father were righteous. He compares Lot's warning, "lest you be swept away in the sin of the city." Radak adds that Anatot's people did later have survivors who repented, and he notes the 128 men of Anatot who returned from Babylon. God did not tell Jeremiah this, because the decree was originally harsh.

### Verses 10–13: Why this is happening
The people will ask what their sin is. Jeremiah is to answer that their ancestors abandoned God and served other gods, and that "you have acted worse than your ancestors," each following his own evil heart (16:12). Therefore they will be hurled to a land they have not known, where they will serve other gods (16:13).

### Verses 14–15: The new Exodus
"הִנֵּה־יָמִים בָּאִים... וְלֹא־יֵאָמֵר עוֹד חַי־יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלָה אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם" ("a time is coming when it shall no more be said, 'As God lives who brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt'") [Jeremiah 16:14]. Instead the oath will be "who brought them out of the northland, and out of all the lands to which they had been banished."

### Verses 16–18: Fishermen and hunters
**Radak** [Radak on Jeremiah 16:16] reads the images as two kinds of enemy.
- The fishermen stand for those who kill by the sword, since fish die when caught.
- The hunters stand for those who take people into exile alive.
- Radak says "I am sending" means God stirs up their spirit to come, as if He had sent for them.
- He notes that Targum Yonatan translates it as nations who kill.

The reason given is that God's eyes are on all their ways. He will repay them "doubly" because they filled His land with the corpses of their idols (16:18).

### Verses 19–21: The nations will recognize God
Jeremiah calls God "my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in a day of trouble." Nations will come from the ends of the earth and say their ancestors inherited "utter delusions" and that "no-gods" cannot be made by mortals. God says He will teach them His power and might, "and they shall learn that My name is GOD." The chapter ends on a note of universal recognition after the punishment.

## What I did not cover
I retrieved Rashi on 15:1, 15:4 and 15:10, and Radak on 15:1, 15:19, 16:2 and 16:16. I did not retrieve Metzudat David, Ibn Ezra, Malbim or others on the remaining verses. Abarbanel on 16:1 also exists and repeats Radak's question. Ask me to pull any of these if you'd like a deeper look at a particular verse.

answer:
**Summary:** Parashat Lech Lecha ([Genesis 12:1–17:27]) is the Torah's first extended account of Abram, later called Abraham. God commands him to leave his homeland and promises him land, descendants, and blessing. The rest of the parasha tests and develops that promise through famine, war, the covenant with God, the birth of Ishmael, and the commandment of circumcision.

## Key Takeaways
- God's opening call is "Lech lecha," a command to leave behind everything familiar, paired with a threefold promise of nationhood, blessing, and a great name.
- Abram's journeys and trials include famine, Egypt, the separation from Lot, and the war of the kings.
- In the Covenant Between the Parts, Abram trusts God's promise of offspring, and God "reckoned it to his merit."
- Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and Ishmael is born.
- Abram and Sarai become Abraham and Sarah, and circumcision is commanded as the sign of the covenant.

## The story in order

**1. The call (12:1–9).** God says: "לֶךְ־לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ" ("Go forth from your native land and from your father's house to the land that I will show you") [Genesis 12:1]. The promise follows: "I will make of you a great nation… and you shall be a blessing… all the families of the earth shall bless themselves by you" [Genesis 12:2-3]. Abram is seventy-five when he leaves with Sarai, Lot, and their household. He passes through Shechem and Beth-el, builds altars, and calls in God's name. God promises the land to his offspring.

**2. Famine and Egypt (12:10–13:4).** A famine drives Abram to Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, out of fear for his life. Pharaoh takes her, but plagues strike his house and he returns her. Abram leaves Egypt with great wealth. The Ramban ([Ramban on Genesis 12:10]) criticizes Abram for this, calling it an inadvertent sin. Others read the episode as a foreshadowing of the later exile in Egypt and Exodus.

**3. Separation from Lot (13:5–18).** Their herdsmen quarrel, so Abram offers Lot first choice of land. Lot chooses the well-watered Sodom plain. God then renews the promise of the land to Abram, and Abram settles in Hebron.

**4. The war of the kings (14).** Four kings defeat five, including the king of Sodom, and capture Lot. Abram pursues them with 318 men and rescues Lot and the captives. He refuses any spoils from the king of Sodom. Malki-Tzedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses him, and Abram gives him a tithe.

**5. The Covenant Between the Parts (15).** God tells Abram: "Fear not, Abram, I am a shield to you; your reward shall be very great." Abram answers that he is childless. God takes him outside and says, "Look toward heaven and count the stars… So shall your offspring be." Then: "וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה" ("And he put his trust in GOD, who reckoned it to his merit") [Genesis 15:6]. In the covenant ceremony (*brit bein ha-betarim*), God foretells that his descendants will be strangers in a land not theirs, enslaved and oppressed for 400 years, and then go free with great wealth. God also defines the borders of the land.

**6. Hagar and Ishmael (16).** Sarai is childless and gives her maidservant Hagar to Abram. Hagar conceives and looks down on Sarai. Sarai deals harshly with her, and Hagar flees. An angel tells her to return and promises that her son will be called Ishmael. Abram is eighty-six at his birth.

**7. Covenant of circumcision (17).** When Abram is ninety-nine, God appears to him. God changes his name to Abraham ("father of a multitude of nations") and Sarai's to Sarah, and promises that Sarah will bear a son, Isaac, within a year. God commands circumcision: "every male among you shall be circumcised… at the age of eight days" [Genesis 17:10-12]. The covenant will continue through Isaac, though Ishmael is also blessed. Abraham circumcises himself, Ishmael, and all the males of his household that same day.

## Themes
- **Faith and obedience.** Abram acts on God's word before he sees where it leads. The Mishnah counts ten trials of Abraham ([Pirkei Avot 5:3]). Many count the call of "Lech lecha" among them, though the lists vary.
- **Promise and delay.** Land and children are promised repeatedly, yet the fulfillment is deferred. The parasha is built around this tension.
- **Covenant.** Each of the two covenants carries a different emphasis: the Covenant Between the Parts concerns the land and the nation's future, and circumcision is the physical sign of the covenant.

I haven't pulled commentary on every passage here. If you'd like, I can go deeper on any section, such as Rashi's reading of "lech lecha," the meaning of the Covenant Between the Parts, or Abram's Egypt episode.

**Ben-deker was not the treasurer of Solomon's Temple.** He appears in only one verse, [I Kings 4:9], as one of the twelve district governors (*nitzavim*, prefects) of Solomon's kingdom. The name is spelled "Ben-deker" in the JPS translation. The KJV has "the son of Dekar." As far as I can tell, no source calls him a Temple treasurer.

## Key Takeaways
- Ben-deker was a regional governor, not a Temple official.
- His job was to supply food for the royal court for one month each year.
- His district covered Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan, in the area west of Jerusalem.
- "Ben-deker" may mean "son of Deker," with his personal name left out, as with Ben-hur and Ben-hesed in the same list.
- The Temple is a separate matter in Kings, and I found no treasurer named there.

## What the text says
[I Kings 4:7] says: "וְלִשְׁלֹמֹה שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר נִצָּבִים עַל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכִלְכְּלוּ אֶת־הַמֶּלֶךְ וְאֶת־בֵּיתוֹ חֹדֶשׁ בַּשָּׁנָה". In translation: "Solomon had twelve prefects over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household; each had to provide for one month in the year."

Then verse 9 reads: "בֶּן־דֶּקֶר בְּמָקַץ וּבְשַׁעַלְבִים וּבֵית שָׁמֶשׁ וְאֵילוֹן בֵּית חָנָן". In translation: "Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan."

- **His role:** He was part of the system that supplied the king's household. This was a tax and provisioning system, not a Temple office.
- **The list:** His entry sits among entries such as Ben-hur, Ben-hesed, Ben-abinadab, Baana son of Ahilud, and Ben-geber. Several are known only as "son of so-and-so."
- **His district:** It lay in the Danite and Judahite border region west of Jerusalem. Beth-shemesh is the best-known town in it.
- **Other details:** The text gives nothing more about him. I could not retrieve the commentaries on this verse, so I won't attribute any specific interpretation to a commentator.

## Where the confusion may come from
- **Other officers:** [I Kings 4:1-6] lists Solomon's chief ministers, such as the officer over the prefects and the one over the household. You may be thinking of that list. I have not checked it here, so I won't say who held which post.
- **Temple treasuries:** The Temple's treasuries (*otzrot beit Hashem*) are mentioned elsewhere in Kings and Chronicles. In Chronicles, the Levites and officers are described as over them. I have not retrieved those passages here, so please check the exact references before relying on this.
- **A different source:** If you saw "Ben-decker" as a Temple treasurer in a novel, a game, a film, or a website, it may be a modern invention or a mix-up with another name.

If you tell me where you came across the claim, I can help trace it. I can also look up the Temple's actual administration in Kings and Chronicles.

I couldn't retrieve the Aish Kodesh text. Sefaria's lookup was rate-limited and failed several times in a row. The parasha summary below rests on the verses and well-known commentary. For the Aish Kodesh, I can only give general themes, and I can't verify the details.

**Short answer:** Parashat Noach (Genesis 6:9–11:32) covers the corruption of the world, the Flood, a new covenant with Noah, and the Tower of Babel. The Aish Kodesh is Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, the Piaseczno Rebbe, who taught in the Warsaw Ghetto. His weekly talks on this parasha treat the Flood as a way to understand Jewish suffering and faith in a time of destruction.

## Key Takeaways
- Noah is "righteous… in his generations," and the commentators disagree about whether that is praise or criticism.
- The Flood came because of *chamas* (violence and robbery) and corruption. The ark was the means of survival.
- After the Flood, God promises never to destroy the world again and gives the rainbow as a sign.
- The Tower of Babel shows humanity united in rebellion, and it ends in the dispersal of the nations.
- The Aish Kodesh was written under Nazi occupation, so it reads the parasha as a source of endurance and closeness to God in suffering.

## Summary of the parasha

**1. Noah's character.** "אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ נֹחַ אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים הָיָה בְּדֹרֹתָיו אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים הִתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹחַ" ("This is the line of Noah. Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his age; Noah walked with God") [Genesis 6:9]. The phrase "in his age" is disputed. One reading in the Talmud and Rashi is that he was righteous only relative to a wicked generation. The other is that he would have been even greater in a righteous one.

**2. The corruption.** The earth was filled with *chamas*, and God decides to end the generation. Noah is told to build an ark. Rashi, citing the midrash, notes the view that Noah was "of little faith" and entered the ark only when the waters forced him to.

**3. The Flood.** Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark. The Flood lasts about a year. The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, and Noah sends out a raven and then a dove. The dove returns with an olive leaf.

**4. After the Flood.** Noah offers sacrifices. God promises never again to destroy the world, and the rainbow is the sign of that covenant. The Noahide laws are given.

**5. Noah and his sons.** Noah plants a vineyard and becomes drunk. The incident with his sons leads to the blessing of Shem and Yefet and the curse on Canaan.

**6. Babel.** The people say, "Let us build a city and a tower." God confuses their language and scatters them. The parasha closes with the line from Shem to Avram.

## The Aish Kodesh (general themes only)

- **The Flood and the ghetto.** He taught these talks in the Warsaw Ghetto. He understood suffering through the Flood and the ark, and he looked for faith and protection within that crisis.
- **The ark as a place of refuge.** The Hebrew word *teivah* means both "ark" and "word." A teaching attributed to the Baal Shem Tov is that a person can enter the words of prayer and Torah as a shelter. I believe the Piaseczno Rebbe used this idea, but I couldn't confirm where.
- **God is present in suffering.** A central theme of the Aish Kodesh is that God is close to a suffering Jew and shares in the pain. A Jew should not stop serving God because of that suffering.

Please check the exact wording in the text itself before quoting any of this. If you can tell me which year's talk you want (the talks are dated 5700–5702), I can try again to retrieve it.

answer:
The mitzvah of *yibum* (levirate marriage) is stated in **Deuteronomy 25:5-10**, in Parashat Ki Teitzei. The Sefaria tool failed when I tried to retrieve the text, so I'm quoting from memory and have not checked it against the source.

**Key Takeaways**
- The commandment is in [Deuteronomy 25:5-6](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.25.5-6).
- It applies when brothers lived together (or at the same time) and one died without a child.
- The widow may not marry outside the family. Her brother-in-law (the *yavam*) takes her as his wife.
- The first son carries on the dead brother's name.
- Verses 7-10 give the alternative, *chalitzah*, for a brother who does not want to marry her.

**The text**
Verse 5 reads: "כִּי יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו וּמֵת אַחַד מֵהֶם וּבֵן אֵין לוֹ, לֹא תִהְיֶה אֵשֶׁת הַמֵּת הַחוּצָה לְאִישׁ זָר; יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וְיִבְּמָהּ."

In translation: "When brothers dwell together and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the deceased shall not be married outside to a stranger. Her *yavam* shall come to her, take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a *yavam*."

Verse 6 says the firstborn she bears "shall stand in the name of his dead brother, so that his name not be blotted out of Israel."

**Chalitzah (verses 7-10)**
If the brother refuses, the widow goes to the elders at the gate. She removes his shoe and spits before him, and he is given the name "the house of the one whose shoe was removed."

**Related sources**
- The Talmudic tractate on this subject is Yevamot, which expands on these verses.
- Genesis 38 (Judah and Tamar) shows a pre-Sinaitic form of the practice.
- Ruth 4 shows a related redemption and levirate-type situation with Boaz.
- In practice, Ashkenazi halacha has favored *chalitzah* over *yibum* since roughly the medieval period. Many Sephardic communities continued to prefer *yibum* for longer, until the Chief Rabbinate of Israel ruled in favor of *chalitzah*. A rabbi should guide any real case.

answer:
The Torah doesn't give an explicit reason, so the answer comes from the commentators. The main approaches are these:

- The first light is a different kind of light from the sun's.
- Day 1 sets up the basic order of light and dark, and Day 4 puts the luminaries in charge of that order.
- The sequence shows that God, not the sun, is the source of light and life.

## Key Takeaways
- The text says light was created on Day 1 [Genesis 1:3] and the luminaries on Day 4 [Genesis 1:14-19], so the order is deliberate.
- The Day 4 luminaries have specific jobs: to separate day from night, to serve as signs for the set times, and to shine upon the earth.
- The Sages read the Day 1 light as a special, spiritual light that was set aside for the righteous (Chagigah 12a, as Rashi cites).
- Reading the verses plainly, the sequence shows that God's creation does not depend on the sun.

## What the text says
On Day 4 God says: "יְהִי מְאֹרֹת בִּרְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַיּוֹם וּבֵין הַלָּיְלָה" ("Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to separate day from night"). They are to be "signs for the set times, the days and the years," and "to shine upon the earth" [Genesis 1:14-19]. The sun and moon are described as lights that "dominate" (*memshelet*) day and night.

On Day 1, then, "light" already existed, and day and night already alternated ("there was evening and there was morning"). Day 4 does not create light. It creates *me'orot*, "light-bearers," that have a function within a system already running.

## Approaches

**1. A separate, primordial light (Midrash and Kabbalah).** The Sages teach that the Day 1 light was extraordinary. Rashi cites this on [Rashi on Genesis 1:4], quoting the aggadah: God "saw that the wicked were unworthy of using it, so He set it apart, reserving it for the righteous in the world to come" (Chagigah 12a). I'm citing the aggadic idea as Rashi gives it. I couldn't retrieve the Talmud page itself. Later Kabbalistic and Chassidic teaching develops this into a spiritual "hidden light" (*or ganuz*).

**2. A plain-sense reading: the order comes first.** Rashi gives a plain-sense explanation of the same verse. God saw that the light was good, and it was not fitting for light and darkness to be used "in a confused manner," so He fixed one's sphere to the day and the other's to the night [Rashi on Genesis 1:4]. On this reading Day 1 sets up the light/dark cycle, and Day 4 gives it fixed, measurable "carriers" that mark time and seasons.

**3. Light is not the sun's property.** Many readers note that the Torah puts light before the sun, and so denies that the sun is the true source of light or life. That matters against ancient sun worship. This is a common explanation, but I'm not attributing it to a particular commentator here. It also fits the order of creation: the heavenly bodies are placed in the sky as servants, not as independent powers.

**4. Purpose on Day 4.** The luminaries serve three jobs. They separate day from night. They mark *moadim* (set times, the basis of the Jewish calendar). They give light to the earth. The sun and moon matter especially because they determine the months, years and festivals, which is why Day 4 stresses "signs for the set times."

## Bottom line
Day 1 gives light itself and the rhythm of day and night. Day 4 gives the sun, moon and stars their roles as timekeepers and light-givers. The Sages add that the first light was a special one, and the Torah's order also teaches that light comes from God, not from the sun.

answer:
**Title: "Very Good… Death? The Craziest Word in Bereshit"**

Bereshit Rabbah reads the last verse of creation, "very good," as "death is good." It sounds absurd, but it may be the most hopeful idea in the parasha. I didn't retrieve the midrash on Torah as God's blueprint, so I leave it out here.

## Key Takeaways
- On the sixth day God calls everything *tov me'od* ("very good"). Rabbi Meir's Torah read this as *tov mot* ("death is good") [Bereshit Rabbah 9:5].
- The Sages offer several reasons why death is built into a "very good" world.
- Rashi opens with a different surprise: the Torah starts with creation to settle who owns the land [Rashi on Genesis 1:1:1].
- The shared idea is that our limits (mortality, ownership, struggle) are part of what makes the world good.

## The Setup: A Strange Version of the Torah
After six days of creation, the verse says: "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good" (*vehinei tov me'od*, [Genesis 1:31]). I did not fetch this verse, so the Hebrew is from memory.

The midrash says: "In Rabbi Meir's Torah they found written: 'And behold, it was *tov me'od*' – and behold, *tov mot*, death is good." (My translation, from the Hebrew text in [Bereshit Rabbah 9:5].)

The two words differ by one letter. *Me'od* (מאד) becomes *mot* (מות) when the *alef* is swapped for a *vav*. The midrash notes that the sources say this was an interpretation Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar taught in Rabbi Meir's name. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman remembered hearing it while riding on his grandfather's shoulders. That is a nice picture of Torah passed down through generations.

This is midrash, not *pshat* (plain meaning). The plain meaning is that creation was exceedingly good. The midrash asks what the word "very" adds that the earlier "good"s did not.

## Why Would Death Be "Good"? The Sages Argue
The midrash then gives a debate about why death was decreed at all. Each answer is a different theory of what a good world needs.

**1. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina: death is a penalty for human arrogance.** Adam was worthy of never tasting death. God foresaw that Nebuchadnezzar and Hiram of Tyre would make themselves gods, so mortality was imposed. This is a harsh, humbling answer.

**2. Rabbi Yonatan: death keeps goodness honest.** If only the wicked died, the wicked would fake repentance and collect mitzvot as a strategy. The midrash puts it this way: "so that the wicked should not feign repentance… the result would be acting [virtuously] for insincere motives." If death were the reward for being bad and life the reward for being good, nobody could serve God without an ulterior motive. Mortality for everyone keeps mitzvot from being a bargain.

**3. Rabbi Yochanan: death is rest.**
- For the wicked, death ends their angering of God: "There the wicked cease from raging" [Job 3:17].
- For the righteous, death ends the daily battle with the evil inclination: "There the weary are at rest" [Job 3:17].

**4. Reish Lakish: death sets up double reward.** The righteous were worthy of never tasting death and accepted it anyway, so they get a double portion. The wicked caused that death, so they pay double.

## Rashi's Question: Why Start Here at All?
Rashi opens with a different challenge. If the Torah is a book of commandments, it should begin with the first commandment, "This month shall be for you…" [Exodus 12:2]. Why start with creation?

Rashi cites Rabbi Yitzchak, who reads [Psalms 111:6]: "He declared to His people the strength of His works, in order to give them the inheritance of the nations." If the nations say to Israel, "You are robbers," Israel can answer: "All the earth belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He; He created it and gave it to whom He pleased."

## Putting It Together (my own connection)
Rashi and the midrash seem to point to one idea. We are not the owners of the world, and we are not its masters.
- Rashi says the land is not ours by right. It is God's, and He gives it and takes it back.
- The midrash says life is not ours by right either. Death keeps us from acting as if we were gods, as Nebuchadnezzar and Hiram did.

Both treat limits as part of a good world. Without them, we could not do mitzvot for their own sake, we would never rest, and we would always be tempted to think we are God.

## Closing Thought
We usually treat limits as flaws in an otherwise perfect world. The Torah's first chapter says the opposite: the world became *tov me'od* only when it included limits, with humans placed inside it as guests, not owners. Rabbi Meir's reading suggests that the best response to our limits is to live each day as if it matters, because it does.

*Shabbat Shalom, and chodesh tov!*
