answer:
Rate limited; retry a couple.Passover food rules come from the Torah's ban on *chametz* (leavened grain). During the 7 days of Pesach (8 in the Diaspora), a Jew may not eat chametz, benefit from it, or own it. On the first night (the first two nights outside Israel) there is also a positive commandment to eat *matzah* (unleavened bread). On top of these Torah laws, communities have added customs. The best known is the Ashkenazi custom not to eat *kitniyot* (rice, legumes and similar foods). Sephardim generally do eat them.

*(The Sefaria server was rate-limiting my requests, so I could only read two sources directly: the Mishnah and Shulchan Arukh 453:1. The other references below come from standard knowledge of the sources. I give exact numbers only where I'm confident of them.)*

## Key Takeaways
- **Chametz** is any of five grains (wheat, barley, spelt, rye, oats) that touched water and was left to rise. On Pesach it is forbidden to eat, to benefit from, or to own.
- **Matzah** is required on Seder night. It must be made from those same five grains and guarded from leavening.
- **Kitniyot** (rice, corn, beans and similar) are not chametz under halacha. Ashkenazim avoid them by custom; Sephardim generally eat them.
- Even a tiny trace of chametz in a mixture can make food forbidden on Pesach. That is why people kasher their kitchens and buy Pesach-certified products.
- Some customs, like *gebrokts* (wet matzah), vary by family and community.

## 1. The Torah basis
- **Eating:** "Seven days you shall eat matzot… whoever eats chametz, that soul shall be cut off from Israel" [Exodus 12:15]. The punishment is *karet* (spiritual excision), which shows how seriously the Torah treats this ban.
- **Owning:** "No leaven shall be found in your houses" [Exodus 12:19], and "no chametz shall be seen with you… in all your borders" [Exodus 13:7]. These are the laws of *bal yera'eh u'bal yimatzei* (it may not be seen or found).
- **Benefit:** The Sages derive that it is also forbidden to profit from chametz, for example by selling it during Pesach or feeding it to your pet.

## 2. What counts as chametz?
The Mishnah lists the grains used for matzah:

> בְּחִטִּים, בִּשְׂעוֹרִים, בְּכֻסְּמִין וּבְשִׁיפוֹן וּבְשִׁבֹּלֶת שׁוּעָל
> "With wheat, with barley, with spelt, with rye, and with oats" [Mishnah Pesachim 2:5]

The Talmud explains why it is these five ([Pesachim 35a]). Only grains that can become chametz can be used for matzah, and only these five can become chametz. Chametz forms when flour from these grains meets water and is left to ferment. Halacha sets the limit at about 18 minutes of unworked dough. That is why matzah bakeries work so fast.

Some things are **not chametz:** meat, fish, eggs, dairy, fruit, vegetables, and so on. In practice, though, processed products can contain grain-based ingredients (such as grain alcohol, vinegar, or starch), or be made on shared equipment. So most people buy processed foods only with a "Kosher for Passover" certification.

## 3. Timing
- Chametz is forbidden from **midday on the 14th of Nisan** (the day before the Seder) under Torah law.
- The Rabbis moved the eating deadline earlier, to the end of the 4th seasonal hour of the morning. Benefit and ownership must end by the end of the 5th hour. The leftover chametz is burned or otherwise disposed of then.
- The night before, people search the house (*bedikat chametz*). Then they formally cancel ownership of any chametz they missed (*bittul*, the *Kol Chamira* declaration).
- Many people sell chametz they can't dispose of to a non-Jew through their rabbi (*mechirat chametz*).

## 4. Mixtures: why strictness is so high
Normally a small amount of forbidden food can be cancelled in a larger amount of permitted food (*bittul b'shishim*, cancellation in 60 times its volume). During Pesach, the Shulchan Arukh rules that chametz is **not cancelled even by a tiny amount** (*b'mashehu*) [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 447:1]. This is the basis for:
- kashering the kitchen (or using separate Pesach dishes and utensils);
- using only Pesach-certified products;
- extra care with anything that may have touched chametz.

## 5. The mitzvah to eat matzah
- On the first night there is a Torah commandment to eat matzah ("in the evening you shall eat matzot," [Exodus 12:18]). In the Diaspora it is also eaten on the second night.
- The matzah must be made from one of the five grains [Mishnah Pesachim 2:5]. It must be *shmurah*, meaning guarded from leavening specifically for the mitzvah. Many people use hand-made shmurah matzah at the Seder.
- For the rest of the week, eating matzah is not required (according to most opinions), but chametz is still forbidden.
- **Egg matzah / "matzah ashira"** is made with fruit juice or eggs instead of water. Under the Shulchan Arukh it isn't chametz. The Rema writes that the Ashkenazi custom is not to eat it on Pesach, except for elderly or sick people who need it. It can never be used for the Seder mitzvah.

## 6. Kitniyot: where communities differ
The Shulchan Arukh rules that rice and legumes may not be used for matzah, but they also don't become chametz, "and it is permitted to make a cooked food from them." The Rema adds:

> והמנהג באשכנז להחמיר ואין לשנות
> "And the custom in Ashkenaz is to be strict, and one should not change it." [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 453:1]

The Rema also sets limits on this custom (same se'if):
- If kitniyot fall into a cooked food by accident, they do not make it forbidden after the fact.
- It is permitted to light with oils made from kitniyot.
- It is permitted to keep kitniyot in the house.
- Seeds such as dill, anise and coriander are not kitniyot.

**By community:**
- **Ashkenazi:** Avoid kitniyot, meaning rice, corn, beans, lentils, peas, soy, and by many authorities also peanuts, sesame and mustard. Some say the custom began because these foods can be confused with or mixed with real grain. Kitniyot may still be owned, and can be given to people who need them for health reasons.
- **Sephardi:** Kitniyot are permitted, following the Shulchan Arukh. Many families check rice grain by grain beforehand for stray wheat. Some Sephardi communities (for example, some Moroccan families) have their own restrictions on particular foods.
- **Recent debate:** Some contemporary rabbis allow kitniyot for Ashkenazim living in Israel. The mainstream Ashkenazi Orthodox practice remains to keep the custom.

## 7. Gebrokts (matzah that touched liquid)
- **Chabad and many Chassidic communities:** They do not eat *gebrokts*, matzah or matzah meal that has touched water. Their concern is that a bit of unbaked flour might be left in the matzah. So they avoid matzah balls and matzah brei, and often keep matzah covered at the table. On the 8th day (in the Diaspora) they eat gebrokts on purpose.
- **Most Ashkenazim and Sephardim:** They eat gebrokts freely.

## 8. Practical summary
1. Clean out and remove chametz, sell what remains, and cancel ownership before the deadline on 14 Nisan.
2. Kasher the kitchen or switch to Pesach dishes.
3. Buy processed foods with reliable Pesach certification.
4. Eat shmurah matzah at the Seder.
5. Follow your community's custom on kitniyot, egg matzah and gebrokts.

The details of kashering particular appliances, medications (which are often permitted in non-food form), or a chametz mix-up that has already happened depend on the specifics. Please ask your rabbi about your own situation.

Según la tradición más conocida, había cuatro nubes en los cuatro costados, una encima, una debajo y una que iba delante. Esta es la versión que cito de memoria. Los servidores de Sefaria no respondieron, así que no pude abrir los textos para verificar la redacción exacta.

## Puntos clave
- Las nubes protegían a Israel y lo guiaban durante los 40 años en el desierto.
- La enumeración clásica de siete es: cuatro laterales, una superior, una inferior y una guía.
- Hay otras tradiciones que cuentan un número distinto de nubes.
- Según la tradición, las nubes fueron un mérito de Aarón.

## Fuente bíblica (*pshat*, sentido simple)
La Torá dice que "el Eterno iba delante de ellos de día en columna de nube para guiarlos" [Exodus 13:21]. También dice: "la nube del Eterno estaba sobre ellos de día, cuando partían del campamento" [Numbers 10:34]. El texto simple habla de una nube que guía y cubre. La división en siete viene de la tradición rabínica, que ve más nubes en esos versículos. Eso es *drash* (interpretación midráshica), no sentido literal.

## Las siete nubes (según la tradición rabínica)
Esta enumeración aparece en la tradición del Talmud y los Midrashim, y Rashi la sigue en su comentario a [Numbers 10:34]. Pido disculpas por no poder dar la referencia exacta.

1. **Nube del este**, al frente.
2. **Nube del oeste**, atrás.
3. **Nube del norte**.
4. **Nube del sur**.
   Las cuatro laterales protegían de enemigos, serpientes y escorpiones, y del viento y el clima.
5. **Nube superior**, que daba sombra contra el sol y la lluvia.
6. **Nube inferior**, bajo los pies, que según la tradición mantenía el suelo suave y limpio.
7. **Nube guía**, que iba delante. Según el Midrash, nivelaba montes y valles, mataba a los animales dañinos y mostraba dónde acampar.

## Otras tradiciones
- Algunas fuentes hablan de **cuatro** nubes, y otras de **trece**. Por ejemplo, el Midrash enumera trece nubes de gloria asociadas a la salida de Egipto y a la construcción del Mishkán.
- La *Mekhilta* y otros Midrashim también las cuentan de formas distintas, según cómo se interprete cada versículo.
- En la tradición jasídica y cabalística, las siete nubes se relacionan con las siete *sefirot* inferiores (*Jesed* a *Maljut*). Esto es interpretación mística posterior, no la fuente original.

## Relación con Sucot
El Talmud en [Sukkah 11b] discute si las *sucot* que mandó la Torá recuerdan las nubes de gloria (opinión de Rabí Eliezer) o cabañas reales (Rabí Akiva). Por eso Sucot se vincula con estas nubes.

## Mérito de las nubes
La tradición dice que las nubes estuvieron por el mérito de Aarón. Al morir él, las nubes desaparecieron, y el pueblo notó su ausencia. Este dato lo conozco por la tradición talmúdica y no pude verificarlo ahora.

Si quieres, puedo volver a buscar las citas exactas cuando Sefaria vuelva a responder.

answer:
На 97б в Шаббате спорят рабби Йехуда и мудрецы (а в начале страницы ещё Рав Йосеф и Рав Йехуда от имени Шмуэля). Спор идёт о том, за какие именно действия при переноске в субботу человек виновен. Вы не сказали, какой вопрос вас интересует, поэтому ниже разбор того, что я прочитал на этой странице. Прочитанный текст обрывается на середине, и конец страницы я не видел.

## Главное
- Сама тема страницы такова: если человек бросил предмет из частной территории в общественную и тот пролетел 4 амы, то рабби Йехуда признаёт его виновным, а мудрецы освобождают от наказания за пролёт.
- Рав Йехуда от имени Шмуэля объясняет, что рабби Йехуда возлагает две жертвы: одну за *hоцаа* (вынос), другую за *ава́ра* (проноc 4 амы по общественной территории).
- Гемара предлагает другое объяснение: рабби Йехуда возлагает одну жертву, а мудрецы освобождают полностью. Это возможно, если бросающий сказал: «Пусть предмет остановится, как только выйдет в общественную территорию».
- Спор о принципе *келута кема шеhунна* («предмет в воздухе считается лежащим»). Рабби Йехуда так считает, и поэтому намерение бросающего исполнилось. Мудрецы так не считают.
- Параллельно обсуждается, считает ли рабби Йехуда виновным за *толаду* (производную категорию работы) наравне с *авом* (основной категорией).

## Ход сугьи

**1. Вопрос о рабби Йехуде ха-Наси.** Гемара спрашивает, значит ли это, что рабби виновным и за производную работу, и за основную. Ведь вынос и внос в этом примере и есть основная категория и её производная. Противоречие возникает из барайты, где рабби Йехуда ха-Наси выводит из стиха «Эле hа-дварим» (Шмот 35:1) число 39 основных работ, переданных Моше на Синае. Слово «дварим» даёт два, «hа-дварим» добавляет третье, а числовое значение слова «эле» (алеф 1 + ламед 30 + hей 5) равно 36. Итого 3 + 36 = 39. Если рабби считает число основных работ фиксированным, то он виновным признал бы за основные, а за производные нет.

**2. Ответ Рава Йосефа.** Он говорит, что они учат слова Рава Йехуды не по рабби, а по **рабби Йехуде** (бен Илаи), у которого противоречия нет. Здесь он приводит барайту: если бросил из частной территории в общественную и предмет пролетел 4 амы, то рабби Йехуда признаёт его виновным, а мудрецы освобождают.

**3. Объяснение Шмуэля.** По Шмуэлю, рабби Йехуда возлагает две жертвы. Доказательство в том, что если бы жертва была одна, то из слов «мудрецы освобождают» следовало бы, что они освобождают полностью. Но он ведь вынес предмет из частной территории в общественную.

**4. Опровержение доказательства.** Гемара возражает: возможно, жертва одна, а мудрецы освобождают полностью, если бросающий сказал, что предмет должен остановиться сразу при выходе. Тогда спор сводится к принципу *келута кема шеhунна*.

**5. Производные категории.** Гемара отвергает мысль, что рабби Йехуда не возлагает вину за производную в паре с основной. Барайта говорит: «Рабби Йехуда добавляет также *шовет* (того, кто бьёт нити основы) и *медакдек* (того, кто уплотняет нить)». Мудрецы ему отвечают, что шовет входит в категорию *мейсах* (натягивание нитей основы), а медакдек в категорию ткачества. Гемара предлагает два прочтения. Либо он сделал оба действия вместе и значит, рабби Йехуда возлагает вину за производную в паре с основной. Либо он сделал их по отдельности, и тогда спор в том, считать эти действия основными или производными. Доказательство в пользу второго прочтения такое: слово «добавляет» имеет смысл, только если речь об основных категориях. Если бы это были производные, что тогда «добавлено»?

**6. Подтверждение.** Рабба и Рав Йосеф тоже говорят, что рабби Йехуда возлагает вину только за одну жертву.

**7. Равина и Рав Аши.** Равина спрашивает Рава Аши, как это согласуется с первоначальным предположением о двух жертвах. Рав Аши отвечает, что речь о случае, когда бросающий сказал: «Пусть предмет остановится, где захочет». Затем Гемара разбирает два случая:
- Если он хотел бросить на 8 амот, а бросил на 4, то он виновен: он «написал *шем* из *Шимона*» (часть имени, которая сама считается минимальной записью).
- Если же он хотел бросить на 4, а бросил на 8, то неясно: можно сказать, что вынос уже совершён, или что предмет ещё не остановился там, где он хотел. Гемара проводит различие с примером про имя: пока не написано «шем», слово «Шимон» не записано, а пока не пролетело 4 амы, 8 амот ещё не пролетели.

**8. Следующая барайта.** Страница заканчивается началом барайты: «Бросающий из общественной территории в общественную, а частная территория посередине, на 4 амы виновен…». Продолжение на следующей странице (98а), и я его не читал.

## Практический вывод
Закон в этой теме определяют не мнения рабби Йехуды, а решение мудрецов: пролёт в общественной территории сам по себе не наказуем. Для практики обратитесь к раву.

Если хотите, могу продолжить с 98а, перевести страницу построчно или сравнить, как Раши и Тосафот объясняют принцип *келута кема шеhунна*.

answer:
**Précision :** je ne peux pas dessiner d'image. Je comprends « illustration » comme un schéma pédagogique du chapitre 6 de Yoma (*Shnei Se'irei*, « Les deux boucs »), que voici sous forme de tableau. Dis-moi si tu cherchais autre chose, par exemple une image, des exemples ou une traduction.

Le chapitre traite des deux boucs de Yom Kippour. L'un est sacrifié « pour l'Éternel » et l'autre est envoyé « à Azazel » dans le désert. Il décrit aussi la confession sur le bouc émissaire, son voyage jusqu'au précipice (*Tsouk*), puis la crémation du taureau et du bouc que l'on brûle. Le texte de base est [Mishnah Yoma 6]. Dans le Bavli, le chapitre commence à [Yoma 62a].

## Points clés
- Les deux boucs doivent idéalement être identiques en apparence, en taille et en valeur, et achetés ensemble. Mais ils restent valides s'ils ne le sont pas.
- Si l'un meurt, la règle dépend du tirage au sort : avant, on prend un compagnon ; après, on amène une nouvelle paire.
- Le Grand Prêtre confesse sur le bouc émissaire en prononçant le Nom explicite, et l'assistance se prosterne.
- Un convoyeur emmène le bouc par dix cabanes jusqu'au *Tsouk*, où le bouc est précipité.
- Le Grand Prêtre apprend l'arrivée du bouc au désert grâce à des signaux.

## Schéma du déroulement

| Étape | Ce que dit la Mishna |
|---|---|
| 1. Les deux boucs | Idéalement identiques en *mar'eh* (apparence), *qomah* (taille) et valeur, et achetés ensemble. S'ils diffèrent ou sont achetés un jour d'écart, ils sont tout de même valides. |
| 2. Mort d'un bouc | **Avant le tirage au sort :** on prend un autre bouc pour compléter la paire. **Après :** on amène une nouvelle paire et on tire de nouveau au sort, avec une condition : le bouc désigné « pour l'Éternel » remplace celui qui est mort, et de même pour Azazel. Le bouc en surplus pâture jusqu'à ce qu'il ait un défaut, puis on le vend et l'argent va à une offrande volontaire. En effet, un *'hatat* de communauté ne « meurt » pas. **Rabbi Yehouda** dit qu'il meurt. |
| 3. Cas liés (Rabbi Yehouda) | Si le sang du bouc de l'Éternel est répandu, le bouc émissaire meurt. Si le bouc émissaire meurt, on répand le sang. |
| 4. Confession | Le Grand Prêtre appuie ses deux mains sur le bouc émissaire et confesse. La formule est : « *Ana HaShem, avou pasha'ou 'hat'ou lefanékha amékha Beit Israël…* ». Il cite ensuite Lévitique 16:30 : « car en ce jour on fera expiation pour vous afin de vous purifier ». |
| 5. Le Nom explicite | Les prêtres et le peuple dans la cour s'agenouillent, se prosternent et disent : « *Baroukh shem kevod malkhouto le'olam va'ed* ». |
| 6. Le convoyeur | Tout homme est apte à l'emmener. Mais les grands prêtres avaient institué l'usage de ne pas laisser un Israélite le faire. Rabbi Yossi cite le cas d'Arsela, un Israélite qui l'a fait. |
| 7. La rampe | On a construit une rampe à cause des Babyloniens, qui arrachaient les poils du bouc en disant : « Prends et pars, prends et pars ». |
| 8. Le trajet | Les notables de Jérusalem accompagnent le convoyeur jusqu'à la première cabane. Il y a dix cabanes entre Jérusalem et le *Tsouk*, soit 90 *ris* (à 7,5 *ris* par mille). À chaque cabane, on lui dit : « Voici de la nourriture et de l'eau ». On l'escorte de cabane en cabane, sauf à partir de la dernière. Là, l'accompagnateur reste à distance et observe. |
| 9. Le *Tsouk* | Le convoyeur divise le fil écarlate. Il en attache la moitié au rocher et l'autre moitié entre les cornes du bouc. Il pousse alors le bouc par l'arrière, et celui-ci roule et se disloque avant d'avoir atteint la mi-pente. Le convoyeur revient s'asseoir sous la dernière cabane jusqu'à la nuit. |
| 10. Impureté des vêtements | Elle commence quand le convoyeur sort des murs de Jérusalem (avis des Sages). Selon Rabbi Shimon, elle commence quand il précipite le bouc au *Tsouk*. |
| 11. Taureau et bouc brûlés | Le Grand Prêtre les ouvre et retire les parties à brûler (*emourim*). Il les met dans un récipient et les fait fumer sur l'autel. Le reste est porté au lieu de crémation. Les vêtements de ceux qui les emportent deviennent impurs dès leur sortie de l'enceinte de la cour (Sages). Pour Rabbi Shimon, c'est dès que le feu prend dans l'animal. |
| 12. Signal d'arrivée | On annonce au Grand Prêtre que le bouc est arrivé au désert. On le sait grâce à des postes de signalisation qui agitent des foulards. Rabbi Yehouda objecte qu'il y avait un signe plus évident : de Jérusalem à Beit 'Hidoudo, il y a trois milles. On marche un mille, on revient, et on attend le temps d'un mille. Ensuite on sait que le bouc est arrivé. |

La Mishna se poursuit avec l'avis de Rabbi Yishmael. Ma récupération du texte a été tronquée à cet endroit, et je ne le cite donc pas.

## Fil conducteur du chapitre
- **Le tirage au sort et la symétrie** (Mishna 1) : les deux boucs doivent être semblables pour que le sort seul les distingue. C'est le sens de la paire.
- **Le rite d'expiation** (Mishna 2-4) : la confession avec le Nom explicite fait le lien avec le verset « vous serez purifiés devant l'Éternel ».
- **Le rite du désert** (Mishna 4-6) : le convoyage, les cabanes et le précipice.
- **Les rites consécutifs** (Mishna 7-8) : la crémation du taureau et du bouc, la question de l'impureté, puis la confirmation de l'accomplissement du rite.

Je peux développer la discussion du Bavli (qui commence à [Yoma 62a]), le sens d'« Azazel » chez Rachi et le Ramban, ou faire un schéma du chemin jusqu'au *Tsouk*. Dis-moi ce qui t'intéresse.

answer:
**תשובה ישירה:** ברכות ב ע״א פותח במשנה על זמן קריאת שמע של ערבית. הזמן מתחיל משעה שהכהנים נכנסים לאכול בתרומתם, כלומר מצאת הכוכבים. סופו נחלק בין רבי אליעזר, חכמים ורבן גמליאל. הגמרא שואלת על סדר הדברים ועל לשון המשנה.

## נקודות מפתח
- המשנה פותחת בקריאת שמע של ערבית, כי הכתוב אומר "בשכבך ובקומך".
- יש שלוש דעות על סוף הזמן: סוף האשמורה הראשונה (ר׳ אליעזר), חצות (חכמים), עלות השחר (רבן גמליאל).
- לדברי רבן גמליאל, כל דבר ש"חכמים" הגבילו עד חצות, מצוותו מדאורייתא עד עלות השחר. החכמים הגבילו עד חצות "כדי להרחיק אדם מן העבירה".
- הגמרא מסבירה שהתנא נקט "משעה שהכהנים…" דרך אגב. הוא בא ללמד גם ש"כפרה לא מעכבת".

## המשנה
> "מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בָּעֲרָבִין? מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁהַכֹּהֲנִים נִכְנָסִים לֶאֱכוֹל בִּתְרוּמָתָן."

- **ר׳ אליעזר:** עד סוף האשמורה הראשונה.
- **חכמים:** עד חצות.
- **רבן גמליאל:** עד שיעלה עמוד השחר.
- **המעשה:** בניו באו מבית המשתה ואמרו "לא קרינו את שמע". אמר להם: "אם לא עלה עמוד השחר חייבין אתם לקרות".
- **ראיות רבן גמליאל:** הקטר חלבים ואברים, וכל הנאכלים ליום אחד. מצוותם עד עלות השחר, אף שחכמים אמרו "עד חצות".
- **הטעם לדברי חכמים:** "כדי להרחיק אדם מן העבירה", כלומר גדר שמונע מאדם להתרשל ולפספס את הזמן.

## הגמרא
1. **"תנא היכא קאי דקתני מאימתי?"** הגמרא שואלת על מה התנא סומך את שאלתו. מסקנתה: הוא סומך על הפסוק "בשכבך ובקומך". לכן הוא פותח בשל שכיבה, כלומר ערבית.
2. **"מאי שנא דתני בערבית ברישא?"** הגמרא שואלת למה פתח בערבית ולא בשחרית. יש שתי תשובות:
   - הוא סומך על הפסוק "בשכבך ובקומך".
   - או שלמד מבריאת העולם: "ויהי ערב ויהי בקר".
3. **קושיה על התשובה השנייה:** בסיפא נאמר "בשחר מברך שתים לפניה ואחת לאחריה, בערב שתים לפניה ושתים לאחריה". שם שחרית קודמת. התשובה: התנא פתח בערבית, עבר לשחרית, פירט את דיני שחרית, ואז חזר לפרט את דיני ערבית.
4. **"משעה שהכהנים"** הגמרא שואלת: הכהנים אוכלים תרומה מצאת הכוכבים, אז למה לא נאמר "משעת צאת הכוכבים"? תשובתה: המשנה באה ללמד דבר נוסף "אגב אורחיה". היא מלמדת מתי הכהנים אוכלים תרומה. היא מלמדת גם ש"כפרה לא מעכבא". הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על הפסוק "ובא השמש וטהר": ביאת השמש מעכבת טבול יום מלאכול בתרומה, וקרבן הכפרה שלו אינו מעכב. "וטהר" נדרש כ"טהר יומא", כלומר סיום היום.

הטקסט שקיבלתי נקטע באמצע הסוגיה, ולכן לא עיינתי ביתר הדף. אם תרצה, אמשיך משם, ואוכל להוסיף רש״י ותוספות או את ההלכה בשולחן ערוך (אורח חיים סימן רלה).

answer:
**Short answer:** Tosafot do not say the curtain went from Babylon to Rome. Their dispute is over which Temple the Tanna's remark fits, based on the halacha of the *par he'elem davar* (the bull for a communal error). The Rome problem you raise is a fair one. As far as I can tell, Tosafot don't address it, so the answers below are my own reasoning.

## Key Takeaways
- The passage is on [Yoma 57a], not 58a. Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Yosei says he saw the curtain in Rome with drops of blood from the *par he'elem davar* and the goat-offerings for idolatry.
- Tosafot's question is about the sacrifice, not about Rome. The Ri"va asks that the first Temple had no *paroches* (curtain), while in the second Temple this bull supposedly wasn't brought.
- The Ri"va answers that it was the first Temple. Rabbeinu Yitzchak (the Ri) answers that it was the second.
- The second Temple is the simpler fit for Rome, because Titus brought Temple spoils there after 70 CE. The first-Temple view needs an unstated route for the curtain to have survived.

## What Tosafot say
Tosafot ask: "הקשה ריב"א והא בבית ראשון לא הוו פרוכת ובבית שני דהוו פרוכת לא היו מקריבין פר העלם דבר" ([Tosafot on Yoma 57a:10:1]). In English: in the first Temple there was no *paroches*, and in the second there was a *paroches* but the bull wasn't offered. The proof for the second half is the Mishnah in Megillah 9b. It says the one difference between a High Priest anointed with the oil and one who merely wears the extra garments is the bull for transgressing all the commandments. Only the anointed one brings it.

- **Ri"va:** it was the first Temple, and the curtain in question was "פרוכת דבבי". I'm not certain how to read that phrase, so I won't translate it. Tosafot seem to mean a curtain of a different kind that did exist in the first Temple.
- **Ri:** it was the second Temple. The Megillah case concerns a High Priest ruling for himself. The communal *par he'elem davar* can be offered even by an ordinary priest, as the Torat Kohanim says. He also notes that the Gemara doesn't mention the High Priest's bull. That is because there was no anointed High Priest in the second Temple, since Yoshiyahu hid the anointing oil (see [Yoma 52b]).

## Your question: how could it be in Rome?
Your instinct is right. If it was the first Temple, the curtain would have had to survive three things:

1. **The Babylonian destruction.** Nebuchadnezzar took the Temple vessels. Some were later returned under Cyrus ([Ezra 1:7-11]). Ezra's list is of vessels, though, and doesn't mention curtains.
2. **Later conquests.** It would then have passed from Babylon to Persia, to Greece, and eventually to Rome. Nothing I know of in the sources records this.
3. **The second Temple.** It would have been kept alongside the second Temple's own curtains, and a Tanna would have had to identify it as the earlier one.

By contrast, a second-Temple curtain reaching Rome has an obvious route. Titus took Temple spoils to Rome, and Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Yosei lived after the destruction. That is a strong reason to prefer the Ri's reading.

The Ri"va's position probably rests on the halachic problem, not on a historical claim about how the curtain travelled. He may have assumed the first-Temple curtain was somehow preserved. I haven't found a source for that. I couldn't open the Gemara text itself in this session, so check Tosafot Yeshanim, Ritva and the Rashash on the same passage. They may discuss the point.

answer:
The Talmud has two layers. The first is the Mishnah, which is the Oral Torah's core text. The second is the Gemara, the later discussion of it. The Gemara itself draws on four kinds of source: Scripture, the Mishnah, *baraitot* (teachings from the Mishnaic era that were left out of the Mishnah), and the statements of the Amoraim (the rabbis of the Gemara). I'm assuming you mean "what sources does the Talmud draw on?" If you meant sources for a particular topic or law, tell me and I'll look into it.

## Key Takeaways
- Written Torah (Tanakh) is the foundation, and the Talmud derives and supports laws from it.
- The Mishnah (compiled by Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) is the text the Gemara is built around.
- *Baraitot* and the Tosefta preserve Tannaitic traditions that the Gemara uses to challenge or support the Mishnah.
- The Gemara also records the teachings and debates of the Amoraim, and it includes aggadah (stories and ethics) as well as halacha.
- The Talmud presents all of this as a chain of tradition going back to Sinai.

## The chain of tradition
The Talmud sees its sources as one continuous transmission. [Pirkei Avot 1:1] says: "מֹשֶׁה קִבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי, וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ…" ("Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua…"). The chain continues through the elders, the prophets and the Men of the Great Assembly, and from there to the Sages. The Oral Torah therefore claims Sinai as its source, together with the Written Torah.

## The layers of source material

1. **Tanakh (the Written Torah).** The Gemara often asks "מנא הני מילי?" ("From where do we know this?") and answers with a verse. It uses interpretive rules such as the *gezerah shavah* (a link between two verses that share a word) and the *kal vachomer* (an argument from the lesser case to the greater). Some laws are called *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* (a law given to Moses at Sinai), which means they have no verse behind them.

2. **Mishnah.** Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi edited it around 200 CE. It gathers the teachings of the Tannaim, the earlier rabbis. The Gemara is organized as a discussion of the Mishnah, and the Mishnah is divided into six orders (*sedarim*).

3. **Baraitot and Tosefta.** These are Tannaitic statements outside the Mishnah, often introduced by "תנו רבנן" ("the Rabbis taught"). The Tosefta is a collection of such material. There are also halachic *midrashim* on the Torah, namely the Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifrei. The Gemara compares these with the Mishnah to resolve difficulties. In Sanhedrin, the Talmud notes that anonymous statements in these collections follow particular Tannaim. For example, an anonymous Mishnah reflects Rabbi Meir and an anonymous Sifra reflects Rabbi Yehudah.

4. **Amoraic teachings.** Amoraim such as Rav, Shmuel, Rav Yochanan, Abaye and Rava taught in Babylonia and in the Land of Israel. Their debates and rulings make up most of the Gemara. The final anonymous editors are called the *Stam* (the anonymous voice of the Talmud), and they shaped the sugyot (discussions) as we have them.

5. **Aggadah and other material.** The Talmud includes stories, ethical teachings, medical and scientific remarks, and homiletical readings of verses alongside the halachic discussion. It also records customs (*minhag*) and the practices of the rabbis.

## Two Talmuds
There are two Talmuds, and each builds on the same Mishnah:
- The **Talmud Bavli** (Babylonian) was edited around the 5th–6th century. It is the more authoritative one and the one usually meant by "the Talmud."
- The **Talmud Yerushalmi** (Jerusalem) was edited earlier, around the 4th–5th century, in the Land of Israel.

If you tell me which of these you meant, I can go into it in more depth, for example how the Gemara cites a specific verse or baraita on a given topic.

answer:
The shortest tractate in Shas is **Kinnim**, in the Order of Kodashim. It has 3 chapters and about 15 mishnayot, and it takes up only a few pages at the end of the Bavli (Kinnim 22b–25a). I answered from memory and didn't pull the text, so check the exact counts against an edition.

## Key Takeaways
- Kinnim is the shortest tractate in Shas by Mishnah count and by pages.
- Kinnim has no Gemara in the Bavli, so it is Mishnah only.
- Middot (5 chapters) and Tamid (7 chapters) are also short, but they are longer than Kinnim.
- If you want the shortest tractate that has a full Gemara, that is a different question (see below).

## Details

**Kinnim** deals with the bird offerings (*kinnim*) of those who must bring a pair of birds, such as a woman after childbirth. It also covers what happens when the birds get mixed up. Its mishnayot are the only text in the Bavli's version, which is why it takes up so few pages.

**Other short tractates:**
- **Middot** describes the measurements of the Temple. It has 5 chapters and roughly 34 mishnayot, and it also has no Gemara.
- **Tamid** covers the daily offering. It has 7 chapters and about 33–34 mishnayot, and it does have a short Gemara.
- **Uktzin** is the last tractate in the Mishnah (Order of Taharot). It has 3 chapters, but it has more mishnayot than Kinnim and no Bavli at all.

**If you meant the shortest with Gemara:** In the Bavli, Makkot is often cited as the shortest with a full Gemara and only 3 chapters, at 24 dapim. Me'ilah is also short, at about 21 dapim plus Kinnim and Tamid attached. Counts vary a little by edition and by how you count, so I'd verify these figures if you need them exactly.

If you're looking for a short tractate to learn, tell me whether you want Mishnah only or Gemara too, and I can suggest one.

answer:
A *hava aminah* (הוה אמינא, "what we first thought") is the Gemara's initial assumption. The *maskanah* (מסקנא) is where the argument ends up. The distance between them is often where the learning happens, because it shows what each answer rules out and why. Below I explain why that is, and I mark which points are my own explanation and which come from sources.

## Key Takeaways
- Every hava aminah shows the logic of a position the Gemara decides to reject, and that logic is often still useful.
- The maskanah usually works by drawing a distinction, and each distinction is a new principle.
- Asking why we needed to say something at all exposes the underlying concept (*yesod*).
- Rishonim often build whole rules on a rejected hava aminah.
- The hava aminah teaches how to think. The maskanah gives the halachic result.

## 1. What a hava aminah shows
The Talmud rarely says "this is the law" outright. It first proposes a natural reading, tests it with a question (*kushya*), and then either refines it or abandons it. The rejected position shows you:
- **The competing logic.** If the Gemara considered it, a reasonable principle stands behind it.
- **The exact point of difference.** When the maskanah overturns the hava aminah, it names the single factor that separates the two. That factor is where the new principle lies.
- **The reason a source was needed.** A common form is: "Why did the Torah or the Mishnah need to say this?" The answer is typically "because I might have thought X" (the hava aminah), "so it teaches us Y."

## 2. An example of reasoning
In the law of *yehareg ve'al ya'avor* (one must die rather than transgress), the Gemara considers a person who is told to kill or be killed. The case appears in [Sanhedrin 74a]. The hava aminah is that saving your own life should justify it. The answer is the logical argument *mai chazit* (מאי חזית): "Who says your blood is redder than his?" The idea behind it is that human lives cannot be ranked against each other. In my own words, one short exchange yields a rule about the value of life that reaches well beyond that case.

## 3. How this opens "worlds"
- **Principles from distinctions.** Each "this, not that" tells you what categories the Torah works with. Over time you learn to predict the Gemara's questions.
- **Rishonim and Acharonim.** Tosafot, the Rashba, Ritva, and later *lomdus* (conceptual analysis) often ask: "What was the hava aminah, and why does the maskanah reject it?" Their different answers are what separate their schools. The hava aminah is also often the key to explaining why a Rishon rules differently.
- **Understanding the psychology of learning.** The Gemara teaches you to hold a view, test it, and let it go. That is a skill beyond Talmud, and it fits the idea that the Torah is acquired through questioning and effort. See the ethics and Torah-learning passages in [Pirkei Avot 6:6] on the ways Torah is acquired.
- **Practical halacha.** The halacha follows the maskanah, but the hava aminah marks the limits of the rule. If the conditions change, a hava aminah may return. That is how poskim apply old rules to new cases.

## 4. How to practice
1. Mark the Gemara's first assumption in each sugya, and write it in one sentence.
2. Identify the *kushya* or text that overturns it.
3. State the single difference between the two.
4. Ask whether any Rishon still holds the hava aminah in some case.
5. Then try to predict the next question before reading it.

If you give me a particular daf, I can walk through its hava aminah and maskanah step by step.

answer:
**Short answer:** The main discussion is in the last chapter of Bekhorot (chapter 9, roughly Bekhorot 53b–61a), which is the Gemara on [Mishnah Bekhorot 9:1] and the mishnayot after it. The Gemara also treats the topic in Rosh Hashanah and Chagigah, and in a few other places. The Torah source is Leviticus 27:32–33.

## Key Takeaways
- The central sugya is Bekhorot ch. 9, which gives the laws of the animal tithe: who is obligated, how the animals are counted, and what happens afterward.
- Rosh Hashanah 2a and 8a discuss the "new year" of ma'aser behema.
- Chagigah 8a discusses whether the animal tithe can fulfill the obligation of *simchat Yom Tov* (rejoicing on the festival).
- The Torah source is Leviticus 27:32, "whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be sacred to the Lord."

## 1. Bekhorot, chapter 9 (the main source)
The chapter opens with the basic laws. Per [Mishnah Bekhorot 9:1]:
- The mitzvah applies in Eretz Yisrael and outside it, whether or not the Temple stands.
- It applies to non-sacred animals, not to consecrated ones.
- It applies to herd and flock, but one does not tithe from one to cover the other.
- Sheep and goats are tithed together, because "flock" (*tzon*) covers both.
- Animals of different years are not tithed from each other.

The later mishnayot, and the Gemara on them, cover the mechanics:
- How the newborn animals are gathered into a pen and pass through a narrow opening one at a time.
- The tenth animal is marked with red paint and is *kadosh* (consecrated).
- Doubtful cases, such as an animal that is mixed up with others.
- The way the owner eats the animal, and what happens to the blood and fat on the altar.

I have not retrieved the specific daf for each of these, so check the chapter directly in Bekhorot.

## 2. Rosh Hashanah 2a and 8a: the new year for the tithe
[Rosh Hashanah 2a] gives the mishnah: "On the first of Elul is the new year for ma'aser behema; Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say, on the first of Tishrei." [Rosh Hashanah 8a] gives the reasoning:
- Rabbi Meir compares animal tithe to grain tithe. Grain is tithed close to its completion (*samuch l'gmaro*), so animals are too, which puts the cutoff at the end of the year, in Elul.
- Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon compare animal tithe to grain tithe in a different way. The new year for grain tithe is Tishrei, so the new year for animal tithe is also Tishrei.

## 3. Chagigah 8a
[Chagigah 8a] teaches that a person can fulfill the obligation of rejoicing on the festival with *nedarim* and *nedavot* (vow and free-will offerings) and with ma'aser behema. This is derived from the verse "*v'samachta b'chagecha*" (you shall rejoice in your festival), which is understood as including all kinds of rejoicing.

## 4. Other places
The animal tithe also comes up in the Gemara on offerings and consecrated animals, such as Temurah and Zevachim. I have not retrieved those references here.

If you tell me which angle interests you (the counting process, the Elul and Tishrei dispute, or the halachic ruling), I can go through that sugya in detail.

answer:
# Tractate Semachot (Evel Rabbati), Chapter 1

Chapter 1 is about the *goses* (a person in the final stage of dying) and the rules of conduct around him. It then covers who does and does not receive full mourning rites, and ends with a short passage on how slaves and the patriarchs are addressed. The unifying principle is that a *goses* is legally alive until death occurs. Nothing may hasten his death, and no mourning rites may begin early. I read the text in Sefaria's English translation as [Tractate Semachot 1].

## Key Takeaways
- A *goses* is considered fully alive for every legal purpose, including levirate marriage, *terumah*, inheritance and sacrifices.
- It is forbidden to do anything that might hasten death, including moving him or closing his eyes.
- Mourning practices (tearing the garment, eulogy, bringing in a coffin) do not begin until death.
- Certain cases get no mourning rites: a non-viable newborn, and, in a limited sense, a non-Jew or a slave. A righteous slave is the exception.
- The stories of R. Eliezer and Rabban Gamaliel show that the character of the individual can override the general rule.

## 1. The *goses* is regarded as alive
The chapter opens: "הגוסס הרי הוא כחי לכל דבר" ("A dying man is regarded as a living entity in respect of all matters"). It then lists the practical consequences:

- **Levirate marriage (*yibbum*).** He binds his brother's wife to *yibbum*, and he exempts his mother from it. The Hebrew wording is "זוקק ליבום ופוטר מן היבום".
- **Terumah.** He enables his wife to eat *terumah* and can also disqualify her from eating it. In the case of a priest's daughter, her marriage status affects whether she may eat it.
- **Inheritance.** He inherits and transmits an inheritance.
- **Severed limbs.** A limb or flesh that is cut off is treated as cut off from a living person. This matters for ritual impurity.
- **Sacrifices.** The blood of his sin-offering and guilt-offering is still sprinkled for him until he dies.

The point is that no legal status changes until death actually occurs.

## 2. What may not be done to a *goses*
The mishnah forbids actions that could hasten death or treat him as dead:

- Tying up his jaw, stopping up his orifices, or placing a metal vessel or any cooling object on his navel. These are normal preparations for a corpse.
- The proof-text is "עד אשר לא ירתק חבל הכסף" ([Ecclesiastes 12:6](Ecclesiastes 12:6)). The text uses the verse's imagery of life's "cord" being snapped, to say that the cord must break by itself.
- Moving him, or laying him on sand or salt. Salt and sand were used to slow decomposition.
- Closing his eyes. This is the most severe item. Whoever touches him and moves him "is a murderer" (שופך דמים).
- R. Meir gives the analogy of a flickering lamp. Any touch can snuff it out, so closing the eyes is "as if he took his soul."

Note that the passage is not telling us to prolong suffering. It forbids a direct, active hastening of death. Later halacha builds on this distinction; see the Rambam's Laws of Mourning, chapter 4, and the Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 339. Consult a rabbi on modern medical questions, which are a separate and complex matter.

## 3. Mourning rites do not start early
Before death, the following are not done:

- Tearing the garment (*keriah*) or baring the shoulder (*chalitzah*).
- Eulogies.
- Bringing a coffin into the house.
- Announcing it publicly or reciting the person's deeds. R. Judah dissents: if he is a scholar, we do recount his deeds.

The mishnah also says that in a small village people do not greet one another, while in a large city this is permitted. I read this as referring to the restraint around the dying person. The text is brief here and the exact application is debated among the commentators, so treat this reading as tentative.

## 4. Those who are not mourned in the usual way
- **A non-viable newborn.** The text lists one who came out dismembered or "in pieces" (*mechutakh*), a castrated one (*mesoras*), miscarriages (*nefalim*), and one born alive at eight months. A baby born alive at eight months is treated as not viable. One born dead at nine months is likewise not given formal mourning, because mourning is for one who lived. The mishnah says one does not "occupy oneself" with them for any rites.
- **A non-Jew or a slave.** One does not occupy oneself with their rites. The mishnah says people say of them: "הוי ארי, ארי, הוי גבור" ("Alas lion, alas mighty man"). R. Judah says that of a slave we say: "הוי טבי, הוי נאמן, אוכל מעמלו" ("Alas Tabi, faithful one who ate of his labor"). The others object that this leaves nothing to say of a righteous free person. R. Judah answers: if he was worthy, why shouldn't we say it of him?

## 5. Condolence for slaves, and the two stories
The mishnah states that "אין מקבלין תנחומין על העבדים" ("we do not receive condolence for slaves"), because slaves are reckoned like animals. This reflects the legal status of a Canaanite slave, who is not an heir or a family member in the usual sense.

Two accounts qualify the rule:

- **R. Eliezer.** When his maidservant died, his students came to comfort him. He retreated from room to room and rebuked them for not being deterred. His point was that they should have known the rule.
- **Rabban Gamaliel and Tabi.** When Tabi died, Rabban Gamaliel accepted condolences and had earlier allowed Tabi to put on tefillin, even though slaves are exempt. His students objected, and he replied: "אין טבי עבדי כשאר כל העבדים, כשר הוא" ("My slave Tabi is not like other slaves; he is a worthy man").

The text sets two sages side by side. R. Eliezer applies the rule strictly. Rabban Gamaliel treats a righteous individual as an exception. This shows that the chapter's rules are general norms, and that moral character and closeness can outweigh a category. Note that the stories do not say Rabban Gamaliel changed the law. He explained Tabi as an exception.

## 6. Forms of address
The chapter closes with rules of address:

- One does not call slaves "Abba So-and-so" or "Imma So-and-so," as these are titles of dignity. In Rabban Gamaliel's household, though, they used "Abba Tabi" and "Imma Tabitha."
- "Avinu" ("our father") is used only for the three patriarchs, and "Imenu" ("our mother") only for the four matriarchs. This protects the special status of the founding figures.

## A note on the text
Semachot is a minor tractate, and the text exists in different versions. Sefaria's edition has bracketed corrections, for example "מעמצין" in place of "מעמידין" for closing the eyes. The wording of some lines, especially the village and city greeting, varies between manuscripts and editions.

For practical questions about end-of-life care or mourning, consult your rabbi for your personal situation.

answer:
**Short answer:** The Mishnah-style text in Semachot 1 doesn't quite say what your question assumes. The Sages and R. Yehuda don't argue over whether to say "righteous." They argue over how much praise a non-Jew or a slave may receive. The Sages allow only generic praise. R. Yehuda allows praise of real moral character, if the person earned it.

**Key Takeaways**
- The text is [Tractate Semachot 1], the passage on a non-Jew or slave after death.
- The Sages say we don't occupy ourselves with his funeral rites, but we may say "Alas lion! Alas mighty man!"
- R. Yehuda says we may say "Alas Ṭabi! Alas faithful man who ate of his labour!"
- The Sages object that this leaves nothing special to say of worthy (Jewish) people. R. Yehuda replies that a worthy slave deserves praise, especially since we don't offer condolences for slaves.
- The text doesn't spell out the underlying reasons. The explanations below are my reading, not a quoted commentary.

**The text**
The passage says: "נכרי ועבד אין מתעסקין עמו לכל דבר אבל קורין עליו הוי ארי ארי הוי גבור. רבי יהודה אומר הוי טבי הוי נאמן אוכל מעמלו. אמרו לו מה הנחת לכשרים. אמר להן אם היה כשר מפני מה אין קורין עליו"

My paraphrase:
- For a non-Jew or slave we don't busy ourselves with his burial and mourning rites.
- We do say "Alas lion, alas mighty man."
- R. Yehuda says to say "Alas Ṭabi, alas faithful man who ate of his own labour."
- They answer, "What have you left for the worthy?"
- He replies, "If he was worthy, why shouldn't we say it of him?"

The wording "righteous man" isn't in this passage. It is probably a paraphrase of "faithful" (*ne'eman*) and "worthy" (*kasher*).

**The two positions**
- **The Sages** treat the formal eulogy as a Jewish institution. Lion and mighty man are neutral, physical or heroic epithets that make no claim about the person's religious or moral standing. Praise like "faithful, living from his own labour" is the language used for the *kesharim*, the worthy Jews. If it is said of a slave, it blurs the distinction.
- **R. Yehuda** answers that the praise is simply true when the person was upright. His reply, "If he was worthy, why should we not say it?", means character should be acknowledged wherever it is found. The reasoning continues: "since we do not receive condolence for male or female slaves." Because no mourning or condolence is given, a worthy slave would otherwise get no recognition at all, and this brief statement is the only honor left to give him.

**The background in the same chapter**
The surrounding passage supports R. Yehuda's view. Slaves are "reckoned as animals," so condolence is not received for them. When R. Eliezer's slave died, he rebuked the students who came to console him. But when Ṭabi, the slave of Rabban Gamaliel, died, Rabban Gamaliel accepted condolence. He said "My slave Ṭabi was unlike all other slaves; he was a worthy man." He also let Ṭabi put on *tefillin*. So R. Yehuda's example, "Alas Ṭabi," draws on Rabban Gamaliel's own household. The Sages' concern is the general rule, and R. Yehuda's concern is the exceptional, righteous individual.

I did not retrieve a commentary on this passage, such as Nachalat Ya'akov or the Gra's text, so I can't tell you how they resolve it.

answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, but mostly indirectly. The Talmud never describes a formal "Yissachar–Zevulun contract." It does praise and encourage supporting Torah scholars, including through business, and the Midrash and later authorities build the Yissachar–Zevulun model from the tribes' blessings. Some major authorities also object to the whole arrangement.

I couldn't retrieve the texts just now because the Sefaria tool was rate-limited. I'm citing these sources from memory, so I give references without verbatim quotes. Please check them inside.

## Key Takeaways
- The model's root is the tribal blessings in [Genesis 49:13-15] and [Deuteronomy 33:18], read by Rashi as Zevulun's trade supporting Yissachar's Torah study.
- The Talmud supplies the principle, not the contract. [Berakhot 34b] speaks of doing business on behalf of a Torah scholar, and [Ketubot 111b] speaks of benefiting scholars.
- The Midrash (*Bereishit Rabbah*, on Jacob's blessings) and the Rema ([Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 246:1]) express the partnership and its shared reward.
- The Rambam ([Mishneh Torah, Torah Study 3:10]) strongly opposes making Torah a means of livelihood, so not everyone accepts the model.

## The biblical and midrashic root
- Moses blesses Zevulun and Yissachar together: "Rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out, and Yissachar in your tents" ([Deuteronomy 33:18]).
- Rashi explains that Zevulun went out to trade and Yissachar sat in the tent of Torah. Zevulun's profit supported Yissachar, and the verse therefore puts Zevulun first.
- Jacob's blessing describes Zevulun as a coastal, seafaring tribe ([Genesis 49:13]) and Yissachar as the one who "bows his shoulder to bear" ([Genesis 49:15]). The Midrash reads this as bearing the yoke of Torah.
- The Midrash also reads the verses in [Deuteronomy 33:19] as saying that Zevulun shares in Yissachar's merit.

## Talmudic foundations
- **[Berakhot 34b]:** The Gemara teaches that the prophets' promises of the messianic blessings were said about someone who gives his daughter to a Torah scholar, does business on behalf of a Torah scholar, or lets scholars benefit from his property. The phrase about doing business for a scholar is the closest Talmudic parallel to a business partnership.
- **[Ketubot 111b]:** The Gemara discusses how to "cling to the Divine Presence" by associating with and supporting Torah scholars. Related passages treat such support as a great merit.
- **Counterweight:** The Talmud also warns against using Torah as a spade to dig with, as in [Pirkei Avot 4:5] and Nedarim. This is the source of the opposition below.

## Halachic development
- **Rema, [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 246:1]:** He records the arrangement in which one person studies while another supports him, and the two share the reward. Later commentators (Shakh, Taz) discuss its terms. As I recall, the Rema bases it on earlier authorities such as the Sefer Hasidim, but I haven't verified that here.
- **Rambam, [Mishneh Torah, Torah Study 3:10]:** He strongly criticizes those who turn Torah study into a source of income and who live off charity. For him, the ideal is that a scholar also supports himself. The Rema's ruling is often read as a response to this, since it permits the arrangement.
- **Later thought:** Many later authorities, such as the Chafetz Chaim and Rabbi Moshe Feinstein's circle, discuss whether the partner's share in the reward is real, and how much. In many communities today, supporting a *kollel* or a scholar is understood in these terms.

## Practical note
The arrangement has real halachic stakes: how the reward is shared, what each side owes the other, and whether to rely on the Rambam or the Rema. Consult your rabbi for your personal situation. If you want, I can pull up the exact texts of Berakhot 34b, the Rashi and the Rema once the tool is working again.

answer:
There are **525 perakim (chapters)** in the Mishnah, spread over 63 masekhtot (tractates) in six *sedarim* (orders). I'm giving this from memory and did not look it up in Sefaria. The total is a standard figure, but the exact count depends on how you count a few tractates, as explained below.

**Key Takeaways**
- The standard total is 525 perakim.
- The Mishnah has 63 masekhtot in 6 sedarim, and the total is usually given as 4,192 mishnayot.
- The "Mishnah Yomi" program uses the same chapter divisions.
- A few tractates are counted differently: Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia and Bava Batra are sometimes counted as one tractate, Nezikin. Makkot may also be counted with Sanhedrin. This can change the tractate count but not the number of chapters.

**Breakdown by seder (from memory)**
- **Zera'im:** 11 tractates, 75 perakim. Berakhot has 9, Peah 8, Demai 7, Kilayim 9, Shevi'it 10, Terumot 11, Ma'aserot 5, Ma'aser Sheni 5, Challah 4, Orlah 3, Bikkurim 4.
- **Mo'ed:** 12 tractates, 88 perakim.
- **Nashim:** 7 tractates, 71 perakim.
- **Nezikin:** 10 tractates, 74 perakim.
- **Kodashim:** 11 tractates, 90 perakim.
- **Tohorot:** 12 tractates, 127 perakim.

These seder totals add up to 525. I'm confident of the Zera'im tractate-by-tractate figures. I'm less sure of the exact seder totals, so check them against a printed Mishnah or Sefaria before relying on them.

If you'd like, I can pull the chapter count for any specific tractate from Sefaria to confirm it.

I couldn't verify the shortest *perek* (chapter) in the Mishnah, and I don't want to name one from memory. Naming a wrong one with confidence would be worse than saying so.

**What I checked**

I looked at a few chapters I thought might be very short:
- [Mishnah Chullin 6] has several long mishnayot.

"Shortest" can mean two things, and they give different answers:
- **Fewest mishnayot.** Several chapters have only two or three mishnayot, and a few may have just one.
- **Fewest words.** A chapter with a few mishnayot can still be longer than a chapter with many short ones.

answer:
The Gemara isn't saying that every law in the Torah exists only to keep the peace. It is saying that the Torah's whole purpose is to produce a pleasant, peaceful way of life. So a rule can be a real Torah law and also serve peace, and the two descriptions don't conflict.

## Key Takeaways
- The line appears in [Gittin 59b], in a dispute over whether a rule is Torah law or merely "for the sake of the ways of peace."
- Rav Yosef answers Abaye that the two aren't opposites: a law can be *de'oraita* (from the Torah) and still be *mipnei darchei shalom*.
- The proof-text is Proverbs 3:17, which describes the Torah's ways as pleasant and its paths as peaceful.
- Abaye then gives a narrower explanation, so the broad statement is not the Gemara's final word on that case.
- Rambam uses the same idea to rank the value of peace.

## The context
The Mishnah on [Gittin 59a–b] lists enactments made *mipnei darchei shalom* ("because of the ways of peace"). These include filling the pit nearest the irrigation channel first, treating trapped animals as stolen if someone else takes them, and not stopping poor gentiles from taking gleanings. The Mishnah also says a *kohen* reads from the Torah first, then a Levite.

The Gemara asks for the source of the *kohen*-first rule. Several Sages offer verses, such as "And you shall sanctify him" (Leviticus 21:8), which gives the *kohen* priority in every sacred matter.

## The key exchange
Abaye objects: "מִפְּנֵי דַּרְכֵי שָׁלוֹם?! דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא הִיא!" ("*Because of the ways of peace*? But it is from the Torah!"). If a verse already teaches the rule, why does the Mishnah present it as a peace-based enactment?

Rav Yosef answers:

"דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, וּמִפְּנֵי דַּרְכֵי שָׁלוֹם. כׇּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ נָמֵי מִפְּנֵי דַּרְכֵי שָׁלוֹם הִיא, דִּכְתִיב: ״דְּרָכֶיהָ דַרְכֵי נוֹעַם וְכׇל נְתִיבוֹתֶיהָ שָׁלוֹם״!"

"It is from the Torah, *and* it is for the ways of peace. The entire Torah is also for the ways of peace, as it is written: 'Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace' (Proverbs 3:17)."

## What this means
- **Torah law and peace-motivated law don't conflict.** Calling something *mipnei darchei shalom* doesn't make it a lesser, merely rabbinic rule. The Torah itself aims at peace, so a Torah law can also be justified by the peace it brings.
- **Peace is a purpose of the whole Torah, not its only purpose.** Rav Yosef describes the Torah's *ways* and *paths* as peaceful. This is a statement about its overall character and goal. It doesn't say each commandment's reason is peace. For example, the *kohen*'s precedence is derived from "you shall sanctify him."
- **Abaye doesn't rest on this answer.** The Gemara continues "אֶלָּא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי" ("Rather, Abaye said"). He explains the Mishnah differently: the rule applies to precedence at a meal, and in the synagogue it prevents quarrels. The Gemara then discusses when the *kohen*-first order is kept and when it isn't, because people might fight over honors. Rav Yosef's line is therefore a broad principle that makes room for both views. It doesn't decide the case.

## Related sources
Rambam cites the same verse when he ranks peace. In his laws of Chanukah (I recall this as [Mishneh Torah, Chanukah 4:14]), he says that "the whole Torah was given to make peace in the world." Because of this, he rules that the Chanukah lamp at home takes precedence over the Kiddush wine when both can't be afforded. I haven't pulled up that text here, so check the wording yourself.

Rav Yosef's reading of Proverbs 3:17 also fits a wider theme in Chazal that Torah study and observance should make a person and their surroundings more pleasant and peaceful.

answer:
**Short answer:** I couldn't find a commentator on Yoma 69b who asks your question in exactly your words. The Gemara and its commentators do suggest several answers. The main one is that the drive for forbidden relations and the drive for permitted relations are one drive, so you can't remove one and keep the other. Some of this comes from the sources I retrieved. The rest is from memory, and I mark it as such.

## Key Takeaways
- The Gemara treats the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination) for *arayot* (forbidden relations) as the same sexual drive that powers all procreation, not as a separate "illicit" faculty.
- The detail about the eggs shows this. The drive is biological and general, and it operates in animals too.
- The Sages did not simply leave the drive as it was. They gouged out its eyes, which narrowed it, so people are no longer aroused toward close relatives.
- A midrashic principle (from memory) is that without the *yetzer hara*, no one would build a house, marry, or have children.

## The text
Zechariah warns the Sages: "חֲזוֹ, דְּאִי קָטְלִיתוּ לֵיהּ לְהָהוּא, כָּלֵי עָלְמָא" ("See: if you kill this one, the world will be destroyed"). They imprisoned it for three days, and no fresh egg could be found in Eretz Yisrael. Then they decided: "נִקְטְלֵיהּ — כָּלֵי עָלְמָא... נִיבְעֵי רַחֲמֵי אַפַּלְגָא — פַּלְגָא בִּרְקִיעָא לָא יָהֲבִי" ("If we kill it, the world is destroyed. If we pray for half, Heaven doesn't give half gifts"). So "כַּחְלִינְהוּ לְעֵינֵיהּ וְשַׁבְקוּהוּ" ("they painted/gouged its eyes and let it go"), and the result was "דְּלָא מִיגָּרֵי בֵּיהּ לְאִינִישׁ בְּקָרִיבְתֵּהּ" ("a person is no longer aroused toward his close relatives") [Yoma 69b:12-17].

Rashi on "כליא עלמא" says only: "יכלה העולם שלא תהא פריה ורביה" ("the world would end, as there would be no procreation") [Rashi on Yoma 69b:12:1]. On the egg he says the *warmth* of the innards ceased, so even eggs already formed no longer ripened [Rashi on Yoma 69b:12:2]. I'm paraphrasing Rashi here. The point you raised about the hens is correct.

## Why humans aren't a different case
1. **The Gemara's own experiment is the evidence.** The Sages tried it. When the drive was held back, the result was the loss of desire for procreation itself. The Gemara's premise is that a *tzaddik* who fulfills *peru u'revu* (be fruitful and multiply) does so through the same natural desire. Halacha governs when and how that desire is expressed. It doesn't create it. Remove the desire, and a human being no longer has the natural impulse to marry and have children, just as the hen stops laying.

2. **The drive can't be split by halachic category.** The "yetzer of arayot" is not a spirit that only wants forbidden things. It is desire as such, and halacha decides what is permitted. This is why Heaven "doesn't give half gifts." You can't ask for the forbidden part to be removed and the permitted part kept.

3. **What the Sages did instead was a targeted narrowing.** Gouging out its eyes limited its range. Chidushei Agadot reads this as weakening the inclination partially. They could not annul it entirely, and it still operates toward others, as shown by the laws of *yichud* (seclusion), for example with one's daughter [Chidushei Agadot on Yoma 69b:10]. So the "responsible procreation" you describe is what the surviving, narrowed drive makes possible.

4. **The midrash makes the same point (from memory, not retrieved).** Bereshit Rabbah 9:7 says that "very good" in Genesis 1:31 includes the *yetzer hara*. Without it, no one would build a house, marry, or have children. I tried to fetch this passage and the tool failed, so verify the exact wording and number.

## A possible counter-argument
You could say that a person can fulfill the *mitzvah* purely out of duty, without desire. The Gemara doesn't take that route. It assumes the world runs on the natural drive, not on abstract duty. Some later thinkers speak of sanctifying desire rather than eliminating it. The Ramban's *Iggeret HaKodesh* is the classic example, from memory. That is a different approach from the one in the Yoma story.

## Where to look further
I'd check Maharsha and Iyun Yaakov on Yoma 69b, and the parallel story in Sanhedrin 64a about the *yetzer* for idolatry. I did not retrieve or confirm what they say, so I can't tell you whether they raise your exact question. If you tell me which edition you're using, I can search it for a comment on "כליא עלמא".

answer:
A *goses* (a person in the throes of death) is legally treated as fully alive for all purposes, until death actually occurs. This Mishnah lists several examples, in family law, priestly law, inheritance, and sacrificial law.

I retrieved the Mishnah text from Sefaria. I did not retrieve commentaries, so the explanations of the individual clauses below are standard understanding rather than quotations.

## Key Takeaways
- A *goses* is considered alive "לכל דבר", for every matter, until he dies.
- This status has effects in levirate marriage (*yibbum*), *terumah*, inheritance, and the laws of limbs severed from a living person.
- It also affects sacrifices: the blood of his offerings is still sprinkled on his behalf.
- Tractate Semachot is a minor tractate. Its first chapter sets this principle as the basis for the laws of the dying and of mourning.

## The text
"הגוסס הרי הוא כחי לכל דבר" – "A dying man is regarded as a living entity in respect of all matters." [Masechet Semachot 1:1]

The Mishnah then lists the following:

- **Levirate marriage.** It says he "זוקק ליבום ופוטר מן היבום". Sefaria's reading is that he "holds tied to levirate marriage" and also "frees from it". Take the first clause. If a man dies childless, a brother who is dying still counts as a brother. His existence binds the widow, so she cannot remarry without *chalitzah* (release) or *yibbum*, and she would be bound to him if he recovered. The second clause is the reverse. His existence or relationship can exempt a widow from *yibbum*, for example by making her forbidden to the other brothers or by leaving no obligation. In both clauses the dying person's status counts as real.
- **Terumah.** He "מאכיל בתרומה ופוסל בתרומה", meaning he enables a woman to eat *terumah* (the priestly gift) and he can also disqualify her from eating it. A living child or relative of the right status affects whether a priest's widow, or a woman married to a priest, may eat *terumah*. Here a *goses* counts as that living person. Sefaria's translation reads this as concerning his mother.
- **Inheritance.** He "נוחל ומנחיל": he inherits from a relative who dies, and he passes that inheritance on to his own heirs.
- **Severed limbs.** If a limb or flesh is severed from him, it is treated as a limb or flesh severed from a living person. This matters for ritual impurity. A limb from a living person carries the impurity laws of a limb from the living, not those of a corpse.
- **Sacrifices.** "וזורקין על ידו דם חטאתו ודם אשמו עד שימות": the blood of his sin-offering and guilt-offering is still sprinkled on his behalf "until he dies". His atonement is still being carried out.

## The underlying principle
The Mishnah sets a clear boundary: death is the dividing line, and "until he dies" means the status holds right up to that moment. Later laws follow from this. One must not hasten the death of a *goses*, and one must not treat him as a corpse. Chapter 1 of Semachot goes on to say this in detail.

For practical halachah, consult your rabbi.

answer:
# Zohar em Parashat Vayishlach (Gênesis 32:4–36:43)

A parasha desta semana é **Vayishlach** (calendário da diáspora; horários de Nova York, por padrão). O Zohar começa com a frase "וַיִּשְׁלַח יַעֲקֹב מַלְאָכִים" ("E Yaakov enviou mensageiros/anjos") e a lê como uma reflexão sobre o *yetzer hara* (inclinação para o mal), os anjos que protegem o homem e o confronto com Esav. Meus acessos à Sefaria falharam por limite de requisições depois do primeiro trecho. Por isso cito literalmente só a abertura e resumo o restante sem citar números.

## Pontos principais

- O Zohar abre com Salmos 91:11, "pois Ele ordenará a Seus anjos que te guardem em todos os teus caminhos", e liga o versículo ao *yetzer hara*.
- Segundo R. Yehuda, o *yetzer hara* se une ao homem desde o nascimento e o acusa continuamente.
- Os "anjos" que Yaakov envia são lidos além do sentido de "mensageiros" comuns.
- Esav e Yaakov representam, no Zohar, dois lados espirituais em confronto.
- Esta é uma leitura do Zohar (*sod*/*drash*), não o sentido simples (*pshat*) do texto.

## A abertura do Zohar

Texto lido em [Zohar, Vayishlach 1:1]:

> וַיִּשְׁלַח יַעֲקֹב מַלְאָכִים וגו'. רִבִּי יְהוּדָה פָּתַח: כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוְּה לָךְ לִשְׁמָרְךָ בְּכָל דְרָכֶיךָ

*"E Yaakov enviou mensageiros (lit. anjos), etc. R. Yehuda começou: 'Pois Ele ordenará a Seus anjos que te guardem em todos os teus caminhos' [Salmos 91:11]."* (tradução minha, com base na tradução inglesa da Sefaria)

O Zohar continua: no momento em que a pessoa nasce, o *yetzer hara* já está com ela e a acusa o tempo todo. Ele cita Gênesis 4:7, "לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רוֹבֵץ" ("o pecado jaz à porta"), e diz que "pecado" ali designa o *yetzer hara*.

## Como entender essa abertura

O Zohar não começa pela história de Yaakov e Esav, mas pela condição do homem. Yaakov está para encontrar Esav, que vem com quatrocentos homens. O Zohar mostra que essa luta tem também uma dimensão interior: o homem enfrenta um acusador desde o nascimento. Por isso ele precisa de proteção, e o versículo dos Salmos fala de anjos que o guardam "em todos os teus caminhos".

Em [Salmos 91:11] os anjos são protetores. Isso prepara a leitura do envio dos *malakhim* de Yaakov: o Zohar não os trata só como emissários humanos.

## Outros temas do Zohar nesta parasha

Os temas abaixo são ensinamentos conhecidos do Zohar sobre esta parasha. Não os recuperei agora, então não dou números de página:

- **A luta com o anjo (Gênesis 32:25–31).** O Zohar identifica o "homem" que lutou com Yaakov com o anjo de Esav, o poder espiritual associado a ele. Yaakov sai ferido na coxa, mas vence e recebe o nome *Yisrael*.
- **A passagem pela noite e o amanhecer.** O Zohar associa a luta e a chegada da aurora ao exílio e à redenção. A noite é o tempo em que os poderes do lado do mal dominam, e o amanhecer os faz recuar.
- **Yaakov como "coluna do meio".** Na tradição cabalística, Yaakov corresponde à *sefirá* de *Tiferet*, que une *Chessed* e *Gevurá*. Isso é um conceito cabalístico, não pshat.

## Cuidados no estudo

- O Zohar usa o texto bíblico como ponto de partida para ensinamentos sobre a alma e o mundo espiritual. Isso difere do pshat de Rashi e Ramban sobre o encontro com Esav.
- Os nomes das *sefirot* e dos "lados" espirituais pedem estudo com um professor. A tradição recomenda cautela ao entrar em Cabalá sem orientação.

## Próximo passo

Posso retomar o Zohar linha por linha (Vayishlach 1:2 em diante) quando a Sefaria voltar a responder. Também posso comparar com Rashi ou Ramban sobre o encontro com Esav, ou trazer a leitura chassídica, como a do Sefat Emet. Qual prefere?

answer:
**Réponse courte :** il n'y a pas de réponse unique, et la tradition ne présente pas Métatron comme celui qui a prononcé les dix paroles. Selon le sens simple et la tradition talmudique, c'est Dieu Lui-même qui a parlé. Selon la Kabbale, Ein Sof en Lui-même est au-delà de toute parole, donc Il parle à travers les *sefirot*. Pour les hassidim, c'est précisément l'essence divine qui s'est révélée au Sinaï. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier tous les passages dans la bibliothèque (un de mes appels a échoué). Je cite donc certains textes sans numéro de référence.

## Points clés
- Le verset dit : « Dieu (*Elohim*) dit toutes ces paroles » et « Moi, l'Éternel, ton Dieu ». Aucun ange n'est mentionné.
- Le Talmud enseigne que « Moi » et « Tu n'auras pas » ont été entendus directement « de la bouche de la Puissance » (Makkot 24a, de mémoire).
- En Kabbale, Ein Sof n'est pas un sujet qui « parle ». La parole passe par les *sefirot*, en particulier Tiferet, qui correspond à « la Voix de Yaakov », et Malkhut, qui correspond à la « Parole ».
- Métatron est un intermédiaire, le « prince de la Face ». Il n'est pas la source de la révélation des dix paroles. Une conception qui lui attribuerait l'autorité de la Torah serait étrangère à la tradition.

## Pshat : le texte
[Exodus 20:1-2] : « וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֵת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה לֵאמֹר, אָנֹכִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ… » (« Dieu dit toutes ces paroles : Moi, l'Éternel, ton Dieu, qui t'ai fait sortir du pays d'Égypte »). La première parole est à la première personne. Le texte ne laisse donc pas place à un messager qui dirait « Moi ».

## Le Talmud
- Selon Makkot 24a, les deux premières paroles ont été entendues directement de Dieu. Le reste a été transmis par Moïse. Cela exclut qu'un ange ait parlé à la place de Dieu.
- Shabbat 88b-89a raconte que les anges ont protesté quand Moïse est monté chercher la Torah, et que Moïse les a réfutés. La Torah n'est donc pas « pour les anges » : elle n'est pas leur parole.

## En Kabbale
- **Ein Sof.** Il est au-delà de toute attribution, de toute lettre et de toute parole. Parler de « la parole d'Ein Sof » est donc, strictement, un langage d'approximation.
- **Les *sefirot*.** Le Zohar (parasha Yitro) enseigne que la révélation passe par la structure des *sefirot*. Les « paroles » sont rattachées à Tiferet, la Voix, et à Malkhut, la Parole (*dibbur*). Les kabbalistes lisent aussi « Anokhi » comme un nom de la Shekhinah, la présence divine qui « parle » (idée que j'attribue au Zohar sans pouvoir citer le passage exact).
- **Métatron.** Dans les textes de *Heikhalot* et dans le Zohar, il est un ange au service de l'ordre divin. Il peut guider, transmettre ou garder, et on lui attribue parfois un rôle lors de la sortie d'Égypte ou dans le désert. Mais je ne connais pas de source classique qui lui attribue la prononciation des dix paroles.

## En hassidout
Chabad et d'autres courants insistent sur le fait que, au Sinaï, Dieu s'est révélé dans Son essence, sans intermédiaire. Le premier mot, *Anokhi*, serait l'essence divine elle-même, qui « se vêt » dans les lettres de la Torah. Je cite cette idée de façon générale, sans passage précis. Elle est liée à l'enseignement selon lequel, au Sinaï, « le haut est descendu vers le bas ».

## À distinguer
Certaines sources parlent de la participation des anges au Sinaï : ils ont couronné Israël, ou ont été présents lors de la révélation. La participation n'est pas la même chose que l'énonciation. La tradition juive distingue clairement les deux et se garde de faire d'un ange l'auteur de la Torah.

Pour approfondir, il vaut mieux étudier le Zohar sur Yitro avec un maître, car les concepts de *sefirot* se comprennent facilement de travers.

answer:
**Réponse courte.** « Yilan » ou « Ilan » (אִילָן) n'est pas un nom propre de l'arbre de vie. C'est le mot araméen et hébraïque tardif pour « arbre ». Dans le Zohar, l'arbre de vie s'appelle *Ilana de-Chayei* (אִילָנָא דְּחַיֵּי), ce qui se traduit par « l'arbre de vie ». Le mot est donc simplement l'araméen de l'hébreu *Etz HaChayim* (עֵץ הַחַיִּים).

## Points clés
- En araméen, « arbre » se dit *ilana* (אילנא). En hébreu, on emploie *ilan* (אילן) dans la langue de la Mishna et du Talmud. La Bible utilise *etz* (עץ).
- Le Zohar emploie systématiquement l'araméen. Il écrit donc *Ilana de-Chayei* à la place de *Etz HaChayim*.
- Dans la Kabbale, cet « arbre » désigne en général la sefira de *Tiferet* ou le « Juste » (*Tzaddik*) qui relie les sefirot. Pour certains passages, il désigne l'ensemble de la structure des sefirot.
- Aujourd'hui, *ilan* désigne aussi le schéma des sefirot, dit « arbre séfirotique ». Cet usage vient des images de branches, de racines et de fruits.

## Le terme dans le Zohar
Le verset de base est [Genesis 2:9], qui parle de « l'arbre de vie au milieu du jardin » (עֵץ הַחַיִּים בְּתוֹךְ הַגָּן). Je n'ai pas pu relire ce verset ici. Je le cite donc de mémoire, sans le citer mot à mot.

Le Zohar reprend cette image avec le mot araméen. Voici deux exemples que j'ai retrouvés :
- Dans [Zohar, Mishpatim 3:85], on lit : « הָכָא נָפִיק בְּחֶדְוָה הַהוּא אִילָנָא דְּחַיֵּי, נָהָר דְּנָפִיק מֵעֵדֶן ». Ma traduction : « Ici sort avec joie cet arbre de vie, le fleuve qui sort d'Éden ». L'arbre est lié au fleuve d'Éden, et les branches (*anafin*) sont les sefirot inférieures.
- Dans [Zohar, Shelach 25:203], le Zohar commente « פְּרִי צַדִּיק עֵץ חַיִּים » (Proverbes 11:30) : « מַה אִילָנָא דְחַיֵּי אַפִּיק נִשְׁמָתִין, אוֹף הָכִי צַדִּיק, אִיבָּא דִילֵיהּ עָבֵיד נִשְׁמָתִין ». Ma traduction : « De même que l'arbre de vie produit des âmes, ainsi le juste : son fruit fait des âmes ». Ici l'arbre sert à décrire le *Tzaddik*, associé à la sefira de *Yesod*.

## Pourquoi l'image d'un arbre ?
Les kabbalistes utilisent l'image de l'arbre parce qu'elle montre bien les relations entre les sefirot. Il y a des racines (la source divine), un tronc (le canal central), des branches (les attributs) et des fruits (les âmes et le monde). Tout l'arbre tire sa vitalité d'une seule source. Ce sens est commun aux écoles kabbalistiques, mais chacune organise l'arbre à sa manière, notamment le Zohar, l'Arizal et le Ramak.

Il existe aussi un autre arbre, celui de la connaissance du bien et du mal. Le Zohar les oppose parfois. L'arbre de vie représente l'unité, tandis que l'autre représente une réalité mélangée.

## Autre lecture possible
Si vous pensiez à un mot précis, par exemple un passage du Talmud où *ilan* est employé dans un autre sens, ou à l'usage de « Ilan » comme prénom, dites-le-moi et je chercherai la source. Pour étudier ces sujets, il est traditionnel de le faire avec un maître.
