answer:
Você pode melhorar seus pensamentos com três hábitos: vigiar o que entra na mente, treinar o pensamento com atos concretos e redirecionar um pensamento ruim em vez de brigar com ele. A tradição judaica trata isso como um trabalho gradual e prático. Ninguém espera que a pessoa tenha só pensamentos puros.

Não consegui abrir os textos no Sefaria agora, por causa de um erro de acesso. Por isso parafraseio as fontes e cito só o versículo que conheço bem.

## Pontos principais

- O coração e a mente precisam de guarda ativa: "Mais do que tudo o que se guarda, guarda o teu coração, pois dele procedem as fontes da vida" (*Provérbios* 4:23).
- Os atos moldam os pensamentos, e não só o contrário.
- Em vez de lutar contra um pensamento negativo, é mais eficaz trocá-lo por outro.
- Estudo, ambiente e companhia influenciam o que você pensa.
- Escolha uma prática pequena e constante, e não uma mudança total de uma vez.

## 1. Guardar a mente (*shmirat hamachshavah*)

O verso de [Proverbs 4:23] diz que "dele [do coração] procedem as fontes da vida". Os pensamentos são a origem das ações e do estado de espírito.

O Rabi Shneur Zalman de Liadi, no *Tanya*, ensina que não controlamos que pensamento surge. Controlamos o que fazemos com ele. Ele dá o exemplo de quem é puxado por um pensamento indesejado: a pessoa não deve brigar com ele de frente, mas desviar a atenção para algo sagrado ou útil, como a Torá. Seu princípio é que a luz afasta a escuridão, e a escuridão não precisa ser combatida.

## 2. Agir para mudar o pensar

O Rambam, em *Hilchot De'ot* (*Mishneh Torah, Human Dispositions*, cap. 1–2), explica que os traços de caráter se corrigem com a prática repetida de ações. Se a pessoa quer ser generosa, deve agir com generosidade até isso se tornar natural. Ele compara o processo a um médico que trata o excesso com o extremo oposto por um tempo e depois volta ao equilíbrio. O Rambam também recomenda procurar a companhia de sábios e bons amigos para se ajustar.

O *Sefer HaChinuch* diz algo parecido: "o coração é puxado atrás das ações". Isso vale para o pensamento também.

## 3. Pensar com confiança (*bitachon*) e gratidão

Muitos pensamentos ruins vêm de ansiedade e de comparação. Os *Chovot HaLevavot* (*Deveres dos Corações*), no "Portão da Confiança", ensinam que confiar em D'us traz descanso à mente. Os Salmos dizem algo semelhante, que as consolações de D'us alegram a alma quando há muitas preocupações no coração ([Psalms 94:19]).

Na prática, os *Pirkei Avot* ([Pirkei Avot 4:1]) dizem que rico é quem se alegra com a sua parte. Praticar gratidão diariamente, como nas bênçãos da manhã e no *Modeh Ani*, muda o padrão do pensamento.

## 4. Preencher a mente com o que é bom

O *Mesilat Yesharim* do Ramchal descreve etapas de crescimento: atenção, cuidado e zelo, e depois pureza. Começa-se observando os próprios pensamentos e ações. Um tempo diário de estudo e de reflexão sobre a conduta é a base dessa observação.

Os mestres do *mussar* recomendam também ouvir e ler coisas edificantes e cuidar do ambiente. O que você vê e ouve alimenta o que você pensa.

## O que fazer esta semana

- **Dez minutos por dia** de estudo ou leitura de mussar, por exemplo um trecho do *Mesilat Yesharim* ou um capítulo dos *Pirkei Avot*.
- **Uma frase de substituição** para quando vier um pensamento negativo, como um verso de salmo ou um pensamento de gratidão.
- **Um ato concreto de bondade por dia**, para que o pensar acompanhe o agir.
- **Um balanço curto à noite**, no estilo do *cheshbon hanefesh* (acerto de contas da alma): "O que me puxou hoje? O que funcionou?"
- **Um amigo ou mestre** com quem conversar.

Se os pensamentos são muito pesados, repetitivos ou causam sofrimento, isso pode ir além de uma questão de mussar. Vale conversar com um rabino, um mentor ou um profissional de saúde mental. A tradição judaica valoriza esse cuidado. Se algum pensamento envolver machucar a si mesmo, procure agora uma pessoa de confiança ou o serviço de emergência da sua região.

Se quiser, posso indicar um texto de mussar para começar, ou aprofundar o trecho do *Tanya*. Também posso ajudar se o problema for um tipo específico de pensamento, como ansiedade, raiva ou inveja.

Изучение Талмуда меняет мышление в трёх связанных отношениях. Оно занимает ум содержательным и святым материалом, который вытесняет пустые и нечистые мысли. Оно приучает к точности, честному спору и признанию правоты другого. И, по традиции, оно соединяет разум человека с Божественной мудростью. Ниже я отделяю то, что прямо сказано в источниках, от моих объяснений. Вавилонский Талмуд тут не единственный источник: большинство цитат говорят об изучении Торы вообще, и я применяю их к Талмуду.

## Главное

- Талмуд называет Тору «приправой» и противоядием от дурного начала (*йецер ра*). Занятый Торой ум не отдаётся ему во власть.
- Талмудическая учёба требует точности, проверки доводов и умения слушать оппонента. Это развивает ясное, честное мышление.
- Спор в учёбе, по словам мудрецов, заканчивается любовью, а не враждой.
- В хасидской мысли разум, занятый Торой, соединяется с Божественной мудростью. Это самое глубокое объяснение, и оно не относится к простому смыслу.

## 1. Простой смысл: Тора как противоядие нечистым мыслям

В трактате Кидушин сказано: Всевышний говорит Израилю: «Дети Мои, Я сотворил дурное начало и сотворил для него Тору как приправу (*таблин*). Если вы занимаетесь Торой, вы не отданы в его руки» [Kiddushin 30b]. Там же объясняется, что иначе «грех лежит у входа», и все помыслы дурного начала будут направлены на человека.

Во второй половине отрывка (и в параллели [Sukkah 52b]) школа рабби Ишмаэля учит:

«אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּל זֶה — מׇשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ. אִם אֶבֶן הוּא — נִימּוֹחַ, אִם בַּרְזֶל הוּא — מִתְפּוֹצֵץ»

«Если встретил тебя этот негодяй, затащи его в дом учения. Если он камень — растворится, если железо — раскрошится».

Дом учения здесь назван практическим средством против нечистых помыслов. Основание в том, что ум не может быть полностью занят двумя вещами сразу. Это моё объяснение, а не цитата. Вавилонский Талмуд даёт для такой занятости больше всего материала: сложные споры требуют полной концентрации и не оставляют места праздному воображению.

## 2. Почему именно Талмуд, а не только Танах или Мишна

Мудрецы ставят изучение Талмуда (*гемары*) выше других видов учёбы. В Бава Меция говорится, что изучение Писания и Мишны имеет меньшую ценность, а в Талмуде «нет большей добродетели». Пересказываю по памяти: точную формулировку в полученном мной отрывке проверить не удалось, поэтому ссылка на [Bava Metzia 33a] приблизительная. Причина понятна. В Талмуде не просто сообщается закон. В нём показано, как к нему приходят:

- **Вопрос и ответ** (*куша* и *тируц*). Человек учится не принимать утверждение на веру, а проверять его.
- **Опровержение и доказательство.** Приходится держать в уме несколько версий и видеть, где в каждой слабое место.
- **Называние источника.** Каждое мнение связано с говорящим, и это приучает к честности: слова приписывают тому, кто их произнёс.
- **Признание правоты другого.** Талмуд часто записывает мнение проигравшей стороны и разбирает его на равных. Это воспитывает смирение мысли.

Эти навыки переходят на всю жизнь: человек меньше склонен к поспешным выводам, самообману и оправданию себя.

## 3. Спор, который очищает

Рабби Хия бар Ава говорит: даже отец с сыном и учитель с учеником, занимаясь Торой в одних воротах, становятся «врагами» друг другу, но не уходят оттуда, пока не станут любящими. Он выводит это из слов «Ваэв в Суфе» (Числа 21:14), читая «бе-софа» — «в её конце» [Kiddushin 30b].

Талмудический спор ведётся ради истины, а не ради победы. Поэтому он приучает отделять идею от личности и спорить без злобы. Это тоже очищает мысль: уходят самолюбование и обида.

## 4. Более глубокий уровень: мысль человека и мудрость Всевышнего

В хасидской традиции (Тания, глава 5, цитирую по памяти, не по полученному тексту) говорится, что, когда человек постигает галаху, его разум охватывает Божественную волю и мудрость и «облачается» в них. Поэтому для хасидизма изучение Торы не только тренировка ума, но и соединение с Источником мудрости. Это уже сфера *дераша* и *сода*, а не простой смысл.

Близкая мысль есть у рава Хаима из Воложина в «Нефеш ха-хаим» (часть 4): изучение Торы поддерживает миры и очищает душу самого учащегося. Точных ссылок на главы я не проверял.

## Практически

- Учитесь вслух и регулярно, пусть понемногу: страница в день надёжнее редких долгих занятий.
- Учитесь с партнёром (*хавруса*): спор в паре даёт то самое очищение, о котором говорит рабби Хия бар Ава.
- Когда приходят нечистые мысли, переключайтесь на учёбу, как советует школа рабби Ишмаэля.
- Начинать лучше с преподавателем или по переводу с комментариями: Талмуд трудно читать без подготовки.

Если вы хотите начать учить Талмуд всерьёз, посоветуйтесь с раввином или преподавателем. Он поможет выбрать трактат и уровень.

answer:
**Resposta direta:** Na tradição judaica, o "diabo" não é um deus rival do bem nem um rei do inferno. A Torá não conhece essa figura. Existe o *Satan* ("adversário, acusador"), e os Sábios o identificam com o *yetzer hará* (inclinação para o mal) que está dentro de cada pessoa. Sua intuição está, portanto, muito próxima da leitura clássica, embora haja várias opiniões sobre o Satan ser também um anjo real a serviço de D'us.

## Pontos principais
- No Tanakh, o *Satan* é um funcionário subordinado a D'us, sem poder próprio. Em Jó, só age com permissão.
- O Talmud diz: "ele é o Satan, ele é o *yetzer hará*, ele é o anjo da morte" [Bava Batra 16a].
- O *yetzer hará* "mora" dentro do coração da pessoa [Sukkah 52a]. Isso se aproxima da sua ideia do ego.
- Rambam e os racionalistas leem tudo isso como alegoria das forças da alma. Outros, sobretudo na tradição mística, veem também uma realidade angélica.
- O dualismo (um poder do mal independente de D'us) é rejeitado pelo judaísmo.

## O Satan no Tanakh
Em Jó, o Satan aparece entre os "filhos de D'us" e responde a D'us:

"וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָן… הִנֵּה כׇל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ בְּיָדֶךָ, רַק אֵלָיו אַל־תִּשְׁלַח יָדֶךָ" — "D'us disse ao Adversário: tudo o que ele tem está em teu poder; somente contra ele não estendas a mão" [Job 1:6-12].

Ele funciona como um promotor na corte celestial. Só age dentro do limite que D'us permite e não é um "anti-D'us". Isaías (45:7) afirma que D'us forma a luz e cria as trevas, e que faz a paz e cria o mal. Isso exclui um segundo poder independente.

## "Ele é o Satan, ele é o yetzer hará"
O Talmud, ao comentar Jó, ensina sobre os métodos do Satan: "desce e leva ao erro, sobe e acusa, recebe permissão e tira a alma". Em seguida, Resh Lakish diz:

"הוּא שָׂטָן, הוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע, הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת" — "Ele é o Satan, ele é o *yetzer hará*, ele é o anjo da morte" [Bava Batra 16a].

Ou seja, o "tentador" que seduz, o "acusador" que denuncia e o "executor" são três faces da mesma função.

## O yetzer hará está dentro de nós
O Talmud fala dele como algo interno. Ele "fica escondido (*tzafun*) no coração do homem" [Sukkah 52a]. Também dá sete nomes a ele, entre eles "pedra" e "obstáculo". Rav Asi diz que ele começa fino como uma teia de aranha e acaba grosso como as cordas de uma carroça. Isso descreve bem o processo do hábito que se fortalece a cada vez que cedemos.

O Talmud acrescenta que, no futuro, D'us o abaterá. Para os justos ele parecerá uma montanha, e para os maus, um fio de cabelo. Os dois grupos chorarão [Sukkah 52a].

## Um ponto de equilíbrio com o ego
- **Concordância:** a tentação nasce da própria pessoa. Ninguém pode dizer "o diabo me fez fazer isso". A responsabilidade e o livre-arbítrio são nossos [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 5:1].
- **Nuance:** o *yetzer hará* não é só "ego" no sentido moderno. É o conjunto dos impulsos (desejo, raiva, inveja, orgulho) e, em si, não é mau. Sem ele não haveria casamento, trabalho nem construção. Ele só se torna destrutivo quando age sem limite. O Midrash chega a dizer que o "muito bom" da criação inclui o *yetzer hará* (Bereshit Rabá 9:7).
- **Ego como obstáculo:** os mestres do Mussar e do Chassidismo falam do orgulho e do egocentrismo como a raiz de muitos pecados. Nesse ponto, sua formulação é bem judaica.

## Existe um ser real chamado Satan?
Há uma gama de opiniões:
- **Rambam** (*Guia dos Perplexos*, III, 22): ele lê o Satan de Jó como alegoria. Seria a matéria, a tendência e o desejo que desviam a pessoa. Não consegui abrir esse texto agora, então cito de memória e sem número exato de trecho.
- **Tradição talmúdica e midráshica:** o Satan aparece como um agente angélico, com tarefas e permissão divinas.
- **Cabalá e Zohar:** descrevem forças espirituais do lado do mal (a *sitra achra*, "o outro lado"), mas elas sempre estão subordinadas à vontade de D'us.

Todas as vertentes concordam em um ponto: o Satan não tem poder independente e não é adorado, temido nem invocado. O ser humano continua livre e responsável.

## Prática para esta semana
O Talmud sugere um método: ocupar-se da Torá, recitar o *Shemá* e lembrar o dia da morte [Berakhot 5a]. Na prática, quando a tentação surgir, pare e nomeie o impulso ("estou com raiva, estou com orgulho"). Esse pequeno intervalo é onde o livre-arbítrio age.

Se a pergunta vem de uma luta pessoal, vale conversar com um rabino ou mentor de confiança.

**Resposta curta:** Sim. Segundo a tradição, os "justos das nações" têm parte no Mundo Vindouro, e a era messiânica não os exclui. O apoio material a Torá, sinagogas e kiruv é uma mitsvá real, e a tradição não diz que ela seja desperdiçada. Mas nenhuma fonte clássica trata desse tipo de doação como categoria específica de mérito. Por isso, o que segue é uma extrapolação a partir de princípios, não uma promessa textual.

## Pontos principais
- O Rambam ensina que o não judeu que cumpre as sete leis por obrigação divina é um dos "justos das nações" e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro.
- Isaías 56:6-7 promete aos estrangeiros que se unem a D'us que o Templo será "casa de oração para todos os povos".
- Contribuir para a Torá e para o povo judeu é um ato bom que vai além das sete leis, e o que é bom raramente se perde diante de D'us.
- A condição central, segundo o Rambam, é a motivação: agir porque D'us ordenou, e não só por razão própria.
- Ninguém conhece o "recibo" exato do mérito de cada pessoa. A humildade é a postura adequada.

## 1. A base: o justo das nações
O Talmud e a Tosefta registram a disputa entre R. Eliezer e R. Yehoshua sobre se os justos das nações têm parte no Mundo Vindouro. A conclusão aceita é a de R. Yehoshua: "yesh chasidei umot ha-olam sheyesh lahem chelek le-olam haba" (há justos das nações que têm parte no Mundo Vindouro). Não consegui abrir a Tosefta nesta consulta, então cito esse dado de memória, sem número de referência.

O Rambam codifica isso em [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11]. Não consegui recuperar o texto agora, então parafraseio. Quem aceita as sete leis e cuida delas é um dos justos das nações e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro. Isso vale desde que as cumpra porque D'us as ordenou na Torá, e não apenas por convicção própria. Muitos comentaristas debatem o alcance exato dessa condição.

## 2. A era messiânica
O Rambam descreve a era messiânica em [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 11–12]. Ele a apresenta como um tempo de paz, de conhecimento de D'us e sem inveja nem guerra, em que "o mundo inteiro se ocupará apenas de conhecer a D'us" (cf. [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 12:5]). A era messiânica é, portanto, algo que as nações também vivem e partilham, e não um evento só para judeus. Os profetas dizem o mesmo. Em Zacarias 8:20-23, povos virão buscar D'us em Jerusalém. Em Isaías 2:2-4, "todas as nações" afluirão ao monte do Templo.

## 3. O texto de Isaías sobre os estrangeiros
O profeta diz: "uvnei hanekhar hanilvim al Adonai lesharto… vahavi'otim el har kodshi" (os estrangeiros que se unem a D'us para servi-Lo… eu os levarei ao Meu monte sagrado), e conclui que "Minha casa será chamada casa de oração para todos os povos" [Isaiah 56:6-7]. O texto trata de estrangeiros que se ligam a D'us. É um bom fundamento para a ideia de que quem apoia casas de oração e o serviço a D'us não fica de fora do futuro.

## 4. E a contribuição concreta?
Aqui falo por inferência, não por citação:
- **Sinagogas e Torá:** apoiar o estudo e a oração é uma ação de bem. Faz parte de uma prática religiosa que a tradição valoriza, e o Talmud afirma que D'us não retém a recompensa de nenhuma criatura (princípio conhecido de [Bava Kamma 38a]; cito de memória).
- **Kiruv:** o kiruv visa aproximar judeus da Torá. Ajudar nisso é ajudar o povo judeu a cumprir sua missão, que inclui ser "luz para as nações". Um não judeu que participa disso colabora com o plano de D'us para o mundo.
- **Cuidado:** o kiruv é dirigido a judeus. Não confunda o papel do ben Noach com o de quem busca converter outros não judeus. Judaísmo não exige conversão de não judeus.

## 5. Sobre a motivação
O ponto mais importante é interno: agir pela vontade de D'us. Se a doação nasce do desejo de servir ao Criador e ao Seu plano, ela se alinha ao que o Rambam descreve como o caminho do justo das nações. Os detalhes de "quanto" ou "como" vão além do que as fontes definem. O melhor é praticar as sete leis com seriedade, estudá-las e manter a generosidade.

Para uma orientação prática (por exemplo, como direcionar doações ou como estudar as leis de Noé), vale conversar com um rabino que trabalhe com noaítas.

O judaísmo clássico ensina que o *Gehinom* (a "geena") é, para a maioria das almas, temporário e purificador. A reencarnação (*gilgul*) existe na tradição judaica, mas é um ensinamento da Cabalá e não é aceita por todos. A comunicação com os mortos, central no espiritismo, é proibida pela Torá.

## Pontos principais

- Para a maioria dos sábios, o Gehinom é um processo de julgamento e purificação com duração limitada, e não um castigo eterno.
- O *gilgul* (reencarnação) aparece na Cabalá, com o Zohar e o Arizal, mas Saadia Gaon o rejeitou e Maimônides não o ensina.
- O judaísmo não entende a purificação como uma escola evolutiva de muitas vidas, como faz o espiritismo.
- Consultar os mortos é proibido em [Deuteronomy 18:10-11].
- A fé judaica gira em torno da Torá, da aliança e dos mandamentos. Não é uma doutrina sobre a evolução da alma.

## 1. Gehinom: purificação, não eternidade

A Mishná diz que o julgamento dos ímpios no Gehinom dura doze meses:

> "מִשְׁפַּט רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנֹּם, שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ"
> "O julgamento dos ímpios no Gehinom dura doze meses." [Mishnah Eduyot 2:10] (tradução minha)

O Talmud, em [Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a], desenvolve a ideia. Os intermediários descem, são purificados e sobem. Os totalmente ímpios têm um destino mais severo, e a escola de Hilel inclina o julgamento para a misericórdia. A liturgia judaica reflete isso: o *Kaddish* de luto é recitado por até onze meses, para não sugerir que o falecido seja totalmente ímpio.

Há uma ressalva. Maimônides ensina que os ímpios incorrigíveis não sofrem para sempre. Eles são "cortados" (*karet*) e deixam de existir:

> "הוּא הַמֵּת שֶׁאֵינוֹ חַי לְעוֹלָם אֶלָּא נִכְרַת בְּרִשְׁעוֹ וְאָבֵד כִּבְהֵמָה"
> "Ele é o morto que não vive para sempre; é cortado em sua maldade e perece." [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 8:1] (tradução minha)

Portanto, a ideia de "purgatório" se parece com o Gehinom temporário. Mas o judaísmo não tem um dogma único. Os textos falam de purificação, de justiça e de misericórdia, sem um mapa detalhado do pós-vida.

## 2. Reencarnação: existe, mas é debatida

- **Na Cabalá:** o *gilgul neshamot* ("ciclo das almas") é ensinado no Zohar e sobretudo na escola do Arizal (R. Isaac Luria, séc. XVI). Para o Arizal, a alma volta para completar mandamentos que não cumpriu ou para corrigir erros. Esse ensinamento é central no hassidismo e entre muitos sefarditas.
- **Contra:** Saadia Gaon, em *Emunot VeDeot*, critica a reencarnação com firmeza. Outros filósofos medievais, como Maimônides, não a incluem nos princípios de fé. Os Treze Princípios dele falam de recompensa e castigo e da ressurreição dos mortos, mas não de reencarnação.
- **Hoje:** muitos judeus ortodoxos aceitam o *gilgul* como parte da tradição mística. Outros o tratam como opinião legítima, mas não obrigatória.

## 3. Diferenças em relação ao espiritismo

- **Contato com os mortos:** a Torá proíbe consultar "quem consulta os mortos" (*doresh el hametim*) e os médiuns [Deuteronomy 18:10-11]. Para o judaísmo, isso é proibido mesmo que a intenção seja boa.
- **Finalidade:** no espiritismo, a reencarnação é um caminho de evolução moral progressiva. No *gilgul* cabalístico, é mais uma correção de pendências, ligada aos mandamentos. Os cabalistas o veem como exceção, ou como sinal da misericórdia de Deus, e não como a estrutura normal da existência.
- **Centro da fé:** o judaísmo não se organiza em torno do destino da alma. Ele se organiza em torno da Torá, da aliança de Israel e da santificação da vida neste mundo. A tradição diz que "uma hora de arrependimento e boas ações neste mundo vale mais que toda a vida do Mundo Vindouro" [Pirkei Avot 4:17].

## Para você, como cristão

O judaísmo não exige que não judeus se tornem judeus. Para os justos de todas as nações, a tradição reconhece um lugar no Mundo Vindouro, e o caminho deles são as sete leis de Noé [Sanhedrin 56a-b]. Se quiser, posso explicar essas leis, a diferença entre os conceitos de pecado e redenção no judaísmo e no cristianismo, ou o que a Cabalá diz sobre o *gilgul*. Qual dessas perguntas é a primeira das suas "milhões"?

Para decisões pessoais de fé ou de prática, é bom conversar também com um rabino e com um líder da sua própria tradição.

answer:
Vou verificar o que as fontes dizem antes de responder.**Resposta direta:** não conheço nenhuma fonte clássica (Talmud, Rambam ou Zohar) que fixe uma recompensa específica para o escriba (*sofer*, de Torá, *tefilin* e *mezuzot*) na era messiânica ou no *Olam Haba*, o mundo vindouro. As fontes dizem que o ofício é "trabalho do Céu" e que o escriba recebe um mérito enorme, equiparado ao de quem recebeu a Torá no Sinai. A recompensa no mundo vindouro é ensinada de forma geral, e os detalhes ficam com D'us.

## Pontos principais
- Não há, nas fontes que consultei, uma "tabela de recompensas" específica para escribas.
- O Talmud chama o ofício de "trabalho do Céu" [Eruvin 13a].
- Escrever uma Torá é considerado como ter recebido a Torá no Sinai [Menachot 30a].
- A recompensa no *Olam Haba* é, segundo o Rambam, a proximidade com D'us, e não um prêmio material.
- Afirmações populares do tipo "o escriba terá tal lugar no mundo vindouro" vêm de literatura posterior ou de tradições locais, e não há fonte clássica certa para elas.

## O que as fontes dizem sobre o mérito do escriba

**1. Trabalho do Céu.** O Rabi Yishmael disse ao Rabi Meir, que era escriba:

"הֱוֵי זָהִיר בִּמְלַאכְתֶּךָ, שֶׁמְּלַאכְתְּךָ מְלֶאכֶת שָׁמַיִם הִיא, שֶׁמָּא אַתָּה מְחַסֵּר אוֹת אַחַת אוֹ מְיַיתֵּר אוֹת אַחַת — נִמְצֵאתָ מַחֲרִיב אֶת כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ" [Eruvin 13a].

Tradução: "Meu filho, seja cuidadoso em seu ofício, pois seu ofício é trabalho do Céu. Se você omitir uma letra ou acrescentar uma letra, estará destruindo o mundo inteiro."

Esse texto fala da responsabilidade do escriba, e não de recompensa. Mesmo assim, mostra a dimensão do que ele faz.

**2. Como se tivesse recebido a Torá no Sinai.** Diz Rav, citado em [Menachot 30a]:

"כְּתָבוֹ – מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ קִיבְּלוֹ מֵהַר סִינַי"

Tradução: "Se ele a escreveu, o verso lhe atribui como se a tivesse recebido do Monte Sinai."

Rav Sheshet acrescenta que quem corrige até uma só letra é considerado como se a tivesse escrito. Essa é a fonte talmúdica mais próxima de uma "recompensa" específica, e ela vale tanto para quem escreve quanto para quem revisa.

## Recompensa no mundo vindouro e na era messiânica

- **Era messiânica:** o Rambam ensina que seu objetivo é a liberdade e a paz para se dedicar à Torá e à sabedoria. Isso é diferente do *Olam Haba*. Nesse quadro, o escriba participa como qualquer judeu que cumpre a Torá.
- **Olam Haba:** o Rambam ensina, em *Hilchot Teshuvá* cap. 8, que o prêmio dos justos é a bondade da alma, a ligação com D'us. Não é uma recompensa material. Esse cap. 8 é uma fonte geral, e eu não o abri aqui para citar o texto.
- **Pirkei Avot** ensina que o "Dono da obra" é fiel em pagar o salário dos justos, mas que "o pagamento é no futuro". Isso inclui o escriba, sem detalhar o que ele receberá. Cito de memória, sem número de mishná.

## Sobre afirmações populares

Você pode ter lido que escribas, ou quem financia uma Torá, têm um lugar especial no mundo vindouro. Algumas obras de ética e de Cabalá exaltam muito a escrita de uma Torá e a *mitzvá* nº 613, "escrevam para vocês este cântico" (Devarim 31:19). Não consegui verificar uma fonte específica para essas afirmações, então não as atribuo a ninguém. Se você viu algo concreto, diga onde, e eu o examino.

Para uma situação pessoal, por exemplo se você é escriba ou pensa em se tornar um, consulte seu rabino.

answer:
Em princípio, qualquer pessoa pode se converter, desde que seja sincera, aceite o jugo das mitsvot (mandamentos) e passe por um *beit din* (tribunal rabínico) reconhecido. Na prática, a conversão não é aceita quando o motivo é insincero (por exemplo, só para se casar ou por vantagem), quando a pessoa não aceita todas as mitsvot, quando falta o procedimento correto ou quando não há um beit din legítimo. Os casos de dúvida precisam de um rabino.

## Pontos principais

- Não existe, hoje, nenhuma nação ou povo cujos membros estejam proibidos de se converter.
- A conversão exige três coisas: aceitação das mitsvot, circuncisão (para homens) e imersão no *mikveh* (banho ritual), tudo diante de um beit din.
- O beit din deve primeiro testar a sinceridade, e por isso tradicionalmente desencoraja o candidato no início.
- Quem se converte por motivos ocultos (casamento, dinheiro, status) levanta dúvida sobre a validade, e a decisão cabe ao beit din.
- Não existe obrigação de se converter: o não judeu justo tem seu caminho (as sete leis de Noé).

## Quando é possível

**1. A pessoa vem com sinceridade e aceita as mitsvot.** O Talmud ensina que, quando alguém quer se converter, o beit din pergunta: "O que você viu para querer se converter? Não sabe que o povo de Israel hoje é sofrido e perseguido?". Se responde "Eu sei, e não sou digno", é aceito de imediato:

> "אִם אוֹמֵר: יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי, וְאֵינִי כְּדַאי — מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתוֹ מִיָּד"
> (Se disser: "Eu sei, e não sou digno", aceitam-no imediatamente) [Yevamot 47a]

Ensinam-lhe então parte das mitsvot leves e das graves, os castigos e as recompensas. O Shulchan Arukh codifica isso em [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 268:2]. Diz também que "não se insiste demais nem se é minucioso demais" com o candidato.

**2. O procedimento é feito corretamente.** O Shulchan Arukh descreve o procedimento (no mesmo trecho):
- circuncisão para o homem (e, se já foi circuncidado, a *hatafat dam brit*, uma gota de sangue simbólica);
- espera até a cura;
- imersão no mikveh sem nenhuma barreira, diante de três juízes;
- para a mulher, a imersão é com decoro, e os juízes ficam de costas.

Depois disso, "é como um judeu": mesmo que volte atrás, continua judeu, ainda que pecador.

**3. É feita diante de um beit din.** O Talmud ensina que quem se converteu "entre si e si mesmo", sem tribunal, não é converso [Yevamot 47a]. Por isso, a conversão "por conta própria" não vale.

**4. Vale para qualquer lugar e época.** O Talmud afirma que se aceitam conversos tanto em Israel quanto fora de Israel, e também "hoje em dia" [Yevamot 47a]. A tradição rabínica ensina que, nos casos de dúvida, quem pergunta sobre a conversão de outra pessoa pode precisar apresentar prova (testemunhas) de que ela foi feita.

**5. Também há conversão de crianças.** Segundo o Talmud (Ketubot 11a, de memória), um beit din pode converter um menor "em seu benefício". Os poskim (decisores) discutem as condições, por exemplo a educação religiosa posterior da criança. É um caso para o rabino.

## Quando não é possível, ou há problema

- **Sem aceitação das mitsvot.** Quem quer ser "judeu" mas recusa parte da Torá, ou só quer uma conversão simbólica, não pode ser aceito. A aceitação das mitsvot é a base de toda a conversão. Entre os poskim ortodoxos, a exigência de compromisso com a observância é o ponto central.
- **Motivos insinceros.** O Talmud discute o converso por interesse (por amor a uma pessoa, por riqueza, por poder) em [Yevamot 24b], e o Rambam trata disso em *Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse* cap. 13 (sem número de halachá, pois não consegui abrir o texto agora). Os beit dinim testam a sinceridade, e a posição geral é de cautela. Se a conversão já foi feita, o caso cabe a um rabino, que avalia a situação concreta.
- **Sem beit din reconhecido.** Conversões feitas por um "rabino" isolado, sem autoridade, ou por movimentos não ortodoxos, não são aceitas pela ortodoxia. É uma questão prática importante, porque afeta casamento e status pessoal. Isso é posição do judaísmo ortodoxo, e outros movimentos têm outra visão.
- **Coerção.** Quem é forçado não tem a intenção necessária.
- **Quem já é judeu.** Se a pessoa é filha de mãe judia, não precisa e não pode "se converter". Já é judia, mesmo que não observante. Se há dúvida sobre isso, procure um rabino.

## E os povos que a Torá proíbe?

A Torá proíbe aceitar *Amon* e *Moav* como membros da comunidade (Deuteronômio 23:4), e fala dos sete povos de Canaã e de Amalek. Mas a Mishná (Yadayim 4:4, de memória) ensina que Senaquerib misturou os povos, de modo que ninguém sabe mais quem é quem. Por isso essas restrições não se aplicam hoje, e qualquer pessoa pode se converter.

## Se você é não judeu e se interessa

O judaísmo **não exige** a conversão dos não judeus. O justo de todas as nações tem parte no Mundo Vindouro, e o caminho de um não judeu são as sete leis de Noé (veja [Sanhedrin 56a]). A conversão é uma escolha de quem sente um chamado profundo, e o beit din tradicionalmente testa e desencoraja no começo, para ter certeza de que a pessoa sabe o que está assumindo.

Se você está pensando em se converter, o melhor caminho é procurar um rabino ortodoxo na sua cidade e começar a estudar. A decisão individual, o seu caso e o seu beit din dependem de um rabino que possa conhecer você e fazer perguntas.

Se quiser, posso detalhar o processo de estudo, os custos e prazos, ou o caminho noáquida.

answer:
It sounds like you two found something rare: someone who lets you be yourself, and who is herself around you. Nobody can promise how any friendship will go, but what you describe sounds like the kind of bond that tends to last. It rests on honesty and on helping each other grow, not on being popular.

## Key Takeaways
- Friendship built on being yourselves is what Jewish sources value most.
- You have already helped her, and she has helped you. That mutual giving is a strong sign.
- Standing by her when others mocked you shows real loyalty.
- No one can know the future, but you can do things that help a friendship last.
- If the worry weighs on you, it is worth talking to someone you trust.

## What you described
You were kind to her when she was alone. You didn't care what others said, and you made her feel she could be social too. Her calm and honesty around you also suggest she feels safe with you. Being the person someone can relax around is a real gift.

Noticing that she adapts to other people is not a flaw in her, and it doesn't make her friendship with you fake. Many people, especially at school, change how they act to fit in. What matters is that with you she doesn't have to. That is probably why it feels different.

## What the Torah says about friends
- **Choosing a friend.** The Mishnah says to acquire a friend for yourself [Pirkei Avot 1:6]. The wording suggests that friendship takes effort and choice, not only luck. You chose each other.
- **Two are better than one.** Ecclesiastes says that two are better than one because if one falls, the other can lift her up [Ecclesiastes 4:9-10]. You each have someone to lift you when you're down.
- **Loyalty.** Proverbs says a true friend loves at all times [Proverbs 17:17]. Your steadiness when people bullied you is that kind of love.
- **Love that doesn't depend on anything.** The Mishnah says love that doesn't depend on a particular reason never ends. Its example is David and Jonathan [Pirkei Avot 5:16]. A bond based on who you are, not on status, is the kind that lasts.

I couldn't pull up the exact wording of these verses just now, so I've paraphrased them instead of quoting. Please look them up to read them yourself.

## About "will she truly stay?"
No one can promise the future. People change, schools change, and friends sometimes drift. But some things make a friendship stronger:
- **Say it out loud.** Tell her what you told me, that she matters to you. Asking "are we okay?" is normal and not needy.
- **Keep being honest.** That is the foundation you already have.
- **Don't shrink her world, and don't shrink yours.** She can have other friends and you can too. Having other friends doesn't take away what the two of you have.
- **Notice what she does, not only what you fear.** She has told you that you're the reason she became social. That is a very open thing to say.

The "weird kids" label is painful, but many people with deep, honest friendships were once called odd. Choosing a real friend over popularity says something good about your character.

If the worry about losing her feels heavy, or the bullying still hurts, please talk to a parent, a teacher, a counselor, or a rabbi you trust. You deserve support from more than one person.

I'm glad to keep talking if you'd like. What made you start worrying that she might leave?

answer:
The Sabeans of Job are almost certainly not Hindu devotees of Shiva. The text and the history both point to an Arabian people, and I don't know of any evidence linking them to Hinduism.

**Key Takeaways**
- In [Job 1:15], *Sheva* (שְׁבָא) are raiders who carry off Job's livestock and kill his servants.
- *Sheva* is an Arabian people descended from Cush or Joktan in the genealogies of Genesis, and the name is unrelated to Shiva.
- Sabaeans (South Arabia), the Quranic "Sabians" and the Mandaeans are three different groups that share similar-sounding names.
- Phallic or standing-stone cults did exist in the ancient Near East, but that doesn't show a Hindu presence.
- The Tanakh does not "ignore" idolatry. It names and condemns many foreign cults, and none of them is Indian.

**What the verse says**

The verse reads: "וַתִּפֹּל שְׁבָא וַתִּקָּחֵם… וָאִמָּלְטָה רַק־אֲנִי לְבַדִּי" ("Sheva fell upon them and took them… and I alone have escaped to tell you"). In Job the Sabeans are simply raiders, and the text says nothing about their religion. The Chaldeans raid Job's camels in the next verses.

**Who Sheva were**

- In Genesis, the name *Sheva* appears in the genealogies. I'm citing this from memory because my lookup failed, and I believe it appears in Genesis 10 (as a son of Raamah, a descendant of Cush, and also as a son of Joktan) and in Genesis 25 (as a descendant of Abraham through Keturah).
- The best-known Sheva is the kingdom of Sheba in South Arabia, which is the Sabaeans of ancient inscriptions. It was known for the incense and spice trade, and the Queen of Sheba came from there in [I Kings 10].
- The Sabaeans of Arabia worshipped astral and local deities such as Almaqah, who was associated with the moon. This is a South Arabian religion with its own inscriptions, and it is not Hindu.
- Some commentators say a different Sheva is meant in Job. I haven't checked what Rashi says on this verse, so I won't attribute a view to him.

**The Quranic "Sabians"**

The Quran's *Sabi'un* (for example Quran 2:62) are a different group. They are usually identified with the Mandaeans, a Gnostic baptizing community in Mesopotamia, or with the star-worshippers of Harran. Their name probably comes from a root meaning "to immerse." The resemblance to "Sabean" is a coincidence of names, and it doesn't make them the same people as Job's raiders.

**Shiva and the lingam**

- The name *Shiva* has nothing to do with *Sheva*. The letters, the language family and the history all differ.
- Phallic symbols and standing stones (*matzevot*) did appear in the ancient Near East. Canaanite worship used *matzevot* and *asherim*, and the Torah forbids them in [Deuteronomy 16:21-22].
- Similar symbols can arise independently in different cultures. This alone doesn't show that Hindus were present.
- There was ancient trade between India and Arabia and Mesopotamia. Contact existed, but I know of no evidence for an organized Shaivite cult in Job's setting.

**Why the Tanakh doesn't mention Hinduism**

The Tanakh names the cults that Israel actually met: Baal, Asherah, Molech, Chemosh, Marduk, Egyptian gods, and star and moon worship. Indian religion is far away and not part of that picture. The one clear Indian reference is geographic. *Hodu* (India) appears in [Esther 1:1] as the eastern limit of Achashverosh's empire. Later Jewish thought did discuss Indian religion. Rambam mentions Eastern peoples in his account of the origins of idolatry. The Talmud's reference to "the idolatry of India" (*avodah zarah shel Hodu*) is a separate matter, and I'm not citing a specific text for it.

answer:
You're thinking of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in [Eruvin 13b], and the link to Job is a real one. Both texts ask whether existence is a good. They differ in who asks and in what they do with the answer. The Talmud asks in general terms and ends with a call to action. Job asks from inside his pain, and he is answered by being addressed rather than by an argument.

## Key Takeaways
- The Talmud reports a two-and-a-half-year debate. Beit Shammai said it would have been better had man not been created, and Beit Hillel said it is better that he was.
- The sages then voted. The conclusion was that it would have been better not to be created, but now that man has been created, he should examine his deeds. (I am giving this ending from memory, because the text I retrieved cut off just before it.)
- Job curses the day of his birth and asks why he did not die at birth [Job 3:1-11].
- The Talmud's question is philosophical and its answer is practical. Job's question is existential, and God answers it with a confrontation rather than a proof.
- Many readers note that the Talmud's "better not created" is not a claim that life is worthless. It is a claim about the weight of moral responsibility.

## The Talmudic source
The Gemara in [Eruvin 13b] teaches: "שְׁתֵּי שָׁנִים וּמֶחֱצָה נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל. הַלָּלוּ אוֹמְרִים: נוֹחַ לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא, וְהַלָּלוּ אוֹמְרִים: נוֹחַ לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁלֹּא נִבְרָא."

Translation: "For two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. These said: It is better for man not to have been created than to have been created. Those said: It is better for man to have been created than not to have been created."

The passage then records that they counted votes and concluded in favor of the Beit Shammai position. The practical consequence is that man should "examine his deeds" (*yefashfesh bema'asav*). Another version has "scrutinize his deeds" (*yemashmesh*). Some read the second version as "examine his future deeds."

Two points about this:
- **The context.** The people who decided "better not created" were the same sages who built the world of mitzvot. The statement seems to concern the burden of accountability. A being who can sin and be judged carries a weight that a being who was never created does not carry.
- **The ending.** The conclusion does not recommend despair. It points toward self-scrutiny and action, so the question does not stay theoretical.

## Job's version
Job's outcry in [Job 3:1-11] is the same wish in personal form:
- "יֹאבַד יוֹם אִוָּלֵד בּוֹ" ("Perish the day on which I was born").
- "לָמָּה לֹּא מֵרֶחֶם אָמוּת" ("Why did I not die at birth").

Job is not saying that creation is bad as a philosophical thesis. He is saying that his own life, with its pain, seems not worth having been given. The Talmud's sages reach their conclusion by reasoning about moral responsibility. Job reaches his through loss.

## Where they differ
- **The mood.** The Talmud's discussion is calm and ends in a vote. Job's is raw protest. Job also says "I do not despise my life" elsewhere, and his friends do not accept his complaint, but he does not retract it.
- **What follows from it.** The sages say: since we are here, take responsibility. Job demands an explanation from God. When God finally answers him (from Job 38 onward), He does not justify the suffering. He shows Job the scale and complexity of creation, which Job could not see from where he stood. Job's question is met by a presence that addresses him, not by a solution.
- **Whether the question is answered.** The Talmud treats the question as settled, though sadly. Job ends up not with an argument but with a changed relationship to God. Many readers see this as the book's point: some suffering cannot be explained, but it can be met.

## A way to hold both
You could say the two texts frame the problem from opposite ends. The Talmud says that existence is a heavy gift, and the response is moral seriousness. Job shows that when the weight becomes unbearable, the honest response is to cry out, and the Torah preserves that cry as part of Scripture. Neither text says that the world is simply good or simply bad.

answer:
Your question is a little open, so I read it as: "Which pshat-based sources show how a lasting spiritual impression gets made?" The Torah's own answer is that it comes from three things together. You have to take it to heart, repeat it and build it into daily routine, and keep remembering it. Some of my later sources didn't load, so I paraphrase those and don't quote them.

## Key Takeaways
- The Torah wants words placed "on your heart," not only known in the head ([Deuteronomy 6:6]).
- Impressions last through repetition and fixed daily settings: home, road, bedtime, waking ([Deuteronomy 6:7]).
- Physical reminders (tefillin, mezuzah) turn an inner idea into something you see and touch ([Deuteronomy 6:8-9]).
- Knowing something is not enough. You also have to bring it back to mind, and an experience fades if you don't guard it ([Deuteronomy 4:9], [Deuteronomy 4:39]).
- Teaching others, especially children, is part of how an impression is made.

## 1. "On your heart": internalizing ([Deuteronomy 6:6])
"וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם עַל־לְבָבֶךָ" means "Take to heart these instructions with which I charge you this day."

- The plain sense is that the words are meant to rest on the heart, which is where the Bible places thought and commitment.
- Rashi on this verse, as I recall it, says the words should not be a fixed burden on the mouth. He reads "today" as meaning they should feel new every day. I couldn't retrieve this comment, so check it directly.

## 2. Repetition and routine ([Deuteronomy 6:7])
"וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ וְדִבַּרְתָּ בָּם בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ וּבְשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ" means "Impress them upon your children. Recite them when you stay at home and when you are away, when you lie down and when you get up."

- The verb *shinantam* (שִׁנַּנְתָּם) is related to sharpening. Words are made sharp and clear, and a lasting mark comes from going over them again and again.
- The verse names situations (home, road, night, morning), not a one-time event. The impression is built into the ordinary rhythm of a day.

## 3. Physical reminders ([Deuteronomy 6:8-9])
"וּקְשַׁרְתָּם לְאוֹת עַל־יָדֶךָ... וּכְתַבְתָּם עַל־מְזֻזוֹת בֵּיתֶךָ" means "Bind them as a sign on your hand... inscribe them on the doorposts of your house."

- The text puts the idea in the hand, between the eyes and at the doorway. These are the places where you act, look and pass through.
- Whatever your view of the later halachic details, the plain function is a reminder that you meet in your body and your space.

## 4. Don't let it fade ([Deuteronomy 4:9])
"פֶּן־תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת־הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר־רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ וּפֶן־יָסוּרוּ מִלְּבָבְךָ כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ" means "so that you do not forget the things that you saw with your own eyes and so that they do not fade from your mind as long as you live."

- Even a direct experience like Sinai can fade. The Torah treats lasting impact as something you have to work to keep.
- The same verse gives the remedy: "make them known to your children and to your children's children." Passing it on keeps it alive in you as well.

## 5. Knowing becomes real only when brought back ([Deuteronomy 4:39])
"וְיָדַעְתָּ הַיּוֹם וַהֲשֵׁבֹתָ אֶל־לְבָבֶךָ" means "Know therefore this day and keep in mind..." Two steps are listed here:
1. *Veyadata*: you know it intellectually.
2. *Vahashevota el levavecha*: you actively return it to your heart.

So the impression forms in the second step, when you bring the idea back to mind and let it affect you.

## Two further sources, paraphrased (not retrieved)
- **[Pirkei Avot 4:20]**: Elisha ben Avuyah compares learning in youth to ink written on fresh paper, and learning in old age to ink on erased paper. This is a pshat-level image of how early impressions go deepest.
- **Rambam, *Hilchot De'ot* ch. 1**: character is shaped by repeating actions over and over. A trait becomes part of you through practice, not through one-time inspiration.

If you'd like, I can retry those two and quote them, or I can focus on one angle: childhood education, the role of experience like Sinai, or habit.

answer:
**Short answer:** Judaism doesn't teach that everyone outside the faith goes to hell. The classic view is that righteous non-Jews have a share in the World to Come (heaven), and that Gehinom (the Jewish "hell") is mostly a temporary place of cleansing, not eternal torture. The sources differ on the details, and the afterlife is described with a lot of humility.

## Key Takeaways
- Non-Jews don't need to convert to merit the World to Come.
- The Rambam says a non-Jew who keeps the seven Noahide laws because God commanded them has a share in the World to Come.
- Gehinom is traditionally a limited period of purification for most souls, not endless punishment.
- The Talmud and later authorities disagree about the details, and we don't know the specifics.
- "Believer" in Judaism is mostly about how you live and act, not only about what you profess.

## The main source: the righteous of the nations
The Rambam writes in [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 8:11]:

"כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל שֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת וְנִזְהָר לַעֲשׂוֹתָן הֲרֵי זֶה מֵחֲסִידֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם. וְיֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא"
("Anyone who accepts the seven mitzvot and is careful to observe them is one of the pious of the nations of the world, and has a share in the World to Come.")

He adds a condition. The person must keep them because God commanded them, not only because logic led them there. Some manuscripts and commentators read this condition differently. Others understand it as describing a higher level of piety, not the minimum.

This builds on the Talmudic and Tosefta teaching, usually quoted as "the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come." That is Rabbi Yehoshua's view, against Rabbi Eliezer, who was stricter. The halacha follows Rabbi Yehoshua. I couldn't pull up the exact Tosefta text just now, so I'm citing it by name only.

The seven Noahide laws are:
- Establish courts of justice.
- Don't blaspheme.
- Don't worship idols.
- Don't commit sexual immorality.
- Don't murder.
- Don't steal.
- Don't eat a limb torn from a living animal.

These are discussed in [Sanhedrin 56a–b].

## What "hell" means in Judaism
- Gehinom is usually described as a temporary stage. The Talmud gives the standard duration as up to twelve months for most souls ([Rosh Hashanah 16b–17a]).
- The Talmud says that some who are completely wicked may be destroyed or may stay longer. Even then, the descriptions are brief and debated.
- The Rambam sees the World to Come as the soul's eternal closeness to God. For him, the worst fate is simply losing it, not being tortured ([Mishneh Torah, Repentance, ch. 8]).
- The Ramban describes it differently, with more detailed stages of reward and punishment, in *Sha'ar HaGemul*.

## What about people who don't believe in God?
- Judaism takes belief seriously. The Rambam's Thirteen Principles are the standard Jewish statement of what Jews are expected to believe.
- The Rambam also says Jews who deny core principles lose their share. But Judaism measures non-Jews by a different standard, which is the Noahide laws.
- No human can judge another person's final standing. Someone's upbringing, circumstances, sincerity, and struggles are known only to God. The Torah speaks of God as "judge of all the earth" who does justly ([Genesis 18:25]).

## Practical bottom line
You don't have to convert to be accepted by God in Judaism. A good person who lives ethically and acknowledges one God stands in a dignified place. If you're curious about the Noahide path, or you have personal questions, speaking with a rabbi is a good idea.

If this question comes from something personal, like worry about a loved one, I'm happy to talk about that too.

answer:
Not all of Freud's ideas can be found in the Torah, and some contradict it. A handful of his observations do have real parallels in Torah and Chazal: the inner conflict of drives, the link between dreams and waking thoughts, and the power of the unconscious. The Torah also frames these ideas very differently from Freud, as I try to show below.

## Key Takeaways
- Freud's divided psyche (id, ego, superego) has a loose Torah parallel in the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), the *yetzer tov* (good inclination), and the human being who must rule over both.
- Chazal anticipated the idea that dreams come from a person's inner life, but they also allow for prophecy and Heavenly messages.
- Torah and Freud agree that drives are present from youth, but they disagree on whether a person is determined by them.
- Freud's religion-as-illusion thesis, his reduction of everything to sexuality, and *Moses and Monotheism* have no place in Torah. I would not try to find them there.

## Title: "Its Urge Is Toward You, Yet You Can Master It"

### 1. Pre-conscious drives
The Flood narrative closes with a diagnosis of human nature: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו", "since the devisings of the human mind are evil from youth" [Genesis 8:21]. Freud said that drives exist from infancy. The Torah says something comparable, that the pull is there "from youth." But look at what God does with this fact. He does not condemn humanity. He promises not to destroy the world again. In the Torah, knowing the human drive is a reason for compassion and not a verdict.

Chazal go further. In Bereshit Rabbah (9:7) they say that the verse "and behold, it was very good" includes even the *yetzer hara*, because without it no one would build a house, marry, or have children. I am citing this from memory, so check the exact wording. This is close to what Freud later called the productive power of libido and sublimation: the drive can be directed into building.

### 2. Inner conflict and mastery
The first psychological scene in the Torah is God speaking to Cain: "לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ וְאֵלֶיךָ תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ וְאַתָּה תִּמְשָׁל־בּוֹ", "Sin couches at the door; its urge is toward you, yet you can be its master" [Genesis 4:7]. Here are an impulse crouching at the threshold, a sibling rivalry (Cain and Abel), and the question of what a person does with the impulse. Freud's later model also shows a conflict between instinct and a restraining conscience.

The difference is the last phrase, *ve'atah timshol bo* ("you can master it"). For Freud, the ego mediates between forces it did not choose. The Torah gives the person real moral agency, which Rambam later makes a foundation of Torah in Hilchot Teshuvah (chapter 5). Freud's determinism is the point where the Torah disagrees with him.

The Talmud develops the inner conflict at length. The *yetzer hara* has many names, and "whoever is greater than his fellow, his *yetzer* is greater" (Sukkah 52a; I did not retrieve this text, so I paraphrase it). Kiddushin 30b teaches that if the *yetzer* attacks you, you should drag it to the *beit midrash*. In other words, the answer is to channel it and not to deny it.

### 3. Dreams
The Torah takes dreams very seriously. Joseph's dreams about his brothers, and then Pharaoh's dreams, drive the plot of Genesis. The Talmud's long treatment of dreams is in [Berakhot 55b]. It says that a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read ("חֶלְמָא דְּלָא מְפַשַּׁר כְּאִגַּרְתָּא דְּלָא מִקַּרְיָא"). The same passage also records a view, which I am paraphrasing, that a person is shown in dreams only what is in the thoughts of his own heart. This is the closest thing in Chazal to Freud's claim that dreams express inner life.

Chazal do not reduce dreams to this one explanation. They also say a dream is "one sixtieth of prophecy." The same page of Talmud says that a dream may contain some nonsense and that dreams follow the interpretation they are given. A dream can therefore be inner material, Heavenly message, or noise. The passage also gives a practical remedy for a distressing dream, which is to "better it before three" friends. This is a kind of talk-therapy ritual: you tell someone, and the fear is eased.

### 4. Repression and the unspoken
The Torah is full of things that were felt but not said. "And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind" (Genesis 37:11, cited from memory). Jacob does not reply to the dream. Esau's hatred and Cain's silence before he kills ("Cain said to his brother…") are also moments when what is not said later erupts. This is a reading of the narrative that fits Freud's idea of repression returning. It is my own connection, not a classic commentator's statement.

### 5. Healing the soul
Rambam, in *Shemonah Perakim* and Hilchot Deot (chapter 2), explicitly compares character flaws to illnesses of the soul. He says that one should go to a wise person, a physician of the soul, and he prescribes a regimen of habit and practice. This is much closer to a therapeutic model than anything in the narratives. Freud's idea that insight heals has a very distant echo in Rambam's idea that self-knowledge and discipline heal.

## Where the parallels end
- **Religion as illusion.** For Freud, belief in God is wish fulfillment. The Torah is built on revelation, so the two cannot be reconciled.
- **Everything as sexuality.** Chazal treat sexual drive as one force among others (honor, anger, greed), and they channel it through marriage and holiness. They do not make it the root of everything.
- **Oedipus.** Some readers connect Reuben and Bilhah (Genesis 35:22) to Oedipal ideas. I would not stretch that far. The Torah presents it as a specific sin and not as a universal law.
- **Moses and Monotheism.** Freud's claim that Moses was an Egyptian who was murdered by the Israelites contradicts the Torah's account at every point.

So a fair dvar Torah can say that Torah recognizes the depth of the human drive, and that it was never a secret. The Torah's point is different from Freud's, though. A person is not trapped by what lies beneath the surface. As God told Cain, a person can master it.

If you like, I can expand any one section (for example dreams, with Joseph and Pharaoh read verse by verse) into a full piece, or compare Freud with Rambam and Mesilat Yesharim in more detail.

answer:
Your framing is a serious one in the tradition. The tension is real, and the tradition treats it as a reason to keep asking, not as something to resolve by dropping one side. I would sharpen two points: the Torah does not simply leave slavery alone, and there is a classic way of distinguishing questioning from "making ourselves G-d." I did not retrieve these texts in this session, so I cite them by reference and paraphrase them.

## Key Takeaways
- Abraham's question, "Shall the Judge of all the earth not do justice?" [Genesis 18:25], shows that asking is a legitimate and even model stance.
- The Torah does not endorse slavery as an ideal. It regulates and limits it, and also builds in counter-pressures.
- Maimonides gives a "gradualism" explanation of why the Torah works through existing institutions [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 3 32], but he presents it as his own reading, not as received tradition.
- The tradition holds that moral sensibility is meant to grow through human interpretation of Torah [Bava Metzia 59b], and this is different from judging the Torah from outside.

## The tension you describe
Your theological point is sound. If God is one, infinite, and wholly good, the problem lies in the meeting of that perfection with a world of limited, already-shaped human societies. The Torah does not speak in an abstract moral vacuum. It addresses a world that already had slavery, as it did conquest, kingship, and animal sacrifice. The Torah's laws are therefore a dialogue between the divine standard and where people actually are.

## What the Torah does with slavery
The Torah's text already pushes against the institution, so "why not abolish it?" should be asked against that background:
- **Hebrew servitude is limited and humane.** It lasts six years and ends in release in the seventh [Exodus 21:2]. Release must come with provision, and the Torah grounds this in memory: "you were a slave in the land of Egypt" [Deuteronomy 15:12-15].
- **Dignity is protected.** A Hebrew servant is not to be worked with *avodat perekh* (crushing labor) [Leviticus 25:39-43]. The Talmud's famous exaggeration is that "whoever buys a Hebrew slave buys himself a master" [Kiddushin 22a], because the master must treat the servant as well as himself.
- **A fugitive slave may not be returned** [Deuteronomy 23:16-17]. This is remarkable for its time and place.
- **Non-Hebrew slaves have protections too.** A master who injures a slave must free him [Exodus 21:26-27], and Maimonides rules that a master must not be cruel and must treat slaves with compassion [Mishneh Torah, Slaves 9:8].

So the Torah is not neutral about slavery. Its whole narrative frame, from Egypt to Sinai, is that Israel was freed to serve God and not to be owned.

## Why not abolish it? The classic approaches
- **Gradual education.** Maimonides argues that God usually leads people step by step, and he gives sacrifice as the central example: God did not abolish it outright but redirected and limited it [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 3 32]. Many readers apply the same logic to slavery, though that application is an extension of his argument and not something he says here.
- **Concession to human nature.** The Talmud, in connection with the captive woman, says "the Torah speaks against the evil inclination" [Kiddushin 21b], meaning that some laws regulate what they could not yet eliminate.
- **Torah is entrusted to human interpretation.** "It is not in heaven" [Deuteronomy 30:12], and the Talmud develops this in the story where the sages overrule a heavenly voice [Bava Metzia 59b]. The living tradition continued to narrow the practice. Later authorities worked within the legal framework, and in modern times many rabbis have understood the direction of the Torah's own values as pointing toward ending slavery.

## Asking versus "making ourselves G-d"
Your distinction is a good one. The tradition gives examples on both sides:
- **Abraham** asks from within a relationship of covenant and responsibility [Genesis 18:23-25].
- **Moses** argues for Israel after the golden calf [Exodus 32:11-13], and **Job** demands an answer. In each case the question is addressed to God and not issued as a verdict over God.
- The mark of legitimate asking is that the questioner stays in the conversation and takes on obligation, instead of simply declaring the Torah wrong and walking away.

One caution: the honest answer to "why wasn't it abolished?" is that the sources offer reasons but no certainty. Saying "we don't know" and continuing to wrestle is itself a recognized stance, so you are in good company.

For how this applies to a particular practical question, consult a rabbi or teacher.

answer:
**Short answer:** There is no single Torah "approval" or "disapproval" of AI. Judaism has no ruling on AI as such. Torah tradition generally welcomes human intelligence and technology as tools that serve God's purposes, and it judges each use by its ethics and halacha. Contemporary rabbis are still working out the specific questions, so you will find a range of opinions.

(My source lookups failed just now because of a rate limit. I cite the sources below by reference, and I paraphrase them instead of quoting.)

## Key Takeaways
- Human creativity and skill are treated as a gift from God, not as a rebellion against Him.
- The Talmud discusses artificially created beings, and it treats them as limited and not truly human.
- The moral test is how the tool is used: honesty, avoiding harm, protecting human dignity, and keeping the mitzvot.
- Rabbinic authorities differ on the specific cases, such as halacha rulings, Shabbat, and relationships with machines.

## The foundations: technology as partnership
- **Human work is part of the plan.** Adam was placed in Eden "to work it and guard it" [Genesis 2:15]. The world is left for us to develop and improve, within limits.
- **Skill is a divine gift.** Bezalel, who built the Tabernacle, was filled with "wisdom, understanding, and knowledge" for craftsmanship [Exodus 31:3]. The Torah honors those who make things with their intelligence.
- **Wisdom is a virtue.** The Torah calls the nation "wise and understanding" because of its Torah [Deuteronomy 4:6]. Learning and discovery are not suspect in themselves.

## Talmudic precedent: artificial beings
- Rava created a man (a *gavra*) by Divine names and sent him to Rabbi Zera. Rabbi Zera spoke to him, and when he did not answer, said, "You were made by the sages; return to your dust" [Sanhedrin 65b].
- Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Oshaya would study the laws of Creation (*Hilchot Yetzirah*) on Shabbat eve and make a calf to eat [Sanhedrin 67b].
- Later authorities, notably in the *golem* literature, used these passages to say that an artificial being lacks speech and a full soul. A machine can imitate intelligence but is not a person. It cannot be counted in a *minyan* or be held to the commandments.

Modern halachic writers often cite these sources when they discuss AI. They are analogies, not direct rulings.

## Ethical tests for any use
- **Honesty.** Deception, fake content, and fraud remain forbidden whoever or whatever produces them [Leviticus 19:11].
- **Harm to others.** Using AI for gossip, slander, or exposing someone's private information runs into the prohibitions on *lashon hara* (harmful speech) and "do not stand by your neighbor's blood" [Leviticus 19:16]. Do not put a "stumbling block before the blind" [Leviticus 19:14], including by misleading people.
- **Responsibility.** A person cannot hand off moral responsibility to a tool. Halacha generally holds the person who sets the process in motion accountable.
- **Human dignity.** Because each person is made in God's image [Genesis 1:27], AI should not be used to demean or exploit people. It also should not replace the human relationships that Judaism values.

## Open questions rabbis discuss
- **Halachic rulings.** Many authorities say AI may help with research and finding sources. A real *posek* (halachic decision-maker) must still rule, because AI can be wrong or invent sources.
- **Torah learning.** AI can be a useful study aid, but it cannot replace a teacher or the living chain of tradition.
- **Shabbat.** Rabbis are discussing whether and how AI and automated systems can be used on Shabbat, and whether this raises problems of creating (*melacha*) or of using electronics.
- **Moral risks.** Surveillance, job displacement, and the concentration of power all bear on Jewish ethics of justice and care for the vulnerable.

## Bottom line
In the Jewish view, the question is less "is AI permitted?" than "what are we doing with it?" Used honestly, to help people, learn, heal, and build, it fits the Torah's call to develop the world. Used to deceive, harm, or replace human responsibility, it conflicts with the Torah. For specific cases, such as Shabbat or halachic questions, consult your rabbi.

answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. It hurts, and the pain shows that your conscience is alive and that you care about your connection to Hashem. Judaism teaches that this feeling of distance is real, but it isn't permanent. The path back is open, and you have already taken the first step.

## Key Takeaways
- Feeling distant from Hashem after sin is a recognized experience, and tradition says it is reversible.
- Heartbreak over what you did is not a sign that you are abandoned. It is closeness in disguise.
- *Teshuvah* (repentance) is often a process, not one moment. Not feeling it "work" right away doesn't mean it failed.
- Your sense of "a lost piece of me" deserves care and support, not only self-judgment.

## "Hashem is close to the brokenhearted"
The verse says: "קָרוֹב יְהֹוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב, וְאֶת־דַּכְּאֵי־רוּחַ יוֹשִׁיעַ" – "God is close to the brokenhearted; those crushed in spirit are delivered" [Psalms 34:19]. The verse does not say Hashem is close only after you feel whole. It says He is close to those who are broken, and that includes you now.

## The distance is real, but so is the return
Rambam describes the contrast between before and after *teshuvah*. Before, "your sins separate between you and your God" (Isaiah 59:2). After, the person "is clinging to the *Shechinah*" (the Divine Presence), and "calls out and is answered immediately" [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 7:7]. Rambam presents this as the nature of *teshuvah*: the barrier you feel can be removed.

The Talmud goes further. It says that "in the place where *ba'alei teshuvah* (those who return) stand, the completely righteous cannot stand" [Berakhot 34b]. Someone who has fallen and come back is not second-class. The return itself is treasured.

## Why it may not feel fixed yet
- **Teshuvah is a process.** Rambam's core steps are to stop, to regret, to confess (*vidui*), and to resolve for the future. Regret and resolve can take time to settle, and the sense of Hashem's closeness often returns gradually.
- **Shame and guilt differ.** Guilt says, "I did something wrong." Shame says, "I am ruined." Torah asks for the first. It never asks you to believe the second. Shame can make Hashem feel absent even when He isn't.
- **Some of what you describe may be partly psychological.** Intrusive images, trouble concentrating, and feeling numb or "emptied" are real effects of distress. They are not a verdict about your soul. If they persist, a therapist, ideally one comfortable with religious clients, can help alongside your rabbi.

## What you can do this week
1. **Speak to Hashem plainly.** Say the words in your own language. Say what happened, that you are sorry, and that you want to come back. Say also that you miss Him. Honest speech is *vidui* and *tefillah*.
2. **Do small, concrete mitzvot.** Examples are a regular prayer, a few lines of Tehillim, giving *tzedakah*, or an act of kindness. Small steady steps rebuild connection better than one intense push.
3. **Put practical safeguards in place.** Use filters, change your environment, and avoid being alone with the device in your trigger situations. These are part of the resolve for the future.
4. **Talk to someone.** Find a rabbi, mentor, or counselor you trust. You don't have to carry this alone, and many people have been where you are.
5. **If you slip again, begin again.** A fall doesn't cancel the *teshuvah* you already did.

If the pain gets so heavy that you feel hopeless or think of harming yourself, please reach out right away to someone you trust or to local emergency services. Your life matters more than any of this.

Please consult your rabbi about your specific situation. If you want, tell me more about what's weighing on you, and we can look at sources together.

answer:
Torah study is how a Jew comes to know what God wants, and it is also how a person builds a relationship with God and shapes their character. In Jewish tradition it is a commandment in its own right, and it also makes every other commandment possible. My source lookups failed just now, so I've paraphrased below instead of quoting exact texts. Please check the references yourself.

## Key Takeaways
- Study is itself a commandment: "you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them" [Deuteronomy 6:7].
- Without learning, one cannot know how to keep the other commandments, so learning is a precondition for living a Jewish life.
- The Sages place Torah study above the other commandments because it leads to all of them [Mishnah Peah 1:1, Kiddushin 40b].
- Torah is also a way of connecting to God, through His wisdom and will.
- Study is meant to change the person, not only to inform them.

## Pshat: a direct commandment
The Torah commands study and teaching in the Shema: "You shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them…" [Deuteronomy 6:7]. Elsewhere, Joshua is told that the book of the Torah should not depart from his mouth and that he should meditate on it day and night [Joshua 1:8]. Rambam codifies this as a duty on every Jew, rich or poor, healthy or ill, young or old [Mishneh Torah, Torah Study 1:8]. Each person is also obligated to teach their children.

## Practical need: you can't do what you don't know
- Rambam holds that a person must learn in order to know how to act [Mishneh Torah, Torah Study 3:3]. Without study, one cannot properly keep Shabbat, kashrut, or the laws of honesty and kindness.
- The Talmud asks whether study or action is greater. The conclusion is that study is greater because it leads to action [Kiddushin 40b].
- The Mishnah lists good deeds whose reward continues and then says that Torah study is equal to them all [Mishnah Peah 1:1].
- *Pirkei Avot* says that an ignorant person cannot be pious [Pirkei Avot 2:5].

## Relationship: Torah as connection to God
- The Torah is described as God's wisdom and will given to us. Studying it is a way of "knowing" Him, as far as a human being can.
- Rambam sees knowing God through His wisdom as the root of love and awe of Him [Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:1-2].
- Kabbalah and Chassidut teach that God and the Torah are deeply united. Learning is therefore a meeting with God, and not only a transfer of information.
- The Sages compare Torah to water, to a healing remedy, and to a "tree of life" [Proverbs 3:18].

## Character and meaning
- The Torah is meant to refine a person. Mesilat Yesharim builds from Torah learning toward watchfulness, zeal, purity, and holiness.
- The Talmud says: "I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its antidote" [Kiddushin 30b].
- Study also gives continuity. Each generation receives the Torah from the previous one and passes it on, so learning keeps the Jewish people connected through time.
- A famous teaching says that Israel, the Torah, and God are bound together (a teaching often quoted from the Zohar).

## Does everyone have to be a scholar?
No. The obligation is set (*kevi'ut*) times of study daily, according to one's capacity, along with earning a living and acting well [Pirkei Avot 1:15]. Many also fulfill it by supporting others' learning. For non-Jews, there is no obligation to study the full Torah. Rambam does encourage learning the seven Noahide laws [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9].

If you tell me what prompted the question, I can suggest where to begin, whether that's the weekly parasha, *Pirkei Avot*, or something else. A local rabbi or teacher can also guide your path in learning.

answer:
**Short answer:** No. The Rambam says this isn't a limit on God's power, because these "things" aren't real possibilities that God fails to do. They are contradictions, and a contradiction is just words that describe nothing. The Rambam's own words are in [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 3 15].

## Key Takeaways
- The Rambam lists God creating another god like Himself, annihilating Himself, becoming a body, or changing as logically impossible.
- Impossibility is a fixed feature of the logic of reality. It isn't something an agent produced, so there's nothing for God to "overcome."
- Not doing the impossible is explicitly "not weakness and not a lack of power."
- The real dispute among thinkers is about which things count as impossible (for example, creation *ex nihilo*), not whether impossibilities exist.
- Each item on the list would contradict God's own nature as necessary, unique, and perfect.

## What the Rambam says
He opens by stating that the impossible "has a permanent and constant property, which is not the result of some agent," so we don't speak of God having power over it. He says no one who understands logic denies this. Among the examples agreed on by all, he lists that God cannot "produce a being like Himself, or annihilate, corporify, or change Himself."

He then concludes that in all of these cases it is "not a weakness on His part nor a lack of power" that He doesn't change them.

## Why these aren't limitations
Think of a "square circle" or a "stone so heavy that its maker can't lift it." These phrases sound like tasks, but they describe nothing. Asking whether God can do them is like asking for a color that's also a sound. The failure is in the sentence, not in the One being asked to act.

Applying this to each of the Rambam's examples:
- **Duplicating Himself:** For God to have an equal would mean two beings who are each absolutely unlimited and necessary. That is a contradiction. It also would mean one of them was *made*, which would make him not God. This follows from God's unity (see [Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7]).
- **Destroying Himself:** God's existence is *necessary*, not contingent. The Rambam begins his code with this: God is the "foundation of foundations" and everything else depends on Him, while He depends on nothing ([Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1-3]). A being whose existence is necessary can't also be one that might cease to exist.
- **Becoming a body or changing:** God is incorporeal and perfect. Change would mean going from lacking something to having it, or the reverse. Perfection admits no such change ([Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:11-12]).

Inability to do such things is actually a mark of perfection. A being who *could* destroy itself, change, or be duplicated would be dependent and finite. In that sense it would be *less* than God.

## Where the Rambam does *not* limit God
The Rambam is not minimalist about divine power. He insists in the same chapter that creation *ex nihilo* is possible, against Aristotelian philosophers who called it impossible. His whole point is to draw the line of "impossible" narrowly, at actual contradiction, and not to say God is bound by nature's laws. Elsewhere he also affirms that God can and does act outside the natural order, such as in miracles.

## Other views
Not everyone is comfortable with this framework. Some thinkers, such as Descartes in the philosophical tradition, held that God's power extends even over logic. Within Jewish thought, some later thinkers, especially in Kabbalah and Chassidut, speak of God's infinite power as beyond all our categories. Others respond that this misses the Rambam's point, since the Rambam holds that logic isn't a rule above God. It reflects God's own truth. These discussions are subtle, and I'd recommend learning the full chapter with a teacher.
