answer:
Your question could mean a few things. I've assumed you mean the Leviathan that God "plays with" (Psalms 104:26 and Avodah Zarah 3b). I've also covered the related idea of the Torah "playing" before God. If you meant a different source, tell me and I'll look at that one.

## Key Takeaways
- The plain verse says Leviathan was formed *lesachek bo*, "to sport with." That describes creation's grandeur and God's effortless mastery over it.
- The Talmud turns this into a picture of God's day. Torah study, judgment, and sustaining the world come first, and "play" with Leviathan is the fourth three-hour block.
- Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says God plays *with* His creatures, not *at their expense*. Rav Aḥa says the play stopped after the Temple's destruction.
- Proverbs 8:30 has a parallel image: the Torah as God's "delight," playing before Him as He created the world.
- The sources are deliberately anthropomorphic. The usual reading is that they point to joy, freedom, and purpose in creation, not to literal amusement.

## The verse
Psalms 104 praises the wisdom in creation. It says: "There go the ships, and Leviathan that You formed to sport with" [Psalms 104:26]. The sea is vast, and its greatest creature is only a toy to its Creator. Rashi connects this to the Talmud's "three hours a day" and to Job's question about Leviathan, "Will you play with him like a bird?" [Rashi on Psalms 104:26].

## The Talmud's picture
Rav describes the divine "day" in four parts [Avodah Zarah 3b:7-10]:
1. God studies Torah.
2. God judges the world. When He sees the world deserves destruction, He moves from the throne of judgment to the throne of mercy.
3. God sustains all life, "from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice."
4. God "sits and plays with Leviathan."

Two comments follow in the Gemara:
- **Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak:** "He plays with His creatures, but He does not play at their expense, except on that day alone." On this reading, God's "play" is gentle. The one exception is the day of Jerusalem's destruction, when He "laughed" at the expense of His creatures.
- **Rav Aḥa:** "From the day the Temple was destroyed, there is no play for the Holy One." The "play" is the joy of a world in harmony with God. With the Temple gone, that joy is withheld.

## What the allegory means
Commentators and later thinkers read it in several ways. These are interpretations, not the text itself.
- **Effortlessness.** Leviathan stands for the most overwhelming force in nature. For God it is a plaything, so no creature threatens His rule.
- **Creation as joy, not necessity.** God did not need the world. He made it freely, as an expression of delight. This fits Proverbs 8:30–31, where the Torah says she was God's "delight every day, rejoicing before Him at all times, rejoicing in His inhabited world."
- **Leviathan as the hidden or sealed-off.** The Midrash and Kabbalistic tradition treat Leviathan as a symbol of great hidden spiritual forces. Their "play" is the quiet, unseen side of divine providence. I'm describing this tradition generally and haven't cited a specific text.
- **Chasidic readings.** Chasidic teachers often say that God's "play" is the joy He has when we connect with Him. This explains why the "play" is tied to the Temple and to Israel's closeness to Him. I haven't pulled a specific source here, so treat this as a general description.

## A note on language
The Torah speaks "in the language of people." Ascribing play to God is a way of speaking about His relationship to creation. It doesn't say that God has needs or moods like a person. The Rambam makes this point in general about anthropomorphic descriptions [Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1]. I haven't pulled the exact chapter.

If you tell me where you came across the phrase, I can look at that specific source.

answer:
Una precisión primero: el sábado 3 de octubre de 2026 cae el 22 de Tishrei de 5787. Ya no es Sucot propiamente dicho sino **Sheminí Atzéret** (el "octavo día de asamblea"). El domingo 4 de octubre (23 de Tishrei) fuera de Israel es **Simjat Torá**, el lunes es *Isru Jag* (el día siguiente a la fiesta) y el resto de la semana termina en **Shabat Bereshit** (10 de octubre), seguido de **Rosh Jódesh Jeshván**. Lo que se hace cada día depende de si vives en Israel o en la Diáspora, así que abajo separo las dos opciones.

*(Una nota: según mi sistema, la fecha de hoy es 23 de noviembre de 2026. Igual preparé el calendario para la semana del 3 de octubre que pediste.)*

## Puntos clave
- **Sábado 3/10:** Sheminí Atzéret. En Israel es al mismo tiempo Simjat Torá.
- **Domingo 4/10:** en la Diáspora es Simjat Torá. En Israel es Isru Jag.
- **Lunes 5/10:** en la Diáspora es Isru Jag. Se suele comer y beber un poco más de lo normal.
- **Sábado 10/10:** Shabat Bereshit y Shabat Mevarjim de Jeshván. Rosh Jódesh Jeshván cae el domingo 11 y el lunes 12.

---

## Sábado 3 de octubre (22 de Tishrei): Sheminí Atzéret
La Torá lo establece como una fiesta aparte, que va pegada a Sucot (Levítico 23:36).

**Cómo se celebra:**
- Es *Yom Tov* (día de fiesta): no se trabaja y se hacen comidas festivas. Este año además cae en Shabat, así que rigen todas las leyes de Shabat.
- En la Amidá se menciona "יום שמיני עצרת הזה" (este octavo día de Atzéret). El Remá aclara que no se le llama "jag" (festividad), porque la Torá nunca lo llama así [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 668:1].
- En el Musaf se dice la **Tefilat Guéshem** (la oración por la lluvia). A partir de ese momento se agrega "Mashiv haruaj umorid haguéshem" en la Amidá.
- La mayoría de las comunidades ashkenazíes dicen **Yizkor**, el recuerdo de los difuntos.
- **La sucá:**
  - **En la Diáspora** se come en la sucá de día y de noche, porque existe la duda de que sea en realidad el séptimo día de Sucot. Pero **no se dice la bendición** de "leishev basucá". En el kidush se dice *Shehejeyanu* [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 668:1].
  - **Jabad** come en la sucá en Sheminí Atzéret, pero no en Simjat Torá. Algunas comunidades jasídicas tienen costumbres distintas.
  - **En Israel** ya no se come en la sucá.
- **En Israel**, este mismo día es también Simjat Torá: se hacen las *hakafot* (vueltas con los rollos de la Torá) y se termina y se empieza la Torá. Mira lo que explico para el domingo.

## Sábado por la noche y domingo 4 de octubre (23 de Tishrei)

### En la Diáspora: Simjat Torá
- **La noche:** kidush con Shehejeyanu [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 669:1]. Luego vienen las **hakafot**: se sacan todos los rollos de la Torá y se dan vueltas alrededor de la *bimá* (la plataforma de lectura) cantando y bailando. El Remá lo describe así: "והכל משום שמחה" ("y todo es por la alegría").
- **La mañana:** otra vez hakafot, y después se sacan tres rollos:
  1. En el primero se lee **Vezot Haberajá**, hasta el final de la Torá. Ese honor se llama *Jatán Torá*.
  2. En el segundo se empieza **Bereshit**. Ese honor se llama *Jatán Bereshit*.
  3. En el tercero se lee el *maftir* del día.
  - La *haftará* es "Vayehí ajarei mot Moshé" (Josué 1) [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 669:1].
- **Otras costumbres** que recoge el Remá:
  - Se llama a la Torá a todos los presentes, repitiendo la misma porción tantas veces como haga falta.
  - En la aliyá de **"Kol hanearim"** suben todos los niños juntos y se les lee "Hamalaj hagoel" (el ángel que redime).
  - Se hace un banquete para celebrar que se terminó la Torá [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 669:1].
- **Sefaradíes:** las mismas ideas, con sus melodías y su orden de *hakafot*. En muchas comunidades se subastan los honores de Jatán Torá y Jatán Bereshit.

### En Israel: Isru Jag
- Al terminar el sábado se hace la *havdalá* (la ceremonia de despedida del Shabat). En muchos lugares se organizan además *hakafot sheniyot* (segundas hakafot), a menudo con música, como gesto de solidaridad con la Diáspora.
- El domingo es Isru Jag (lo explico en el lunes).

## Lunes 5 de octubre (24 de Tishrei): Isru Jag en la Diáspora
- El Remá escribe: "ונוהגין להרבות קצת באכילה ושתיה ביום אחר החג והוא אסרו חג" ("se acostumbra comer y beber un poco más el día después de la fiesta, que es Isru Jag") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 429:2].
- No se dice *Tajanún* (las súplicas diarias).
- Ese día se puede desarmar la sucá.

## Martes 6 a viernes 9 de octubre (25 a 28 de Tishrei): días normales
- Se vuelve a la rutina. Muchos ven aquí el momento de llevar a la vida diaria la inspiración de los Yamim Noraím (los días solemnes de Rosh Hashaná y Yom Kipur) y de Sucot.
- **El Tajanún varía según la comunidad:**
  - Muchas comunidades sefaradíes y Jabad no lo dicen hasta que termina Tishrei.
  - En muchas comunidades ashkenazíes se vuelve a decir después de Isru Jag.
  - Lo mejor es seguir lo que haga tu sinagoga.

## Sábado 10 de octubre (29 de Tishrei): Shabat Bereshit
- Se lee la **parashá Bereshit**: se empieza otra vez la Torá desde el principio en la lectura semanal.
- Es **Shabat Mevarjim**: se bendice el mes de Jeshván. El *molad* (la luna nueva) es el domingo a las 9:43 a. m. y 2 *jalakim*.
- Como es víspera de Rosh Jódesh, la haftará suele ser **"Majar Jódesh"** (Samuel I 20).
- Jabad da mucha importancia a este Shabat. Según su enseñanza, "como uno se establece en Shabat Bereshit, así será todo el año".

## Domingo 11 y lunes 12 de octubre: Rosh Jódesh Jeshván
- Se agregan *Yaalé veyavó* (la oración especial de Rosh Jódesh), medio *Halel* y *Musaf*.

---

Si me dices tu ciudad, te paso los horarios exactos de encendido de velas y de havdalá. También podemos estudiar juntos Vezot Haberajá o el comienzo de Bereshit. Para las costumbres de tu propia comunidad, te recomiendo consultar con tu rabino.

answer:
Los textos para leer en Sukkot salen de Levítico 23, de Números 29 y de los profetas. La Guemará (Meguilá 31a) los fija para el primer día, para Jol HaMoed (los días intermedios) y para Shemini Atzéret. Las "7 Nubes de Gloria" son una tradición midráshica: no encontré una lista de siete con cita exacta en la Guemará, y las fuentes varían, así que lo marco abajo.

## Puntos clave
- El primer día se lee Levítico 22:26–23:44 y la haftará es Zacarías 14. En la diáspora el segundo día repite la Torá, con haftará de Reyes I 8.
- En Jol HaMoed se leen los sacrificios de la fiesta (Números 29). En el Shabat de Jol HaMoed se lee "Reé atá" (Éxodo 33:12 en adelante), con haftará de Ezequiel 38–39.
- Shemini Atzéret lleva Deuteronomio 14:22–16:17 (*Kol HaBejor*). Simjat Torá lleva *Vezot HaBeracá*.
- La sucá recuerda las Nubes de Gloria según R. Eliezer (Sucá 11b). La tradición de siete nubes es un midrash, no un pshat (sentido literal) del texto.

## 1. Las lecturas

La base es [Meguilá 31a]: "Yom tov harishón shel jag korin befarashat moadot shebetorat kohanim, umaftirin 'Hineh yom ba laShem'… veshear kol yemot hajag korin bekorbanot hajag. Yom tov haajarón korin 'Kol habejor'… umaftirin 'Vayhi kejalot Shlomó'. Lemajar korin 'Vezot haberajá', umaftirin 'Vayamod Shlomó'."

En español: el primer día de la fiesta se lee la parashá de las festividades de Levítico, con la haftará "He aquí viene un día para HaShem". Los demás días se leen los sacrificios de la fiesta. El último día se lee "Todo primogénito". Al día siguiente se lee "Y esta es la bendición".

Las lecturas actuales son estas:

| Día | Torá | Haftará |
|---|---|---|
| 1.º día de Sukkot | Levítico 22:26–23:44, y de maftir Números 29:12–16 | Zacarías 14:1–21 |
| 2.º día (solo diáspora) | Igual que el 1.º | Reyes I 8:2–21 |
| Jol HaMoed | Números 29:17–34, repartido según el día | – |
| Shabat de Jol HaMoed | Éxodo 33:12–34:26 (*Reé atá*), y de maftir los sacrificios del día | Ezequiel 38:18–39:16 (la Guemará dice "*beyom bó Gog*") |
| Shemini Atzéret | Deuteronomio 14:22–16:17, y de maftir Números 29:35–30:1 | Reyes I 8:54–9:1 |
| Simjat Torá (en Israel coincide con Shemini Atzéret) | Deuteronomio 33–34 y Génesis 1:1–2:3, y de maftir Números 29:35–30:1 | Josué 1 |

Notas que verifiqué en la Guemará:
- **Shabat de Jol HaMoed:** Rav Huna dice que se lee "*Reé atá*" y se lee de haftará "*beyom bó Gog*" ([Meguilá 31a]).
- **Haftará del segundo día:** la Guemará cita "*Vayikahalú el hamélej Shlomó*" ([Meguilá 31a]).
- **Los demás datos de la tabla:** el reparto exacto de Números 29 por día, Josué 1 en Simjat Torá y las páginas de Éxodo 33–34 son la costumbre vigente. No los recuperé de las fuentes en esta consulta.

**Diferencias por comunidad:**
- **Israel y diáspora:** en Israel hay un solo día de Yom Tov al principio y Shemini Atzéret es también Simjat Torá. En la diáspora hay dos días de cada uno, y el reparto de Números 29 en Jol HaMoed cambia según el día.
- **Ashkenazi:** se lee el rollo de Kohélet (Eclesiastés) en el Shabat de Jol HaMoed.
- **Sefaradí y Jabad:** las lecturas de Torá son esencialmente las mismas. Algunos detalles de las costumbres (Kohélet, el reparto de los días) varían según la comunidad.
- **Mitzvot propias de la fiesta:** también se recitan Hallel completo, el lulav y el etrog, y los Hoshanot. Hoy, 23 de noviembre de 2026, Sukkot ya pasó. La próxima vez será en 2027.

## 2. Las Nubes de Gloria

**El texto base.** La Torá dice: "*Basukot teshvú shivat yamim… ki vasukot hoshavtí et benei Yisrael*" ([Levítico 23:42-43]). Es decir: "Habitarán en cabañas siete días… porque en cabañas hice habitar a los hijos de Israel".

Los Sabios discuten a qué se refiere. La Guemará pregunta sobre la sucá: "*hanija lemán damar ananei kavod hayú*", es decir, esto cuadra con quien dice que fueron nubes de gloria. La otra opinión dice que hicieron cabañas verdaderas ([Sucá 11b]). Por eso la sucá recuerda las Nubes de Gloria, según R. Eliezer. Sus raíces están en el Éxodo: la nube que guiaba de día y la columna de fuego de noche.

**Las siete nubes.** La tradición midráshica (que se cita también en comentaristas posteriores) cuenta siete funciones. En algunas versiones, las fuentes cuentan cuatro o cinco nubes, o las reparten de otra forma. Esta es la lista más conocida, que explico como midrash:

1. **Nube del lado este.** Protegía a Israel por ese lado.
2. **Nube del lado oeste.** Hacía lo mismo por el oeste.
3. **Nube del lado norte.** Protegía por el norte.
4. **Nube del lado sur.** Protegía por el sur. Las cuatro primeras formaban una pared de protección alrededor del campamento.
5. **Nube de arriba.** Daba sombra contra el sol y la lluvia en el desierto, y protegía de las calamidades.
6. **Nube de abajo.** Según el midrash, allanaba el terreno y mantenía el suelo limpio. Esa idea se asocia a que sus ropas no se gastaban.
7. **Nube que iba delante.** Guiaba la marcha, levantaba los valles y bajaba las montañas, y mataba a las serpientes y escorpiones del camino. Es la columna de nube de Éxodo 13:21.

Los midrashim también dicen que la nube limpiaba y planchaba la ropa de Israel. Dicen además que las nubes se retiraron con la muerte de Aharón y regresaron por el mérito de Moshé. El mérito de Aharón también se asocia con ellas.

**Relación con la sucá y los Ushpizín.** La sucá actualiza ese amparo. El Zohar y la tradición cabalista hablan de siete huéspedes (*ushpizín*): Avraham, Yitzjak, Yaakov, Moshé, Aharón, Yosef y David. Algunos los relacionan con las siete nubes, pero eso es una conexión cabalística posterior, no una enseñanza de la Guemará.

*Consulta a tu rabino* para saber qué costumbre sigue tu comunidad en las lecturas y en los detalles de la fiesta.

answer:
Today's daf is **Arakhin 6** (Daf Yomi, 23 Nov 2026). It starts with gifts from gentiles and with changing the purpose of pledged *tzedakah* (charity). It then moves to a new mishnah about a dying person (*gosess*) and a person being led to execution, and whether they can be the subject of vows or valuations.

## Key Takeaways
- Gentile donations to the Temple are refused at the start of the building and are accepted at the end, but only if the gift is not "defined" (identifiable as theirs).
- A gentile's *terumah* is buried if there is doubt whether he meant it for Heaven, which is a Temple dedication.
- You may change the use of a coin you pledged to charity until it reaches the *gabbai* (charity collector). After that you may not.
- A synagogue lamp may be repurposed for another *mitzvah*, but not for a voluntary use. If the donor was a gentile, wait until his name is forgotten.
- A *gosess* cannot be the subject of a vow or valuation. Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya and Rabbi Yose disagree about the person led to execution.

## Part 1: Gentile donations to the Temple (6a)
- **The contradiction:** One baraita says "we accept" a gentile's pledge for Temple maintenance (*bedek habayit*). Another says "we do not accept."
- **Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:** The first baraita is about the end of the building, and the second is about the beginning.
  - Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: At the beginning, we accept "not even water and salt."
  - At the end, we do not accept a defined item (*davar hamsuyam*). We do accept an undefined one.
  - Rashi on Arakhin 6a explains that at the beginning we are concerned about "weakening of hands." This means the Jews might come to rely on gentile funding. A defined item brings disgrace, and the gentiles would boast about it.
- **Example of a defined item:** Rav Yosef gives the spiked iron plates, a cubit square, that kept ravens off the Sanctuary roof (*amah kliya orev*).
- **Challenge:** Rav Yosef cites Nehemiah's request to the Persian king for timber from the royal forest [Nehemiah 2:8]. Abaye answers that a government does not retract its word. He quotes Shmuel: if the government says "I will uproot mountains," it does so.

## Part 2: A gentile's *terumah* and a donated beam (6a)
- **Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav:** When a gentile separates *terumah* from his grain pile, we examine his intent.
  - If he meant it "with the knowledge of Israel," it goes to a *kohen*.
  - If not, it must be buried (*genizah*). We worry that "perhaps in his heart it was for Heaven," meaning *hekdesh*.
- **Objection:** A baraita says that a gentile donated a beam with God's Name written on it. The Name is cut off (*yagod*) and buried, and the rest is used.
  - Question: Does this imply that a beam without a Name needs no burial?
  - Answer: No, it needs burial too. The baraita adds that even with the Name written on it, we cut off the Name and use the remainder. This is because a Name written where it does not belong has no holiness (*shem shelo bimkomo lav kadosh*). The Gemara supports this from a mishnah about names written on the handles of utensils.

## Part 3: "This *sela* is for charity" (6a–6b)
- **Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuha:** One who says "this *sela* is for charity" may change it. The Gemara debates how far this goes:
  - Rabbi Yochanan: it applies whether he changes it for himself or for another person.
  - Rabbi Zeira: it applies only if he said "*alai*" (it is incumbent on me). If he said "*harei zo*" (behold this), he must give that very coin.
  - Rava: the reverse is more logical. With "*harei zo*" he may use it so that he is liable for it. So there is no difference between the two wordings.
  - Rav Zevid of Nehardea's version of the tradition: it is permitted in all cases, whether for himself or another, and with either wording.
  - Rashi explains that the person is treated like one who takes a deposit. He takes responsibility for it and replaces it.
- **Baraita:** Until the coin reaches the *gabbai*, you may change it. Afterwards you may not.
- **Rabbi Yannai:** He borrowed from the charity fund and repaid it. The Gemara says this was acceptable because it benefited the poor. A depleted fund moves people to give more.

## Part 4: Changing a synagogue lamp (6b)
- **Baraita:** If a Jew donated a *menorah* or lamp to a synagogue, it is forbidden to change it.
- **Rabbi Chiya bar Abba:** Thought this applied to every use.
- **Rav Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:** It applies only to a voluntary use (*davar reshut*). For a *mitzvah* use it is permitted.
  - He proves this from a gentile's donation. Until the donor's name is forgotten, we may not change it, because a gentile would protest. A Jew would not protest if the item went to another *mitzvah*.
- **Story of Sha'azrak the Arab merchant:** He donated a lamp to Rav Yehuda's synagogue, and one of the Sages repurposed it. The versions differ on who did it and who was angry (Rachava, Rava, the Pumbedita attendants, Rabba). Those who changed it thought he was unlikely to return and protest. Those who objected thought he might come back.

## Part 5: New mishnah – the *gosess* and the one led to execution (6b)
- **Mishnah:** A *gosess* or someone being taken to execution cannot be the subject of a vow (*nidar*) or of a valuation (*ne'erach*).
  - Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya: he can be valued, because the Torah fixes the amounts.
  - Rabbi Yose: he can vow and value, and if he causes damage he is liable.
- **Gemara:**
  - A *gosess* has no monetary worth and cannot be "stood and valued."
  - For the one led to execution, the Gemara quotes [Leviticus 27:29], "*kol cherem lo yipadeh*" (nothing devoted shall be redeemed). It limits this with "*min ha'adam*" (of man), meaning not every person. This applies only after the verdict is final.
  - Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka: The verse teaches that death at human hands is not atoned for by payment. Death at the hands of Heaven can be, as in "*im kofer yushat alav*" [Exodus 21:30].
  - **Rabbi Yose's dispute with the first Tanna:** Both agree he can vow, value and dedicate. They disagree only about liability for damage.
    - Rav Yosef: they disagree over whether an oral loan can be collected from heirs.
    - Rava: they disagree over whether a debt written in the Torah counts as a written document.

answer:
This week's parasha is **Vayishlach** (וישלח), read on Shabbat, November 28, 2026. The Torah reading is [Genesis 32:4-36:43]. The haftarah is Obadiah 1:1-21.

**Key Takeaways**
- Yaakov prepares for his meeting with Esav through gifts, prayer, and readiness for battle.
- Yaakov wrestles with a mysterious figure and is renamed Yisrael.
- The parasha also includes the episode of Dinah and Shechem, Yaakov's return to Beit El, the deaths of Rachel and Yitzchak, and the lineage of Esav.
- The haftarah of Obadiah is a prophecy about Edom, which is Esav's descendants.

**Outline by aliyah**
1. [Genesis 32:4-13]: Yaakov sends messengers to Esav and hears that Esav is coming with 400 men. He divides his camp and prays.
2. [Genesis 32:14-30]: Yaakov sends gifts ahead, crosses the Yabbok, and wrestles with a man until dawn. He is given the name Yisrael.
3. [Genesis 32:31-33:5]: Yaakov limps away. The prohibition of the *gid hanasheh* (sciatic nerve) is introduced. Yaakov and Esav meet.
4. [Genesis 33:6-20]: The brothers part. Yaakov settles in Sukkot and then Shechem.
5. [Genesis 34:1-35:11]: The episode of Dinah and Shechem. Yaakov goes to Beit El and buries the idols. God blesses him again.
6. [Genesis 35:12-36:19]: Rachel dies giving birth to Binyamin. Reuven's act with Bilhah is recorded. Yitzchak dies. Esav's descendants are listed.
7. [Genesis 36:20-43]: The families of Seir and the kings of Edom.

**Themes often discussed**
- Rashi on the opening verses, drawing on midrash, says the "messengers" were actual angels. Yaakov's three-part preparation is often described as gifts, prayer, and war.
- The wrestling match is traditionally read as a struggle with Esav's guardian angel. It is also read as Yaakov's inner transformation.
- The haftarah of Obadiah continues the theme of Edom's downfall.

answer:
**This year is 5787, the 5th year of the shemitah cycle. The second tithe is *maaser sheni*** (redeemed onto a coin), not *maaser ani* (the tithe for the poor). I checked the date: today is 13 Kislev 5787. The last shemitah was 5782, and the next is 5789.

**Which year your produce belongs to:**
- **Vegetables:** go by when they're picked. Anything picked now counts as year 5, so the second tithe is *maaser sheni*.
- **Tree fruit:** go by when the fruit first formed (*chanatah*), measured from Tu BiShvat. Most fruit picked now formed after Tu BiShvat 5786 (the previous year), which was year 4. That's also *maaser sheni*.
- **Exception:** fruit that formed before Tu BiShvat 5786 belongs to year 3 (5785). For that fruit the second tithe is *maaser ani*, which isn't redeemed. This is rare, mostly long-hanging citrus.

## Blessings
Only say these over produce that is **definitely untithed (*tevel vadai*)**, for example from your own garden or a field you know wasn't tithed. Over produce that is only *doubtfully* tithed (*demai*), separate the tithes without a blessing.

1. Before separating:
   **בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לְהַפְרִישׁ תְּרוּמוֹת וּמַעַשְׂרוֹת**
   (Blessed are You… who commanded us to separate *terumot* and *maasrot*, the priestly gifts and tithes.)
2. For redeeming the *maaser sheni*:
   **…וְצִוָּנוּ עַל פִּדְיוֹן מַעֲשֵׂר שֵׁנִי**
   (…who commanded us concerning the redemption of *maaser sheni*.)
   Many poskim say this blessing only when you redeem at the produce's full value. If you use the usual "one *perutah* (smallest coin unit) of a coin" method, many advise leaving it out. Ask your rav which practice to follow.

## How much to remove
- Set aside **a little more than 1%** of the produce.
- Recite the standard separation text (*nusach*) that designates this portion as *terumah* (the priestly portion) and *terumat maaser* (the tithe of the tithe). The text also designates which part of the produce is *maaser rishon* and *maaser sheni*, so you don't remove those physically.
- This is printed on cards from Machon HaTorah VeHaAretz and in many siddurim. Saying it ends with the *maaser sheni* being "redeemed with its fifth on one *perutah* of the designated coin."
- The separated portion is holy and can't be eaten. Wrap it in a bag and put it in the trash or compost respectfully.

## The coin
- Set aside one coin for this. It should be worth many *perutot* (roughly a few agorot each in today's money), so a 1-shekel coin or higher works. Each time you redeem, you use up one *perutah* of its value.
- When the coin is "full," say a short text to redeem it onto a tiny coin worth one *perutah*. Then destroy that small coin or throw it into the sea, and start again with the large coin.
- Many people instead use a "coin" held by an organization like Machon HaTorah VeHaAretz or Keren Hashviis, by including it in the text they say.

The blessing details are where practice varies most, so please consult your rabbi for your own case.

answer:
**He becomes bar mitzvah in Adar I.** If a boy was born in Adar I of a leap year, and the year he turns 13 is also a leap year, his bar mitzvah is in Adar I, on the same day of the month he was born. A boy born in Adar II has his in Adar II. The rule is to match the month he was actually born in.

*(Note: Sefaria's library wasn't responding when I tried to look up the texts, so the sources below are cited from memory. I paraphrase them rather than quote them. Please check the inside text of [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 55:10] and the commentaries there.)*

## Key Takeaways
- **Leap year to leap year:** born in Adar I means bar mitzvah in Adar I, and born in Adar II means Adar II.
- **Leap year to regular year:** a boy born in either Adar I or Adar II has his bar mitzvah in the one Adar of that year.
- **Regular year to leap year:** a boy born in Adar of a regular year has his bar mitzvah in Adar II, according to the Rema. This is the accepted practice, though some disagreed.
- **Months, not days, are counted.** In a leap year that's 13 months, so a younger boy can sometimes become bar mitzvah before an older one.

## The basic rule
The age of 13 is counted in calendar years, from the day of birth to the same day 13 years later. It isn't counted by the number of days that pass. A leap year has 13 months, and the extra month still counts as part of that one year.

The Shulchan Arukh discusses this in the laws of counting a boy for a minyan [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 55:10]. Its ruling is that the bar mitzvah falls in the Adar the boy was born in: Adar I for a boy born in Adar I, and Adar II for a boy born in Adar II. Both are real, named months. So when the 13th year also has two Adars, the birth month is simply there again.

## The other combinations
1. **Born in a leap year, turns 13 in a regular year.** The regular year has only one Adar, so a boy born in either Adar I or Adar II has his bar mitzvah in that Adar.
2. **Born in a regular year, turns 13 in a leap year.** This is the case people argue about. In his gloss there, the Rema rules, following the Mahari"k, that the boy only becomes bar mitzvah in Adar II. The reasoning is that the Adar of a regular year is the Adar next to Nisan. Some earlier authorities held Adar I. Practice follows the Rema, and many Sephardi authorities agree in this case as well. Since the halachic consequences are real (counting for a minyan, Torah-level obligations), a family in this situation should ask their rav.

## A strange result
The Acharonim point out something odd that follows from this system. Imagine two boys born in a leap year, one on 29 Adar I and the other the next day, 1 Adar II. If their 13th year is a regular year, the younger boy becomes bar mitzvah on 1 Adar. The older boy has to wait until 29 Adar, four weeks later. This happens because the law counts months and years, not days.

## In practice
- The *aliyah* (being called to the Torah), counting toward a minyan, and full obligation in the mitzvot all start on the halachic date worked out above, at nightfall.
- Many families hold the celebration at another time. But a boy only counts for a minyan, and only fulfills obligations for others, from the actual date.
- Use a Hebrew–Gregorian converter (I can do this for you if you give me the birth date) to check whether both years are leap years.

For your own situation, please ask your rabbi, especially in the regular-year-to-leap-year case.

answer:
The 17th of Tammuz (*Shiv'ah Asar b'Tammuz*) is a public fast day marking five disasters in Jewish history. The best known are Moses breaking the Tablets after the Golden Calf and the breach of Jerusalem's walls before the Temple was destroyed. It begins the Three Weeks of mourning that end on Tisha B'Av. The prophets promised that one day it will become a festival. Next year it falls on Thursday, July 22, 2027 (17 Tammuz 5787).

## Key Takeaways
- The Mishnah lists five calamities on 17 Tammuz: the Tablets were broken, the daily offering stopped, the city walls were breached, Apostemos burned a Torah, and an idol was placed in the Sanctuary.
- The Talmud works out the date of the broken Tablets by counting Moses' 40 days on Mount Sinai.
- The Shulchan Arukh counts it as one of the four required fasts commemorating the destruction.
- It starts the Three Weeks (*Bein HaMetzarim*). Ashkenazim begin mourning customs now; many Sephardim start them later.
- Zechariah foretold that the "fast of the fourth month" will turn into a day of joy.

## The five calamities
The source is the Mishnah [Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6]:

> חֲמִשָּׁה דְבָרִים אֵרְעוּ אֶת אֲבוֹתֵינוּ בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר בְּתַמּוּז... נִשְׁתַּבְּרוּ הַלּוּחוֹת, וּבָטַל הַתָּמִיד, וְהֻבְקְעָה הָעִיר, וְשָׂרַף אַפּוֹסְטֹמוֹס אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, וְהֶעֱמִיד צֶלֶם בַּהֵיכָל
> "Five things happened to our ancestors on the seventeenth of Tammuz… the Tablets were broken, the *tamid* (daily offering) stopped, the city was breached, Apostemos burned the Torah, and an idol was set up in the Sanctuary."

1. **The Tablets were broken.** This is the first and most basic disaster, when Moses came down and saw the Golden Calf ([Exodus 32:19](Exodus 32:19)).
2. **The *tamid* stopped.** The daily offering could no longer be brought during the siege. The Gemara says this is known by tradition.
3. **The walls of Jerusalem were breached.** This began the final stage before the Temple was destroyed three weeks later.
4. **Apostemos burned a Torah scroll.** He was apparently an official of the Greek or Roman period. His exact identity is unclear.
5. **An idol was placed in the Sanctuary.** The Gemara connects this to Daniel's "abomination of desolation." Commentators disagree about who did it; some say King Manasseh, others say Apostemos.

## How the Talmud works out the dates
The Gemara [Taanit 28b] explains two of these items:

- **The Tablets.** The Torah was given on 6 or 7 Sivan, and Moses went up the mountain on the 7th for 40 days. The rest of Sivan (24 days) plus 16 days of Tammuz makes 40: "בְּשִׁיבְסַר בְּתַמּוּז נְחֵית, אֲתָא וְתַבְרִינְהוּ לְלוּחוֹת" ("on the seventeenth of Tammuz he came down and broke the Tablets").
- **The breach of the walls.** Jeremiah says the city was breached on the *ninth* of the fourth month. Rava explains: "כָּאן — בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה, כָּאן — בַּשְּׁנִיָּה". In other words, the First Temple's walls fell on 9 Tammuz and the Second Temple's on the 17th. Because the Second Temple's destruction is closer to us, the fast was set on the 17th.
- The Jerusalem Talmud offers another view: the First Temple breach was also on the 17th, but in the chaos of the time the date was recorded wrongly.

## The prophetic source and its hopeful side
Zechariah calls this day the "fast of the fourth month" (Tammuz, counting from Nisan) and gives a promise [Zechariah 8:19]:

> צ֣וֹם הָרְבִיעִ֡י וְצ֣וֹם הַחֲמִישִׁי֩... יִהְיֶ֤ה לְבֵית־יְהוּדָה֙ לְשָׂשׂ֣וֹן וּלְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּֽלְמֹעֲדִ֖ים טוֹבִ֑ים
> "The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth month… shall become occasions for joy and gladness, happy festivals for the House of Judah."

So the day carries two meanings: it mourns what was lost, and it looks forward to redemption. Rambam (Laws of Fasts, ch. 5) explains that these fasts are not mainly about hunger. Their purpose is to stir *teshuvah* (repentance) by remembering our ancestors' sins, which are like our own, and what they led to.

## Halacha in practice
- **Required fast.** "חייבים להתענות... ובשבעה עשר בתמוז" ("we are required to fast… on the seventeenth of Tammuz") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 549:1]. This is a minor fast: it runs from dawn to nightfall, and only eating and drinking are forbidden.
- **Exemptions.** Pregnant and nursing women, and people who are ill, are generally exempt or treated leniently. Anyone with a health concern should ask a rav.
- **Prayers.** Selichot and Avinu Malkeinu are said, and *Aneinu* is added to the Amidah. The Torah reading is *Vayechal* (Exodus 32), the story of the Golden Calf and God forgiving the people, at Shacharit and Mincha. At Mincha the haftarah is *Dirshu* (Isaiah 55), though many Sephardi communities do not read a haftarah at Mincha.

## The Three Weeks
The 17th of Tammuz begins *Bein HaMetzarim* ("between the straits," from Lamentations 1:3), which ends on Tisha B'Av:
- **Ashkenazim:** The Rema writes: "ונוהגין להחמיר שאין נושאים מי"ז בתמוז ואילך עד אחר תשעה באב" ("the custom is to be strict and not hold weddings from the 17th of Tammuz until after Tisha B'Av") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 551:2]. By custom, Ashkenazim also avoid haircuts and live music from the 17th.
- **Sephardim:** The Shulchan Arukh itself limits joyful activities, including weddings, only from Rosh Chodesh Av [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 551:2]. Many Sephardim avoid haircuts only during the week of Tisha B'Av. Customs vary, so follow your community.

For your own situation, especially health questions about fasting or wedding dates, please consult your rabbi.

Rate limited. Retry one or two.En principe, une femme doit faire une prière chaque matin. Pour la majorité des décisionnaires, elle doit réciter la *Amida* (les 18 bénédictions, prière dite debout) de Cha'harit, comme les hommes. On recommande aussi de dire au minimum le premier verset du *Chema Israël*, ainsi que les bénédictions du matin. Pour une femme très occupée (par exemple avec de jeunes enfants), certains se contentent d'une courte prière personnelle. Cette pratique repose sur un avis plus souple, qui n'est pas la position principale.

## Points clés
- La Michna dit que les femmes sont **dispensées du Chema** mais **obligées de prier** [Mishnah Berakhot 3:3].
- Le Rambam et le Ramban ne sont pas d'accord sur ce qui suffit. Le Michna Beroura tranche selon la majorité des décisionnaires : il faut dire la Amida du matin et de l'après-midi (*Min'ha*) [Mishnah Berurah 106:4].
- On recommande aussi de dire *Chema Israël* et la bénédiction *Emet veYatsiv*, qui fait le lien entre le Chema et la Amida.
- Il y a une différence entre communautés : les ashkénazes et Habad disent la bénédiction *Chéassani kirtsono* avec le nom de Dieu, les séfarades sans le nom de Dieu.

## 1. Le fondement : une obligation de prier
La Michna enseigne : « נָשִׁים וַעֲבָדִים וּקְטַנִּים פְּטוּרִין מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּמִן הַתְּפִלִּין, וְחַיָּבִין בִּתְפִלָּה » (« Les femmes, les esclaves et les mineurs sont dispensés de la lecture du Chema et des téfilines, mais obligés de prier ») [Mishnah Berakhot 3:3]. La raison donnée : la prière est une demande de miséricorde, dont chacun a besoin.

Le Michna Beroura présente deux avis (ma traduction résumée) [Mishnah Berurah 106:4] :
- **Le Rambam** : l'obligation de prier vient de la Torah, mais sans texte fixe. Une seule prière par jour, avec les mots qu'on veut, suffit pour la Torah. D'après le Maguen Avraham, c'est pour cela que beaucoup de femmes avaient l'habitude de dire seulement une courte demande le matin, juste après s'être lavé les mains.
- **Le Ramban** : la prière vient des Sages (*Anché Knesset HaGuedola*), qui ont fixé la Amida le matin et l'après-midi. Les femmes y sont obligées comme les hommes.
- **La décision** : « וכן עיקר כי כן דעת רוב הפוסקים » (« c'est l'avis principal, car c'est celui de la majorité des décisionnaires »), comme le tranche aussi le Chaagat Arié. Il faut donc encourager les femmes à dire la Amida. Il est aussi bon qu'elles disent au moins *Chema Israël*, puis *Emet veYatsiv*, pour enchaîner la délivrance et la prière (*samkhout gueoula litefila*).
- **Le soir** : la prière du soir (*Arvit*) n'est pas une obligation pour les femmes, et la plupart ne la disent pas.

## 2. L'ordre concret de la prière du matin
1. **Modé ani** au réveil : une phrase de remerciement à Dieu qui nous rend l'âme. Elle ne contient pas le nom de Dieu, on peut donc la dire avant de se laver les mains.
2. **Lavage des mains** (*nétilat yadayim*) et sa bénédiction, puis *Acher yatsar*.
3. **Les bénédictions de la Torah** (*Birkot HaTorah*) : les femmes les disent, selon la pratique admise par le Choul'han Aroukh.
4. **Les bénédictions du matin** (*Birkot HaCha'har*). À la place de *Chélo assani icha*, la femme dit **« Chéassani kirtsono »** (« qui m'a faite selon Sa volonté ») :
   - **Ashkénazes et Habad** : avec le nom de Dieu, selon le Rema.
   - **Séfarades** : sans le nom de Dieu, selon le Ben Ich 'Haï et le Rav Ovadia Yossef.
5. **Les Psaumes du matin** (*Pessouké deZimra*) : ils sont recommandés si on a le temps. Selon le Rav Ovadia Yossef, les femmes séfarades ne disent pas le nom de Dieu dans *Baroukh chéamar* et *Yichtaba'h*. Beaucoup d'ashkénazes les disent normalement.
6. **Le Chema** : au moins le premier verset, et si possible tout le Chema avec ses bénédictions, jusqu'à *Emet veYatsiv*.
7. **La Amida de Cha'harit** : c'est le cœur de l'obligation selon la majorité des décisionnaires.

## 3. Selon les communautés
- **Ashkénazes** : la Amida du matin et de l'après-midi, comme le tranche le Michna Beroura. Chema et Emet veYatsiv fortement recommandés.
- **Séfarades** : le Rav Ovadia Yossef enseigne aussi que les femmes sont obligées de dire la Amida de Cha'harit et de Min'ha. Pour les bénédictions dont l'obligation est incertaine, il demande de les dire sans le nom de Dieu (*Chéassani kirtsono*, *Baroukh chéamar*).
- **Habad** : le texte est celui de l'Ari (*Noussa'h Ari*). Le Rabbi de Loubavitch encourageait les femmes à dire les bénédictions du matin, le Chema et la Amida.

## 4. Si l'on manque de temps
Une mère de jeunes enfants qui n'arrive pas à prier longuement peut s'appuyer sur l'avis du Rambam et du Maguen Avraham. Elle dit alors au moins les bénédictions du matin et une courte prière personnelle, dans la langue de son choix, même en français. Si possible, elle ajoute *Chema Israël*. C'est un minimum en cas de besoin, pas l'idéal décrit plus haut.

Pour commencer, il existe de bons siddourim (livres de prière) bilingues hébreu-français, en version ashkénaze, séfarade ou Habad.

Le serveur de Sefaria a limité mes requêtes. Je n'ai donc pas pu vérifier directement le passage du Rema sur *Chéassani kirtsono*, ni les ouvrages du Rav Ovadia Yossef. Ces points sont cités de mémoire, sans numéro de référence précis.

Pour votre situation personnelle (votre communauté, votre emploi du temps, vos enfants), consultez votre rabbin.

**Salmo 42 (en la numeración hebrea, [Psalms 42])**. Traducción mía al español, basada en el texto hebreo y en la versión de la JPS:

**1** Al director. Maskil de los hijos de Coraj.
**2** Como la cierva que anhela las corrientes de agua, así mi alma te anhela a Ti, oh Dios.
**3** Mi alma tiene sed de Dios, del Dios vivo. ¿Cuándo llegaré y me presentaré ante Dios?
**4** Mis lágrimas han sido mi pan día y noche, mientras me dicen todo el día: «¿Dónde está tu Dios?».
**5** Esto recordaré y derramaré mi alma dentro de mí: cómo pasaba entre la multitud y avanzaba con ellos hasta la casa de Dios, con voz de júbilo y alabanza, una muchedumbre en fiesta.
**6** ¿Por qué te abates, alma mía, y te turbas dentro de mí? Espera en Dios, pues aún le alabaré por las salvaciones de su presencia.
**7** Dios mío, mi alma se abate dentro de mí; por eso te recuerdo desde la tierra del Jordán, desde los Hermones, desde el monte Mizar.
**8** Un abismo llama a otro abismo al fragor de tus cascadas; todas tus olas y tus rompientes han pasado sobre mí.
**9** De día ordenará el Señor su bondad, y de noche su canto estará conmigo: una oración al Dios de mi vida.
**10** Diré a Dios, mi roca: «¿Por qué me has olvidado? ¿Por qué ando enlutado, oprimido por el enemigo?».
**11** Como quebrantando mis huesos, me afrentan mis adversarios, diciéndome todo el día: «¿Dónde está tu Dios?».
**12** ¿Por qué te abates, alma mía, y por qué te turbas dentro de mí? Espera en Dios, pues aún le alabaré: salvación de mi rostro y mi Dios.

## Notas breves
- **Estructura:** el salmo tiene tres partes, y los versículos 6 y 12 repiten el mismo estribillo. Muchos lo consideran una unidad con el Salmo 43, que repite el estribillo en [Psalms 43:5]. No es una lectura de un comentarista concreto que yo haya consultado.
- **Autoría:** «los hijos de Coraj» son una familia de levitas cantores. *Maskil* es un término de significado incierto, que suele entenderse como un canto de instrucción o de reflexión.
- **Anhelo de Dios:** el salmista está lejos del Templo, en la región del Jordán y el Hermón. Recuerda las peregrinaciones festivas y se consuela hablando consigo mismo: «espera en Dios».
- **Dificultades de traducción:** el v. 5 («*edaddem*», «avanzaba con ellos») es una palabra poco común. El v. 9 se puede leer como petición o como confianza. Y «*yeshuot panav*» (v. 6) tiene una lectura distinta en el v. 12 («*yeshuot pani*»).

Si quieres, puedo añadir lo que dicen Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre este salmo, o tratar su uso litúrgico.

# Salmo 41 (traducción mía del hebreo)

Es un salmo de David. Habla de quien cuida al pobre y recibe protección, y del salmista enfermo, traicionado por un amigo cercano, que confía en que Dios lo levantará. Cierra con la bendición que termina el primer libro de los Salmos. [Psalms 41]

## Puntos clave
- Los versículos 2-4 prometen protección y sostén en la enfermedad a quien se ocupa del necesitado.
- Los versículos 5-10 describen la enfermedad, la confesión del salmista, los enemigos que hablan mal de él y la traición de un amigo íntimo.
- Los versículos 11-13 piden que Dios lo levante, expresan confianza en Él y terminan con la doxología.

## Texto

**1** Al director del coro. Salmo de David.

**2** Dichoso el que se ocupa con inteligencia del pobre (*dal*); en el día malo lo librará el Eterno.

**3** El Eterno lo guardará y le dará vida, y será dichoso en la tierra; no lo entregarás al deseo de sus enemigos.

**4** El Eterno lo sustentará en el lecho del dolor; tú transformas toda su cama en su enfermedad.

**5** Yo dije: «Eterno, ten piedad de mí; sana mi alma, porque he pecado contra ti».

**6** Mis enemigos hablan mal de mí: «¿Cuándo morirá y perecerá su nombre?».

**7** Y si alguien viene a verme, habla falsedad; su corazón junta maldad; sale afuera y lo cuenta.

**8** Juntos murmuran contra mí todos los que me odian; contra mí planean el mal:

**9** «Una cosa perversa (*devar Belial*) se le ha pegado; el que yace ya no volverá a levantarse».

**10** Hasta el hombre de mi paz, en quien confiaba, el que comía mi pan, levantó contra mí el talón.

**11** Pero tú, Eterno, ten piedad de mí y levántame, y les pagaré.

**12** Por esto sé que me quieres: porque mi enemigo no canta victoria sobre mí.

**13** Y a mí, por mi integridad me sostuviste, y me pusiste ante ti para siempre.

**14** Bendito el Eterno, Dios de Israel, desde siempre y hasta siempre. Amén y amén.

## Notas breves
- *Maskil el dal*: el verbo *haskel* sugiere pensar y actuar con sabiduría, no solo dar limosna. Por eso la tradición lo asocia con la visita al enfermo y el cuidado del necesitado.
- El versículo 10 (*hirbil alai akev*, «levantó el talón») se refiere a una traición. La tradición lo ha relacionado con Ahitófel y Absalón. Ese vínculo es una interpretación de los comentaristas, no algo que diga el texto. Puedo buscar los comentarios de Rashi o Radak si te interesa.
- El versículo 14 no pertenece al contenido del salmo. Es la bendición que cierra el primer libro de los Salmos (capítulos 1-41).

Si quieres, puedo añadir el comentario de Rashi, Radak o Metsudat David, o las fuentes talmúdicas sobre este salmo.

# Salmo 77 (Tehilim 77)

Este salmo es la oración de alguien que sufre. Pasa de la angustia y la duda ("¿me rechazará el Eterno para siempre?") a la memoria del Éxodo, y esa memoria le devuelve la confianza. La traducción al español es mía, basada en el texto hebreo de [Psalms 77].

## Puntos clave
- El salmo es "de Asaf" y tiene tres movimientos: clamor (vv. 2-4), crisis de fe (vv. 5-11) y recuerdo de las maravillas de Dios (vv. 12-21).
- El salmista no ofrece una respuesta teórica a su duda. Se consuela recordando la redención de Egipto.
- Termina de forma abrupta, con Dios guiando a Su pueblo "como a un rebaño" por medio de Moisés y Aarón.

## Texto (traducción propia)

**1** Para el director del coro, sobre Yedutún; de Asaf, salmo.
**2** Mi voz clama a Dios, y yo grito; mi voz a Dios, para que me escuche.
**3** En el día de mi angustia busqué al Señor; mi mano de noche se extiende sin cesar; mi alma rehúsa ser consolada.
**4** Recuerdo a Dios y me conmuevo; medito, y mi espíritu desfallece. *Sela*.
**5** Tú sujetaste los párpados de mis ojos; estoy turbado y no puedo hablar.
**6** Pienso en los días de antaño, en los años de siglos pasados.
**7** Recuerdo mi canto en la noche, converso con mi corazón, y mi espíritu indaga:
**8** ¿Rechazará el Señor para siempre, y no volverá a complacerse?
**9** ¿Ha cesado para siempre Su bondad? ¿Se ha acabado la promesa para todas las generaciones?
**10** ¿Ha olvidado Dios tener piedad? ¿O ha cerrado en la ira Sus entrañas de compasión? *Sela*.
**11** Y dije: "Esta es mi dolencia: que haya cambiado la diestra del Altísimo".
**12** Recordaré las obras de Yah; sí, recordaré Tus maravillas de antaño.
**13** Meditaré en toda Tu obra y hablaré de Tus hazañas.
**14** Oh Dios, santo es Tu camino; ¿qué dios es grande como Dios?
**15** Tú eres el Dios que hace maravillas; diste a conocer Tu poder entre los pueblos.
**16** Con Tu brazo redimiste a Tu pueblo, a los hijos de Jacob y de José. *Sela*.
**17** Te vieron las aguas, oh Dios; te vieron las aguas y temblaron; también se estremecieron los abismos.
**18** Las nubes derramaron agua; los cielos dieron su voz; también Tus saetas iban de un lado a otro.
**19** La voz de Tu trueno rodaba como una rueda; los relámpagos iluminaron el mundo; la tierra se estremeció y tembló.
**20** En el mar fue Tu camino, y Tu sendero en las muchas aguas; y Tus huellas no se conocieron.
**21** Guiaste a Tu pueblo como a un rebaño, por mano de Moisés y Aarón.

## Comentario breve

**1. El clamor (vv. 2-4).** El salmista se aflige de noche, con insomnio ("Tú sujetaste los párpados de mis ojos", v. 5). Recordar a Dios no lo consuela por ahora. Más bien lo agita: "Recuerdo a Dios y me conmuevo".

**2. La crisis (vv. 6-11).** Las preguntas de los vv. 8-10 son una duda sobre los atributos de Dios. Los vv. 8-9 apuntan a la bondad y a la promesa divinas. El v. 10 apunta a la compasión. El v. 11 es difícil y se entiende de varias maneras. Mi traducción sigue una lectura frecuente: "mi dolencia es que la diestra del Altísimo haya cambiado". Otra lectura entiende que el salmista reconoce que la causa es su propia culpa. Esto último lo recoge la traducción de Sefaria: "es mi culpa". Ahí cambia el tono. De preguntar pasa a *recordar* (vv. 12-13). Quizá por eso el texto tradicional tiene aquí una variante: el *ketiv* (lo escrito) dice "recordaré" y el *kerí* (lo que se lee) dice "recordaré las obras de Yah".

**3. La memoria como respuesta (vv. 12-21).** El salmista confía en que Dios actuó en el pasado. Por eso su lenguaje cambia: "Tu camino es santo" (v. 14). Recuerda la salida de Egipto y el cruce del mar, con "los hijos de Jacob y de José" (v. 16). José aparece junto a Jacob, quizá porque sostuvo a la familia en Egipto. Las aguas "te vieron" y temblaron (v. 17), como si el mar mismo reconociera a su Creador. El v. 20 dice "Tus huellas no se conocieron". Dios actúa, pero Su modo de actuar queda oculto. Esto da consuelo y también humildad: no siempre vemos el camino de Dios.

**4. El final (v. 21).** El salmo concluye con un pastor y un rebaño, con Moisés y Aarón como guías. Su mensaje es que el Dios que condujo a Israel a través del mar sigue guiándolo, aunque no se vean Sus huellas.

Si quieres, puedo añadir lo que dicen Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre versículos concretos, en especial el v. 11.

answer:
Je ne connais aucune source classique qui relie ces deux expressions aux 22 lettres de l'alphabet. En revanche, un calcul simple donne une correspondance numérique, qui est une observation personnelle et non une tradition.

## Points clés
- Les deux expressions sont dans [Exodus 3:1] : « אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ » puis « וַיִּנְהַג אֶת־הַצֹּאן ».
- Ensemble, elles comptent 5 + 6 = 11 lettres, soit la moitié de 22. Cela ne repose sur aucune source.
- Leur valeur numérique totale est 542 + 547 = 1089, soit 33².
- La guématria est ici une *drash* (lecture homilétique) et non une preuve.

## Le texte (pshat)
« וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתְנוֹ כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן וַיִּנְהַג אֶת־הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר ».
Traduction (la mienne) : « Moïse faisait paître le petit bétail de Jéthro, son beau-père, prêtre de Madian, et il mena le troupeau au-delà du désert. »

Le premier « צֹאן » est celui de Jéthro, introduit sans article. Le second est « הַצֹּאן », avec l'article défini, parce qu'il désigne le troupeau déjà mentionné. L'ajout du *hé* est donc d'ordre grammatical.

## Le calcul (valeurs : א=1, ה=5, ן=50, צ=90, ת=400)
- אֶת־צֹאן : 1 + 400 + 90 + 1 + 50 = **542**, soit 5 lettres.
- אֶת־הַצֹּאן : 1 + 400 + 5 + 90 + 1 + 50 = **547**, soit 6 lettres.

Ce qu'on peut en dire :
- **Nombre de lettres** : 5 + 6 = 11, la moitié de 22. On peut y voir, de façon imagée, la moitié de l'alphabet, mais c'est une coïncidence.
- **Lettres distinctes** : seules cinq lettres apparaissent, א, ת, צ, נ et ה (le *noun* final compte comme *noun*). Cela fait 5 lettres sur 22 et n'a rien de remarquable.
- **Somme** : 1089 = 33², un fait arithmétique sans portée traditionnelle.

## Où chercher le sens traditionnel
Les commentateurs ne s'attardent pas sur les lettres de ces mots. Ils s'intéressent à la figure du berger. Selon le Midrash (Shemot Rabbah, sur ce passage), D. a éprouvé Moïse par les brebis, comme dans l'épisode du chevreau fatigué qu'il porte sur son épaule. Cette compassion le qualifie pour conduire Israël. L'idée que le désert (« אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר ») prépare à la révélation du Buisson ardent est également classique.

Si vous avez rencontré ce lien avec les 22 lettres chez un auteur précis, dites-moi lequel et nous pourrons l'examiner.

answer:
**Direct answer:** Gematria doesn't claim that two words *mean* the same thing, or that their concepts are equal in size. It claims that the same numerical value is a *signal of a hidden link*, and that link is then read as a hint, not a proof. Your objection is a sound one. Traditional sources also treat gematria as a secondary tool, not a proof.

## Key Takeaways
- Gematria does not say two concepts are quantitatively equal. It says a shared number points to a hidden connection.
- Chazal called it an "appetizer" of wisdom, a supporting tool and not a main course.
- Kabbalah and chassidut give it a metaphysical basis: Hebrew letters are the building blocks of reality, so a number is part of a thing's makeup.
- Gematria is drash, a homiletic reading. It does not establish law or doctrine on its own.

## 1. Sameness of number ≠ sameness of concept
Your objection is right if gematria claimed "love = one", so that the two are identical. The classic use is different. Words that share a value are said to *illuminate* each other. In the Hebrew examples below, each pair adds up to 13:
- *Ahavah* (אהבה, love) = 1+5+2+5 = 13
- *Echad* (אחד, one) = 1+8+4 = 13

The tradition does not say love is "the same as" oneness. It uses the number to invite reflection: love is what unites two into one. The numbers don't create the relationship, they only point to it, and a bare number can be coincidence unless the idea already fits.

## 2. The earliest sources treat it as a tool
- The Mishnah says "תקופות וגימטריאות פרפראות לחכמה": calendrical calculations and gematria are "the condiments (or dessert) of wisdom" [Pirkei Avot 3:18]. That means they are ornaments to wisdom, not its foundation.
- The Talmud notes that Abraham's 318 servants [Genesis 14:14] equal the numerical value of Eliezer, so the verse hints that Eliezer alone was worth them all [Nedarim 32a]. Even there it works as a homiletic hint on a verse, not a legal proof.
- Gematria is also listed among the interpretive methods, but halachic and doctrinal conclusions are not drawn from it alone. It is typically seen as an *asmachta* (a hint that supports something established elsewhere).

## 3. The deeper rationale: letters as the structure of creation
Your question assumes that words are just labels, and labels aren't quantities. Kabbalah rejects that assumption.
- *Sefer Yetzirah* describes God creating the world through the Hebrew letters and their combinations. Letters are building blocks, not conventions.
- The Baal HaTanya develops this in *Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmunah* (the second part of Tanya). The letters of the ten utterances of creation continually sustain each thing, so a thing's Hebrew name is the channel of its life-force.
- If a word's letters are its inner makeup, then its numbers are part of that makeup too. Two things with the same number would then share something in their spiritual root. That is the logic, not a mathematical identity.

## 4. Practical limits
- Gematria is *remez/drash* (hint and homily), not *pshat* (plain meaning). It does not decide halacha.
- Many different words share any given number, so a good gematria works because the idea already fits. A mere numerical match doesn't make an insight.
- Some authorities, rationalist in outlook, were wary of reading too much into such connections. They saw gematria as at most a pleasing mnemonic or hint.

If you give me the two words you had in mind, I can work through their values and see what the tradition says about that particular connection.

answer:
**Direct answer:** *Har* (הַר) is itself the most direct, standard Hebrew word for "mountain", in the Torah and in modern Hebrew. It is not a vague word for "elevated" that needs a more literal substitute. Its range of meaning is real, but the core sense is a mountain or hill.

## Key Takeaways
- *Har* (plural *harim*, construct *harei*) is the ordinary word for mountain in Biblical, Mishnaic and modern Hebrew.
- Other words describe nearby ideas such as hill, high place, rock or mound, and none of them replaces *har* as "mountain".
- The "elevated" flavor you noticed comes mostly from how *har* is used in poetry, in sacred contexts and in midrash.

## Where *har* means a literal mountain
- Noah's ark rests on "the mountains of Ararat" (*harei Ararat*) in [Genesis 8:4].
- The flood covers the "high mountains" in [Genesis 7:19-20].
- Lot is told to flee to "the mountain" (*he-harah*) in [Genesis 19:17].
- Israel encamps "opposite the mountain" at Sinai in [Exodus 19:2].

In these verses *har* is a physical mountain, and the word is used the same way in modern Hebrew. Place names built on it include *Har HaZeitim* (Mount of Olives) and *Har HaBayit* (Temple Mount). The adjective *harari* (הררי) means "mountainous".

## Related words (not synonyms for "mountain")
- ***Giv'ah*** (גִּבְעָה): a hill, smaller than a *har*. It often appears alongside *harim* in parallelism, as in "mountains and hills".
- ***Bamah*** (בָּמָה): a high place, usually a platform or altar site on a height. It is a cultic term, not a geographic one.
- ***Tzur*** and ***sela*** (צוּר, סֶלַע): rock or crag, not a mountain.
- ***Tel*** (תֵּל): a mound, often the ruins of an ancient city.
- ***Ramah*** (רָמָה): "height", from the root *ram* ("high"). It is mostly a place name.

## Where the "elevated" sense comes from
- **Poetic and figurative use.** *Har* can stand for a great power or kingdom, or for something imposing. It can also mean the highland region itself, as in "the hill country".
- **Sacred geography.** Mountains are where revelation and the Temple happen: Sinai, Moriah, Zion.
- **Midrash and drash.** The Talmud connects *Har HaMoriah* with *hora'ah* (teaching), as the place from which instruction goes out to Israel (see [Ta'anit 16a]). This is homiletic wordplay, not etymology. It reflects a tradition of reading *har* as a point of ascent to God. Isaiah's vision of "the mountain of the Lord's house" ([Isaiah 2:2-3]) is in the same spirit.

So *har* is the word to use for a mountain, and its spiritual overtones come from what mountains stand for in the Torah.

answer:
No. "Kayin" (קַיִן, Cain) and *kenaynahora* have no connection, either linguistically or historically. The resemblance is only in the sound.

**What the phrase is**
- *Kenaynahora* (also written *kein ayin hara* or *kanehora*) is a Yiddish expression. It comes from the Hebrew/Aramaic phrase "בְּלִי עַיִן הָרָע", or in Yiddish pronunciation "kein ayin hara" (קײן עין הרע). It means "no evil eye."
- Its components are *kein*, "no" (German *kein*), plus *ayin hara* (עַיִן הָרָע), "the evil eye."
- It is said after mentioning good fortune, such as health, a child's success, or a simple blessing. The speaker hopes the praise won't draw the harmful gaze of jealousy.
- The word *kein* here is not Hebrew *ken* (כֵּן, "yes/so"). It is the Germanic Yiddish "no/none."

**What Kayin means**
- The Torah explains the name itself: "וַתֹּאמֶר קָנִיתִי אִישׁ אֶת־ה'", "I have acquired a man with the Lord" [Genesis 4:1]. The name is tied to the root ק-נ-ה (*kanah*, "to acquire"). Its form is *Kayin* (קַיִן), with a *yod*, not the *kein* of the Yiddish phrase.
- Cain's story is about jealousy and murder, so someone could make a thematic link to the evil eye. But that would be a homiletic play, not an etymology.

**The evil eye in Jewish sources**
- The concept of *ayin hara* is old. Pirkei Avot lists "עַיִן הָרָע" among the things that remove a person from the world [Pirkei Avot 2:11].
- The Talmud says that Joseph's descendants were protected from the evil eye, based on "בֵּן פֹּרָת יוֹסֵף... עֲלֵי־עָיִן" [Berakhot 20a]. It cites this to explain why the evil eye has no power over them.
- Rashi on Genesis 4 doesn't connect Cain to this phrase, and I know of no classic source that does.

**A possible source of confusion**
- Some people hear "kenaynahora" and think of "Kayin" because both begin with a "ken/kayn" sound.
- There is also the word *kein* (קֵן, "nest"), as in *kan tzipor*, which is unrelated to both.

answer:
**Direct answer:** *Nachash* (נָחָשׁ, serpent) comes from the root נ-ח-ש. The root is usually linked to hissing or whispering, which is the sound a snake makes. The same root also gives the verb "to divine, to read omens" (*nichesh*). The two meanings are often connected, though not always.

## Key Takeaways
- The noun *nachash* is a snake. The most likely origin of the name is the hissing or whispering sound, which is onomatopoeic.
- The verb *lenachesh* means to practice divination or to take omens.
- Linguists and commentators disagree about whether the two meanings share a single origin.
- Related words are *nechoshet* (copper or bronze) and *Nachshon*. Their connection to the root is debated.

## The root and its meanings

**1. Serpent.** The noun appears in [Genesis 3:1]: "וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם מִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה", "Now the serpent was the shrewdest of all the wild beasts." Cognate words in other Semitic languages also mean snake. Examples are Arabic *ḥanash* and Aramaic *ḥiviya*, which is a different word. The sound of the root fits the hiss of a snake. This is the standard explanation, and it is my summary of the linguistic consensus, not a quotation from a source I retrieved.

**2. Divination.** The verb *nichesh* means to take omens or practice divination. Examples are Joseph's cup, "נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ" (Genesis 44:5), and Laban's "נִחַשְׁתִּי" (Genesis 30:27). The Torah forbids it in Leviticus 19:26 and Deuteronomy 18:10. I did not retrieve these verses this time. The two meanings may be linked through the murmuring, whispering sound of incantations. Another suggestion links them through the snake's reputation for cunning or hidden knowledge. This ties in with the "*arum*" (shrewd) of the verse above.

**3. Copper.** *Nechoshet* (נְחֹשֶׁת, copper or bronze) may be related. One explanation is the metal's snake-like gleam or color. Many scholars treat it as a separate root. The name *Nachshon* is also sometimes connected to the root, but it is uncertain.

## Caveats
- This is a linguistic summary. The classical commentators mostly don't discuss the etymology and focus on the snake's role in Eden.
- The 429 errors from the Sefaria tool meant I could not retrieve the verses for divination or for the commentators. If you want, I can look up what Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Radak (*Sefer HaShorashim*) say about the root.

answer:
Yes. Many commentators connect *Ivri* (עברי, "Hebrew") to the root ע-ב-ר (*avar*, "to cross over, pass through"), and it is one of several explanations of the word.

## Key Takeaways
- The root ע-ב-ר means "to cross" or "to pass over", and *ever* (עבר) means "the other side".
- Avraham is first called *HaIvri* in [Genesis 14:13].
- The main explanations are: a descendant of Ever, someone from across the river, and someone who stands on one side against the whole world.
- The "crossed over" reading is the one most often emphasized in midrash and in later Jewish thought.

## Pshat: what the word means
The root ע-ב-ר means "to cross", as in "crossing the river" or "passing through a land". *Ever* means "the far side", for example *ever haYarden*, "across the Jordan". *Ivri* can therefore mean "one from the other side" or "one who crossed".

## The main explanations
- **Descendant of Ever.** Genesis lists Ever (עֵבֶר) as an ancestor in the line of Shem and Avraham ([Genesis 10:21]; [Genesis 11:14]). Ibn Ezra and others take *Ivri* simply as "a descendant of Ever". This is the more literal genealogical reading. Even here, the name Ever itself is often explained as coming from "crossing".
- **From across the river.** Avraham came from the far side of the Euphrates, from Ur and Haran. Rashi on [Genesis 14:13] brings this reading: he was "from the other side of the river".
- **One side against the world.** Rashi on [Genesis 14:13] also quotes a midrash, which I believe is [Bereshit Rabbah 42:8]. The whole world was on one side (*ever*), and Avraham was on the other. In this reading *Ivri* means one who "crossed over" from the idolatry of his surroundings to stand alone for monotheism. This is the drash most people have in mind, and it is a midrashic reading, not the plain sense.

## Later usage
Later thought extends the idea. The Jew is the one who "crosses over", moving beyond the given and breaking from convention. This is homiletic and is not a claim about the word's original meaning.

**Translation:** "They trampled with their heels."

**Direct answer:** The phrase שָׁדְשׁוּ בְּעֲקֵבֵיהֶם means "they threshed (trampled) with their heels." I could not find the exact phrase in Sefaria. The search returned nothing, and my second search failed. So I'm translating the words themselves, not a known source.

**Word by word**
- **שָׁדְשׁוּ** (*shadeshu*) comes from the root ד־ו־שׁ / ד־שׁ־שׁ (*dush*). It is a Mishnaic-Hebrew form meaning to thresh, tread, or trample. It is related to the biblical *dush* and *dayish* (threshing), as in "דָּשָׁה" and "הַדָּשׁ". The root is used for threshing grain by treading it, and figuratively for crushing something underfoot. The ש־ד־ש form is a known variant spelling of the same idea.
- **בְּעֲקֵבֵיהֶם** (*be-akeveihem*) means "with their heels." The word עָקֵב (*akev*) is "heel." It is plural with the suffix "their."

**Context matters.** The sense depends on the source:
- **Literal:** people trampling something with their heels, for example kicking or stamping on something.
- **Figurative:** treating something with contempt, or crushing it. The heel often stands for the lowest part of the body, or for the "heels of the generation."

answer:
Here is my own English translation of [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 192:2], including the Rema's gloss. Sefaria has only a loose French paraphrase of this se'if, so I did not use it. Square brackets mark my explanatory additions. Since the Rema's gloss continues the Shulchan Arukh's ruling, the Mechaber's line comes first for context.

---

### The Shulchan Arukh (R. Yosef Karo)

**שבעת ימים הללו מונים אותה משעה שהיא סומכת בדעתה ומכינה עצמה לחופה אע"פ שלא נתקדשה עדיין:**

These seven [clean] days are counted from the time she makes up her mind [to marry] and prepares herself for the chuppah, even though she has not yet been betrothed [*kiddushin*].

---

### The Rema's gloss (הגה)

**ויש לסמוך הטבילה סמוך לבעילת מצוה בכל מה דאפשר**

The immersion [in the mikvah] should be as close as possible to the *be'ilat mitzvah* [the first marital relations after the wedding].

**(כך משמע במרדכי בשם רשב"ם ור"מ ורוקח בשם אביו ורבותיו ובהגהת מיימוני פי"א דהלכות א"ב)**

(So it appears from the Mordechai, citing the Rashbam [Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir] and the Maharam [Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg], and from the Rokeach, citing his father and his teachers, and from the Hagahot Maimoniyot on chapter 11 of Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah [the Laws of Forbidden Relations].)

**והמנהג לטבול הכלה ליל ד' אע"פ שלא תבעל קודם מוצאי שבת (מרדכי שם)**

The custom is for the bride to immerse on the night of the fourth day [i.e., the night that begins Wednesday, which is Tuesday evening], even though she will not have relations before Saturday night (Mordechai, there).

[Context: in the Rema's time weddings were often held on Friday, so the first relations would be on Saturday night.]

**אבל אין להרחיק הטבילה מן הבעילה יותר מזה**

But the immersion should not be separated from the relations by more than this [about four days].

**ואם לא תבעל במוצאי שבת יש לה לבדוק עצמה בכל יום עד בעילת מצוה (שם בהג"ה ובתוספות פ"ק דיומא דף י"ח)**

If she does not have relations on Saturday night, she should examine herself [with a *bedikah*, an internal check] every day until the *be'ilat mitzvah* (there, in the Hagahot [Maimoniyot], and in Tosafot on the first chapter of Yoma, page 18).

**ודוקא לכתחלה אבל בדיעבד אין להחמיר אם בדקה רק פעם אחת תוך ז' (ב"י)**

This applies only *lechatchilah* [the preferred practice from the outset]. *Bedi'eved* [after the fact], we are not strict if she examined herself only once during the seven [days] (Beit Yosef).

**וכל חתן ישאל לכלה קודם שיגע בה אם שמרה שבעה נקיים (הגהת ש"ד):**

Every groom should ask the bride, before touching her, whether she has kept the seven clean days (Hagahot Sha'arei Dura).

---

### Notes on the translation
- **Night of the fourth day (ליל ד'):** In Jewish reckoning the night comes before the day, so this is the night that begins Wednesday, i.e., Tuesday evening. That reading also fits the Rema's limit: from Tuesday night to Saturday night is about four days.
- **The bedikah "within the seven":** The Rema's "after the fact" ruling refers to the examinations of the seven clean days themselves. If she checked only once during those seven days, we don't invalidate her count.

If you'd like, I can also translate the Shakh and Taz on this se'if. They discuss how many days may pass between the immersion and the wedding, and what is done today.

answer:
A Sephardi woman must cover her hair after marriage. Whether a wig (*peah nokhrit*, literally "foreign hair") counts as a valid covering is a real dispute among Sephardi authorities. **Rav Ovadia Yosef**, whose rulings many Sephardim follow, forbade wigs for Sephardi women and required a cloth covering such as a *mitpachat* (scarf) or hat. **Rav Shalom Messas** and other North African authorities allowed them, and many Sephardi women today follow that view. In practice, the answer depends on which authority and family custom she follows.

## Key Takeaways
- Married women must cover their hair. Most authorities treat this as Torah law, based on [Ketubot 72a].
- The Mishnah mentions a woman going out in a wig [Mishnah Shabbat 6:5]. The Rema says wig hair is not considered exposed hair, even for a woman who covers her own [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 75:2].
- That leniency appears only in the Rema's gloss, not in the Shulchan Arukh's own text. That is the core of Rav Ovadia Yosef's argument that Sephardim, who follow the Shulchan Arukh (whom they call "Maran"), should not rely on it.
- Other Sephardi authorities, notably Rav Shalom Messas, permitted wigs. So did leading Ashkenazi authorities and the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who actively encouraged them.

## The underlying obligation
The Mishnah lists going out with an uncovered head (*rosh parua*) as a breach of *dat Yehudit* (Jewish norms of modesty). The Gemara ties the basic duty to the Torah itself, learning it from the verse about the *sotah* (a woman suspected of adultery): "and he shall uncover the woman's head" (Numbers 5:18) [Ketubot 72a]. Everyone agrees on the duty to cover. The question is only whether a wig does the job.

## The sources for a wig
- **Mishnah:** a woman may go out on Shabbat "with a wig to the courtyard," though not into the public domain [Mishnah Shabbat 6:5]. The limit is about carrying on Shabbat, not modesty. Some authorities, such as the Shiltei HaGiborim, used this Mishnah to argue that a wig counts as a covering.
- **Shulchan Arukh and Rema:** the Shulchan Arukh rules that one may not say the Shema facing a married woman's hair that is normally covered. The Rema adds that this certainly doesn't apply to "foreign hair," meaning a wig: «וכ"ש שער נכרית אפי' דרכה לכסות» ("and certainly foreign hair, even if it is her practice to cover") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 75:2].
- **Mishnah Berurah:** he explains the lenient view, that cut hair is not *ervah* (hair that must be covered) and wearing it is not "uncovering the head." He notes that others disagree. He cites the Pri Megadim: where women commonly wear wigs uncovered, they may rely on the lenient ruling. Where it is not the local practice, the stricter view is correct because of *mar'it ayin* (how it looks to others) [Mishnah Berurah 75:15].

## Sephardi views
**Forbidden: Rav Ovadia Yosef and his school**
- In his responsa (*Yabia Omer*, *Yechave Da'at*) he ruled strongly that Sephardi women should not wear wigs. Rav Yitzchak Yosef's *Yalkut Yosef* follows the same line.
- His reasons, in brief:
  - Maran never recorded the leniency. It is the Rema's.
  - Many authorities forbade wigs, either as uncovering the head or because people can't tell them from real hair.
  - Many of today's wigs look exactly like natural hair, which makes the concern even stronger.
- He accepted a hat or scarf as the proper covering.

**Permitted: Rav Shalom Messas and the North African tradition**
- Rav Shalom Messas (Chief Rabbi of Morocco, later Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem) defended wigs in his responsa. He relied on the Mishnah, the Shiltei HaGiborim and the Moroccan custom.
- Many Sephardi women today wear wigs on this basis, especially in Moroccan, Syrian and Haredi-educated Sephardi communities. Often their husband's or community's rabbi rules this way.

## For comparison: Ashkenazi and Chabad
- **Ashkenazi:** wigs are widely accepted, following the Rema and the Mishnah Berurah above, and Rav Moshe Feinstein permitted them. Some Ashkenazi authorities objected, and some women wear a scarf as an added stringency.
- **Chabad:** the Lubavitcher Rebbe strongly encouraged wigs. His reasoning was that a woman is more likely to keep a wig on consistently than a scarf.

## A side issue: where the hair comes from
Wigs made of human hair also raise the question of whether the hair was used in idol worship. Halacha forbids benefiting from such hair, as with the hair of an idolatrous city [Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 4:12]. The question became urgent in 2004 over Indian temple hair. Anyone who wears a human-hair wig, under any opinion, should buy one with reliable certification.

## Practically
A Sephardi woman who follows Rav Ovadia Yosef should cover her hair with a scarf, hat or snood. One whose family or community follows Rav Messas or similar authorities has solid grounds to wear a wig. The choice is best made together with her husband, in line with her family's tradition. Please consult your rabbi for your personal situation.
